knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when an undirected graph can be oriented to balance a prescribed digraph at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be an undirected graph and $H$ a digraph with $V(G)=V(H)$. There exists an orientation $G'$ of $G$ such that $G'+H$ is Eulerian if and only if, for every $v\in V(G)$, $|\delta_H^+(v)|+|\delta_H^-(v)|+|\delta_G(v)|$ is even, and, for every $X\subseteq V(G)$, $|\delta_H^+(X)|-|\delta_H^-(X)|\le |\delta_G(X)|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected graph can be oriented so that its union with a prescribed digraph is Eulerian exactly when each vertex has even total incidence across the two graphs and the directed imbalance across every vertex subset does not exceed the number of undirected edges crossing that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ an orientation }G'\text{ of }G\text{ with }G'+H\text{ Eulerian}\iff \left[\forall v,\ |\delta_H^+(v)|+|\delta_H^-(v)|+|\delta_G(v)|\equiv0\pmod 2\right]\land\left[\forall X\subseteq V(G),\ |\delta_H^+(X)|-|\delta_H^-(X)|\le |\delta_G(X)|\right].

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Undirected Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple undirected graphs, excluding loops and parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite simple undirected graph is an ordered pair \(G=(V,E)\), where \(V\) is a finite set and \(E\subseteq \binom{V}{2}=\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in V,\ u\ne v\}\). Each edge is therefore an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Because \(E\) is a set of pairs, at most one edge has any prescribed pair of endpoints, and because every member of \(E\) has cardinality two, no edge is a loop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple undirected graph has finitely many vertices and unordered edges joining distinct vertex pairs, with neither loops nor parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\subseteq \binom{V}{2}\).

notation.meaning: set of two-element subsets of V

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite undirected graphs, simple graphs, and complete graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic finite undirected-graph terminology, including multiplicity and loop regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected graph \(G\) consists of disjoint finite sets \(V(G)\) and \(E(G)\), together with an assignment to every edge of an unordered pair of endpoints, which may coincide. An edge is incident with its endpoints, and distinct endpoints are adjacent. Edges with the same endpoints are parallel; an edge with equal endpoints is a loop. A graph is simple if it has neither loops nor parallel edges, and it is complete if it is simple and every pair of distinct vertices is the endpoint pair of an edge. The notation \(e=vw\) is unambiguous only when parallel edges are absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite undirected graph has disjoint vertex and edge sets and assigns two possibly equal endpoints to every edge. Equal endpoint pairs create parallel edges, equal endpoints create loops, simple graphs have neither, and complete graphs are simple graphs containing an edge between every pair of distinct vertices. Writing an edge merely by its endpoints is unambiguous only without parallel edges.
assumptions_latex: V(G)\text{ and }E(G)\text{ are disjoint finite sets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is simple}\iff G\text{ has no loops or parallel edges},\qquad G\text{ is complete}\iff G\text{ is simple and every distinct vertex pair is adjacent}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete graphs, complements, matchings, covers, stable sets, and cliques
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The complete-graph and complement definitions assume simple undirected graphs; the remaining objects are defined for undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complete graph is a simple undirected graph in which every pair of distinct vertices is adjacent; the complete graph on \(n\) vertices is \(K_n\). The complement \(\overline G\) of a simple undirected graph \(G\) has \(V(\overline G)=V(G)\) and exactly the edges missing from \(G\), so \(G+\overline G=K_{|V(G)|}\). For an undirected graph \(G\), a matching is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges; a vertex cover is a set \(S\subseteq V(G)\) incident with every edge; an edge cover is a set \(F\subseteq E(G)\) incident with every vertex; a stable set is a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices; a clique is a set of pairwise adjacent vertices; and an empty graph has no edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete graph joins every vertex pair, and the complement of a simple graph contains exactly its missing edges. A matching has no shared endpoints; vertex and edge covers meet every edge and every vertex, respectively; stable sets contain no adjacent pair; cliques contain every possible adjacent pair; and empty graphs have no edges.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is simple and undirected when defining }K_n\text{ and }\overline G
G\text{ is undirected for matchings, covers, stable sets, and cliques}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated adjacency and incidence conditions define the listed undirected graph object classes.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the graph operations and associated induced-subgraph and chordality terminology in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Deleting an edge removes it while retaining its endpoints; multiplying a \(uv\)-edge replaces it by \(k\ge1\) parallel \(uv\)-edges. Deleting a vertex removes it and all incident edges. A subgraph is obtained by vertex and edge deletions, and a spanning subgraph retains the full vertex set. For \(X\subseteq V\), the induced subgraph \(G[X]=G-(V\setminus X)\) has edge set \(I_G(X)\) and \(i_G(X)=|I_G(X)|\). A hole is an induced circuit with at least four edges, and a graph is chordal iff it has no hole. For nonempty \(Z\subseteq V\), shrinking \(Z\) replaces it by a vertex \(v_Z\) joined to each \(u\in V\setminus Z\) by \(d_G(Z,u)\) parallel edges; contracting a non-loop edge \(uv\) means shrinking \(\{u,v\}\). Multiple-edge contraction is order-independent, and when \(G[Z]\) is connected, shrinking \(Z\) is equivalent to contracting the edges induced by \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge and vertex deletion generate subgraphs; retaining all vertices gives a spanning subgraph, while deleting the complement of a vertex set gives its induced subgraph. A hole is an induced circuit of length at least four, and chordal graphs have no holes. Shrinking a nonempty vertex set replaces it with one vertex while preserving its external edge multiplicities. Edge contraction is the special case of shrinking two endpoints; multiple contractions are order-independent, and shrinking a connected induced set is equivalent to contracting its induced edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The deletion, subgraph, chordality, shrinking, and contraction operations have the stated meanings and equivalences.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite undirected multigraphs and basic incidence notation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loops and repeated edges are allowed; a loop contributes twice to its incident-edge family and hence to degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected graph is a pair $G=(V,E)$, where $V$ is finite and $E$ is a family of unordered vertex pairs, so loops and repeated pairs are permitted. Write $V(G)=V$, $E(G)=E$, $n=|V|$, and $m=|E|$. Repeated copies of the same pair are parallel edges, with multiplicity equal to their number of occurrences; a graph is simple iff it has neither loops nor multiple edges, and loopless iff it has no loops. For $v\in V$, $\delta_G(v)$ is the family of incident edges, with each loop at $v$ occurring twice, $N_G(v)$ is its neighbor set, and $\deg_G(v)=|\delta_G(v)|$. Define $\Delta(G)=\max_{v\in V}\deg_G(v)$ and $\delta(G)=\min_{v\in V}\deg_G(v)$; $G$ is $k$-regular iff every vertex has degree $k$. For graphs $G=(V,E)$ and $G'=(V',E')$, $G+G'=(V\cup V',E\cup E')$, where the edge-family union retains multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite undirected graph may contain loops and parallel edge copies. Its vertex and edge families, incidence and neighbor sets, degrees, maximum and minimum degrees, regular classes, and multiplicity-preserving graph union are defined as stated; loops count twice toward incidence and degree.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is a family of unordered pairs from }V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_G(v),\ N_G(v),\ \deg_G(v),\ \Delta(G),\ \delta(G),\text{ simplicity, looplessness, regularity, and }G+G'\text{ are defined with edge multiplicities and loop incidences retained.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite graphs and their basic operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonempty vertex sets, finite edge sets, no loops unless explicitly allowed, and possible parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected graph is a triple \(G=(V,E,\Psi)\) with finite nonempty \(V\), finite \(E\), and \(\Psi:E\to\{X\subseteq V:|X|=2\}\); a digraph instead has \(\Psi:E\to\{(v,w)\in V^2:v\ne w\}\). Distinct edges with equal images are parallel, and a graph without parallel edges is simple. The incidence map defines adjacency, neighbors, endpoints, incidence, and, for an arc \((v,w)\), its tail \(v\) and head \(w\); loops are excluded unless stated otherwise. Forgetting arc directions gives the underlying undirected graph with the same edge multiplicities, and the digraph is an orientation of it. A subgraph \(H\) satisfies \(V(H)\subseteq V(G)\) and \(E(H)\subseteq E(G)\); it is induced when it contains exactly the edges of \(G\) whose endpoints lie in \(V(H)\), and spanning when \(V(H)=V(G)\). The operations \(G-X\), \(G-e\), \(G+e\), and \(G+H\) respectively delete vertices or edges, add an edge, and take vertex union with disjoint edge union, allowing parallel edges. Graph isomorphism consists of compatible bijections on vertices and edges. Contracting \(X\subseteq V(G)\) replaces \(X\) by one vertex, deletes internal edges, and redirects every boundary edge to that vertex, allowing parallel edges. For undirected \(G\), \(E(X,Y)=\{\{x,y\}\in E(G):x\in X\setminus Y,\ y\in Y\setminus X\}\), \(\delta(X)=E(X,V\setminus X)\), and \(\Gamma(X)=\{v\in V\setminus X:E(X,\{v\})\ne\varnothing\}\). For digraphs, \(E^+(X,Y)=\{(x,y)\in E(G):x\in X\setminus Y,\ y\in Y\setminus X\}\), \(\delta^+(X)=E^+(X,V\setminus X)\), \(\delta^-(X)=\delta^+(V\setminus X)\), and \(\delta(X)=\delta^+(X)\cup\delta^-(X)\). Singleton notation defines degree, in-degree, and out-degree; degree zero means isolated, and equal degree \(k\) at every vertex means \(k\)-regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph is specified by finite vertex and edge sets and an incidence map to unordered pairs for undirected graphs or ordered pairs of distinct vertices for digraphs. The definitions distinguish parallel and simple graphs and introduce incidence terminology, underlying undirected graphs, subgraphs, induced and spanning subgraphs, deletion and addition, disjointness, isomorphism, contraction, cut and neighborhood notation, degrees, isolated vertices, and regular graphs. Loops are excluded by default, while parallel edges may occur and retain their multiplicity.
assumptions_latex: \Psi(e)\text{ has two distinct endpoints for every }e\in E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed constructions define the standard finite-graph objects, operations, cut boundaries, neighborhoods, and degree notions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simple undirected graphs and their basic traversal objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines loopless simple undirected graphs, degrees, walks, paths, cycles, and connectedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simple undirected graph is a pair \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\), where every edge is an unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\subseteq\mathcal N\) with \(i\ne j\); thus \(\{i,j\}=\{j,i\}\), and self-edges are excluded. The degree of a node is the number of incident edges, and the degree of the graph is the maximum node degree. A walk is a finite sequence \(i_1,\ldots,i_t\) satisfying \(\{i_k,i_{k+1}\}\in\mathcal E\) for every \(k<t\). It is a path when no node repeats, and it is a cycle when \(i_1,\ldots,i_{t-1}\) are distinct, \(i_t=i_1\), and \(t-1\ge 3\). The graph is connected exactly when every two distinct nodes are joined by a path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple undirected graph has distinct-node unordered edges and no self-edges. Node degree counts incident edges, and graph degree is the maximum node degree. A walk follows adjacent nodes; a path has no repeated nodes; a cycle returns to its initial node after at least three distinct nodes; and the graph is connected when every distinct node pair has a path between them.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is connected}\iff \forall i,j\in\mathcal N,\ i\ne j\Rightarrow\exists\text{ an }i\text{--}j\text{ path}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull of Simple-Graph Degree Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete linear description of the convex hull of labeled simple-graph degree vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite vertex set \(V\), the convex hull of the degree vectors of simple graphs on \(V\) is the set of all \(x\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfying \(x_v\ge 0\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(x(U)-x(W)\le |U|\bigl(|V|-|W|-1\bigr)\) for every pair of disjoint sets \(U,W\subseteq V\), where \(x(S)=\sum_{v\in S}x_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of labeled simple-graph degree vectors consists exactly of the nonnegative vectors satisfying the stated inequality for every pair of disjoint vertex subsets.
assumptions_latex: V\text{ is a finite vertex set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\{(\deg_G(v))_{v\in V}:G\text{ is a simple graph on }V\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x_v\ge0\ \forall v\in V,\ x(U)-x(W)\le |U|(|V|-|W|-1)\ \forall U,W\subseteq V\text{ with }U\cap W=\varnothing\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected graphs, edge boundaries, and incidence matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the foundational definitions present in the extract, including loops and parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simple undirected graph is \(G=(V,E)\) with \(E\subseteq\binom V2\); vertices \(u,v\) are adjacent when \(\{u,v\}\in E\), and \(\Gamma_G(v)\) is the neighbor set of \(v\). It is complete when every two distinct vertices are adjacent, and its complement \(\bar G=(V,\bar E)\) has \(uv\in\bar E\iff uv\notin E\). A general undirected graph is \(G=(V,E,\varphi)\), where \(\varphi(e)\) is an unordered pair of not necessarily distinct vertices; equal endpoints define a loop and distinct edges with the same endpoints are parallel. For \(X,Y\subseteq V\), \(E_G(X,Y)\) consists of edges joining \(X\setminus Y\) to \(Y\setminus X\), \(d_G(X,Y)=|E_G(X,Y)|\), and \(\bar d_G(X,Y)=d_G(X,V\setminus Y)\). The incidence matrix \(Q\in\{0,1\}^{V\times E}\) satisfies \(Q_{ve}=1\) exactly when \(e\) is incident with \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple undirected graph has vertices and unordered two-vertex edges, with adjacency, neighbor sets, complete graphs, and graph complements defined in the usual way. A general undirected graph assigns each edge an unordered pair of possibly equal endpoints, thereby allowing loops and parallel edges. Edge sets and counts between set differences define boundary notation, and the zero-one incidence matrix records which vertices are incident with which edges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the stated simplification convention for contraction and the associated Menger characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For edge contraction, delete all resulting loops and retain only one copy of each resulting parallel-edge class. A connected undirected graph $G$ is 3-connected if $|V(G)|\ge4$ and deleting any set of at most two vertices does not disconnect $G$. Equivalently by Menger's theorem, every pair of vertices $u,v$ is joined by three openly disjoint $uv$-paths. An edge $e$ of a 3-connected graph is contractible if contracting $e$ under this convention produces a 3-connected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contraction deletes loops and merges parallel copies so that the result is simple. A connected undirected graph is 3-connected when it has at least four vertices and no deletion of at most two vertices disconnects it; equivalently, each vertex pair has three openly disjoint paths. An edge is contractible when its contraction remains 3-connected.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers both directed and undirected variants and the degree/incidence conditions for suppression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Subdividing an edge \(e=uv\) replaces it by a \(u\)-to-\(v\) path whose internal vertices are new; in the elementary case the path is \((uz,zv)\). Suppression is the inverse operation. In an undirected graph, a degree-two vertex \(z\) may be suppressed by deleting \(z\) and adding an edge between its two neighbors. In a digraph, if \(uz\) and \(zv\) are respectively the only arcs entering and leaving \(z\), suppression removes \(z\) and adds the arc \(uv\). Pinching \(k\) edges at a vertex \(z\) means subdividing each selected edge and identifying all \(k\) subdivision vertices with \(z\).

Pinching several edges at one vertex subdivides each edge and identifies the new subdivision vertices.

\text{For directed suppression, }uz\text{ and }zv\text{ are the only arcs entering and leaving }z.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Subdivision, suppression, and pinching produce the stated transformed graphs.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core objects, incidence data, cuts, connectivity, rooted structures, paths, circuits, and standard directed-graph classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed edge \(uv\) has tail \(u\) and head \(v\); loops, parallel arcs, opposite arcs, orientations, reorientations, digraphs, partial orientations, mixed graphs, tournaments, and complete digraphs are defined accordingly. A tournament on \(n\) vertices has \(n(n-1)/2\) arcs, whereas a complete digraph has \(n(n-1)\). The incidence matrix \(Q\) has entry \(+1\) at an arc's head, \(-1\) at its tail, and \(0\) otherwise. For \(X\subseteq V\), \(\varrho_D(X)=|\Delta_D^-(X)|\), \(\delta_D(X)=|\Delta_D^+(X)|\), and \(\Psi_D=\varrho_D-\delta_D\); entrances, induced arcs, and the corresponding notions for bi-sets are defined by head-tail membership. A digraph is weakly connected iff its underlying undirected graph is connected; a dicut is \(\Delta^-(X)\) when \(\delta_D(X)=0\), and a minimal dicut in a connected digraph uniquely determines its shores. It is strong iff \(\varrho_D(X)\ge1\) for every \(\varnothing\ne X\subsetneq V\), equivalently iff \(\delta_D(X)\ge1\) for every such \(X\); it is root-connected from \(s\) iff \(\varrho_D(X)\ge1\) for every nonempty \(X\subseteq V\setminus\{s\}\). An \(s\)-arborescence is a directed tree with \(\varrho(s)=0\) and \(\varrho(v)=1\) for \(v\ne s\); a branching is a directed forest with every indegree at most one. Directed paths and circuits have the stated underlying path/circuit structure and degree bounds. A digraph is Eulerian iff \(\varrho(v)=\delta(v)\) for every \(v\), near-Eulerian iff \(|\varrho(v)-\delta(v)|\le1\), cyclic iff every arc belongs to a directed circuit, and acyclic iff it has no directed circuit. A transitively closed digraph satisfies \(xy,yz\in A\Rightarrow xz\in A\); the strict-order digraph of a poset is acyclic and transitively closed, and its underlying graph is a comparability graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This collection defines directed edges and orientations, digraphs and mixed graphs, tournaments, incidence matrices, directed degrees and cuts, bi-set incidence, weak and strong connectivity, dicuts, root-connectivity, arborescences and branchings, directed paths and circuits, Eulerian and acyclic regimes, transitive closure, and comparability graphs. It includes the equivalent in-cut and out-cut tests for strong connectivity and the uniqueness of the shores of a minimal dicut in a connected digraph.

M=(V,A+F)\text{ is a mixed graph where mixed notions are used}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let V=S\cup T, let \mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_p\} partition S, and let \mathcal T=\{T_1,\ldots,T_q\} partition T, with all classes nonempty and p,q\ge 1. knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite graphs containing both undirected edges and directed arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite mixed graph is a tuple \(M=(V,E,A,\partial,t,h)\), where \(V\) is finite, \(E\) and \(A\) are disjoint finite sets of undirected edges and directed arcs, \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\) assigns an unordered endpoint pair to each edge, and \(t,h:A\to V\) assign a tail and head to each arc. Hence adjacency contributed by \(e\in E\) is symmetric, whereas an arc \(a\in A\) has the ordered incidence \(t(a)\to h(a)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed graph combines undirected edges with directed arcs on one vertex set, preserving unordered and ordered incidence respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\cap A=\varnothing\), with incidence maps \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\) and \((t,h):A\to V\times V\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the same-sign loop convention used in the stated setting and the matrix characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bidirected graph is a triple \(G=(V,E,\sigma)\), where \((V,E)\) is an undirected graph and \(\sigma_{e,v}\in\{+1,-1\}\) is assigned to every incidence \(v\in e\); the two occurrences of a loop may generally have different signs, but here loops are assumed to have equal signs. An edge is positive if all its incidence signs are \(+1\), negative if all are \(-1\), and directed otherwise. Its incidence matrix \(M\in\mathbb Z^{V\times E}\) has \(M_{v,e}=\sigma_{e,v}\) for a nonloop incidence, \(M_{v,e}=2\sigma_{e,v}\) for a loop, and \(M_{v,e}=0\) when \(v\notin e\). An integer matrix is such an incidence matrix if and only if every column satisfies \(\sum_v |M_{v,e}|=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bidirected graph is an undirected graph with a sign at each edge–vertex incidence. Under the same-sign convention for loops, its incidence matrix uses the incidence sign for nonloops, twice the sign for loops, and zero off an edge. Integer matrices of this form are exactly those whose columns have absolute-value sum two.
assumptions_latex: \text{the two incidence signs of every loop are equal}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is a bidirected-graph incidence matrix}\iff \sum_{v\in V}|M_{v,e}|=2\quad\text{for every }e\in E.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partitionable mixed graphs and the matching-forest bifurcation correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines partitionability, records its circuit and contraction characterizations, and gives the directed representation of matching forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed graph \(G=(V,E,A)\) is partitionable into \(R\) and \(S\) if \(V=R\mathbin{\dot\cup}S\), every undirected edge has one endpoint in each class, and every directed arc has both endpoints in one class. Equivalently, every circuit of \(G\) contains an even number of undirected edges; equivalently, contracting all directed arcs yields a bipartite graph. Orient every edge from \(R\) to \(S\) and reverse every arc whose endpoints lie in \(R\), obtaining \(D'=(V,A')\). Then a set \(F\subseteq E\cup A\) is a matching forest in \(G\) if and only if its corresponding arcs in \(D'\) form an \(R\)-\(S\) bifurcation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed graph is partitionable when its undirected edges cross a two-class partition and its arcs remain within the classes. This is equivalent to the even-undirected-edge circuit condition and to bipartiteness after contracting the arcs. Under the stated orientation and reversal, matching forests correspond exactly to R–S bifurcations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is partitionable}\iff\text{every circuit contains an even number of edges from }E\iff G/A\text{ is bipartite},\qquad F\text{ is a matching forest in }G\iff F'\text{ is an }R\text{-}S\text{ bifurcation in }D'.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientations of loopless undirected multigraphs, including constrained orientation families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) be a finite loopless undirected multigraph. An orientation is a pair of maps \(t,h:E\to V\) such that \(\{t(e),h(e)\}=\partial(e)\) for every \(e\in E\); it replaces each undirected edge independently by one of its two possible directions. An orientation regime is any specified family \(\mathcal O\) of such orientations, possibly defined by degree, reachability, connectivity, or prescribed-direction constraints. The unconstrained regime consists of all \(2^{|E|}\) orientations of the distinguishable edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orientation chooses one direction for each loopless undirected edge; an orientation regime is a family of choices satisfying stated constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O\subseteq\{(t,h):\{t(e),h(e)\}=\partial(e)\text{ for every }e\in E\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subpartition characterization of orientations covering an intersecting supermodular function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes feasibility for ordinary undirected-graph orientations, allowing the integer-valued requirement function to take negative values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be an undirected graph and let $h$ be an integer-valued intersecting $G$-supermodular function, possibly taking negative values. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has an orientation covering }h\iff \forall\mathcal P=\{V_1,\ldots,V_t\},\quad e'_G(\mathcal P)\ge\sum_{i=1}^t h(V_i).

knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple hypergraphs with arbitrary nonempty edge cardinalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite hypergraph is an ordered pair \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\), where \(V\) is a finite vertex set and \(\mathcal E\subseteq 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) is a family of nonempty subsets called hyperedges. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines partition-derived, laminar, cross-free, and union-intersection-closed families of sets or bi-sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A partition of V is a hypergraph in which every v\in V has degree 1; a subpartition is a partition of a subset of V. A co-partition of V is obtained by complementing the members of a partition of V. If Z\subsetneq V and \{Z_1,\ldots,Z_t\} partitions V\setminus Z, then \{V\setminus Z_1,\ldots,V\setminus Z_t\} is a co-partition of Z and a co-subpartition of V. A hypergraph is a chain when its members are pairwise comparable by inclusion, laminar when every two members are comparable or disjoint, and cross-free when it has no crossing pair; the same laminar and cross-free definitions apply to bi-set families. A family \mathcal F of sets or bi-sets is a ring-family when it is closed under union and intersection; it is intersecting, respectively crossing, when X\cap Y,X\cup Y\in\mathcal F for every intersecting, respectively crossing, pair X,Y\in\mathcal F. A hypergraph (V,\mathcal F) is intersecting or crossing exactly when \mathcal F has the corresponding property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition is a hypergraph whose vertices all have degree one, and a subpartition partitions only a subset of the ground set. Co-partitions arise by complementing partition members, including the stated construction relative to a proper subset Z. Chains have pairwise comparable members; laminar families have only comparable or disjoint pairs; cross-free families have no crossing pair. These notions also apply to bi-set families. Ring-families are closed under union and intersection, while intersecting or crossing families require this closure only for intersecting or crossing pairs, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F=\{V\setminus Z_i:1\le i\le t\}\text{ is a co-partition of }Z\text{ and a co-subpartition of }V,\text{ with the remaining family classes defined by their stated comparability, crossing, and closure properties.}

knowledge_statements.title: Clutters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite antichain hypergraphs under set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A clutter is a finite hypergraph \(C=(V,\mathcal E)\) whose hyperedge family is an antichain under inclusion: for all distinct \(F,F'\in\mathcal E\), neither \(F\subseteq F'\) nor \(F'\subseteq F\). Equivalently, \(F\subseteq F'\) for members \(F,F'\in\mathcal E\) implies \(F=F'\). Thus every edge of a clutter is inclusion-minimal within its edge family, and no edge properly contains another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clutter is a finite hypergraph in which no hyperedge properly contains another hyperedge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall F,F'\in\mathcal E,\ F\subseteq F'\Rightarrow F=F'\).

knowledge_statements.title: General Set Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite ground sets equipped with unrestricted families of subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite set system is an ordered pair \((V,\mathcal F)\), where \(V\) is a finite ground set and \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) is an arbitrary family of subsets. Unless extra conditions are stated, \(\mathcal F\) may be empty, may contain \(\varnothing\) or \(V\), and need not be uniform, intersecting, inclusion-closed, or an antichain. Its incidence relation is \(I=\{(v,F)\in V\times\mathcal F:v\in F\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set system is a finite ground set together with an otherwise unrestricted family of its subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\subseteq 2^V\) and \(I=\{(v,F):v\in F\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational conventions for sets and set systems; finiteness is the default for combinatorial structures unless stated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A substructure is proper when it is unequal to its containing structure. A family permits repeated elements with multiplicities. For a set \(X\), \(\mathcal P(X)=\{Y:Y\subseteq X\}\), while \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{odd}}(X)\) and \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{even}}(X)\) contain its odd- and even-cardinality subsets. A set \(U\) separates distinct \(s,t\) when \(|U\cap\{s,t\}|=1\), and separates disjoint \(S,T\) when \(U\cap(S\cup T)\in\{S,T\}\). Moreover, \(S\triangle T=(S\setminus T)\cup(T\setminus S)\), \(X+y=X\cup\{y\}\), and \(X-y=X\setminus\{y\}\). Sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_k\) are disjoint when \(S_i\cap S_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\); a partition of \(X\) is a collection of such subsets with union \(X\). Two sets are comparable when one contains the other, and a chain is a pairwise comparable collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper substructure differs from its containing structure, and a family may contain elements with multiplicity. The power set and its odd- and even-cardinality subfamilies are defined in the usual way. Separation, symmetric difference, adjoining or deleting one element, pairwise disjointness, partitions, comparability, and chains have the stated set-theoretic meanings.
assumptions_latex: S\cap T=\varnothing\text{ in the definition of separation of two sets}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The displayed conditions define the stated set-system notions and notation.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dualization of finite incidence systems by transposing membership incidence while retaining indexed dual edges.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Elements of graphs and hypergraphs p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(V,\mathcal E)\) be a finite set system. Its incidence dual is the incidence system \(H^*=(\mathcal E,(E_v)_{v\in V})\), whose vertex set is \(\mathcal E\) and whose dual edge indexed by \(v\in V\) is \(E_v=\{F\in\mathcal E:v\in F\}\). Thus \(F\in E_v\) if and only if \(v\in F\). If the incidence matrix \(M(H)\) has rows indexed by \(V\) and columns indexed by \(\mathcal E\), then \(M(H^*)=M(H)^{\mathsf T}\). When distinct vertices have identical incidences, their equal sets \(E_v\) remain distinct members of the indexed dual-edge family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The incidence dual exchanges the two indexed sides of the membership relation, transposes the incidence matrix, and retains distinct dual-edge indices even when their incident sets coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected node-Menger theorem with parallel terminal edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's bi-set notation: d_G(X) is the relevant boundary size and w(X) the wall size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) be an undirected graph with specified vertices s,t, let \alpha be the number of parallel st-edges, and let G^- be obtained by deleting those edges. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) be a finite loopless undirected multigraph with \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\). A walk of length \(k\ge 0\) is an alternating sequence \(W=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) such that \(\partial(e_i)=\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\). Vertices and edges may repeat. A walk system is any specified family \(\mathcal W\) of such walks in \(G\), possibly restricted by endpoints, length, or other stated predicates. The walk is closed exactly when \(v_0=v_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A walk system in a finite loopless undirected multigraph is a family of alternating vertex-edge sequences in which each intervening edge joins its neighboring vertices; vertices and edges may repeat.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Walks, paths, circuits, and cycles in an undirected graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary walk length counts traversed edges unless an edge-length function is in force. A one-edge circuit uses a loop, and a two-edge circuit uses distinct parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A walk in an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ is a sequence $P=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)$, where $k\geq0$ and $e_i$ joins $v_{i-1}$ and $v_i$ for every $i$. It is a path when $v_0,\ldots,v_k$ are all distinct, closed when $v_k=v_0$, and a circuit when $v_k=v_0$, $k\geq1$, $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ are all distinct, and $e_1,\ldots,e_k$ are all distinct. Reversal reverses the traversal order, and two walks may be concatenated when the last vertex of the first is the first vertex of the second. A chord is an edge outside the traversed edge family that joins two traversed vertices. Walks are vertex-disjoint, internally vertex-disjoint, or edge-disjoint according to the corresponding vertex or edge families. An edge set $F\subseteq E$ is a cycle when every vertex has even degree in $(V,F)$; equivalently, $F$ is the symmetric difference of the edge sets of finitely many circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A walk is an alternating incident vertex-edge sequence. Paths have no repeated vertices; circuits are nonempty closed walks with the stated vertex and edge distinctness. Chords and the standard disjointness notions are defined from the traversed vertices and edges. A cycle is an edge set inducing even degree at every vertex, equivalently a symmetric difference of circuit edge sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\subseteq E\text{ is a cycle}\iff \deg_{(V,F)}(v)\text{ is even for every }v\in V\iff F\text{ is a symmetric difference of edge sets of circuits.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphs, Digraphs, Traversals, and Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite graph-theoretic objects and standard traversal terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite graph is $G=(V,E)$ with $E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|=2\}$; a multigraph may have repeated edges. A digraph is $D=(V,A)$ with $A\subseteq V\times V$. For $e=[u,v]\in E$, $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, $e$ is incident with both, and $\deg(v)$ counts incident edges. A walk is $[v_1,\ldots,v_k]$, $k\ge1$, with $[v_j,v_{j+1}]\in E$ for every $j<k$; it is closed when $k>1$ and $v_k=v_1$, a path when it has no repeated vertices, and a cycle when it is closed with no repetitions except its first and last vertex. Path and cycle length is $k-1$. In a digraph, $\deg^-(v)=|\{(u,v)\in A\}|$ and $\deg^+(v)=|\{(v,u)\in A\}|$; directed walks, paths, cycles, closure, and length are defined analogously using arcs $(v_j,v_{j+1})\in A$. A graph $B=(W,E)$ is bipartite if $W=V\mathbin{\dot\cup}U$ and every edge has one endpoint in each part.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph has a finite vertex set and two-vertex edges; a multigraph may repeat edges. A digraph instead has ordered-pair arcs. Incidence, adjacency, vertex degree, directed indegree and outdegree are defined by edge or arc endpoints. Walks follow consecutive edges or arcs; closed walks return to their initial vertex, paths have no repeated vertices, and cycles are closed paths with only the initial/final vertex repeated. Their length is the number of traversed edges or arcs. A bipartite graph has a partition of its vertices into two parts, with every edge crossing between the parts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated conditions define graphs, digraphs, walks, paths, cycles, degrees, and bipartite graphs.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction by deleting a closed trail and recursively splicing residual Eulerian walks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a vertex $v_1$ in an Eulerian connected component, return $[v_1]$ if it is isolated. Otherwise, construct a closed trail $[v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_n,v_1]$ without repeated edges, delete its edges, recursively construct Eulerian walks in the residual graph from the trail vertices, and splice those walks into the trail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an Eulerian component, form a closed trail without repeating edges, delete its edges, recursively traverse the residual components encountered at its vertices, and splice the resulting walks. The output traverses every edge of the original component exactly once and returns to the starting vertex.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Euler}(v_1)\text{ is a closed walk traversing every edge of the component containing }v_1\text{ exactly once}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Walks, paths, trails, and directed walks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The composite extract supports these traversal definitions at Walk Systems; connectivity, Eulerian, Hamiltonian, tree, and branching material is not assigned here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a graph or digraph, a walk is a finite alternating sequence $W=v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k$ with $k\ge0$, where each edge or arc $e_i$ has endnodes $v_{i-1}$ and $v_i$. Its origin and terminus are $v_0$ and $v_k$, its internal nodes are $v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}$, and its length is $k$. In a digraph, the walk is directed when $e_i=(v_{i-1},v_i)$ for every $i$. A path is a walk whose nodes are all distinct, whereas a trail is a walk whose edges or arcs are all distinct. A directed path is a path that is also a directed walk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A walk alternates vertices with incident edges or arcs and may have length zero. A directed walk follows every arc from the preceding vertex to the succeeding vertex. A path has no repeated vertices, a trail has no repeated edges or arcs, and a directed path is both a path and a directed walk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W\text{ is a path}\iff v_0,\ldots,v_k\text{ are distinct},\quad W\text{ is a trail}\iff e_1,\ldots,e_k\text{ are distinct},\quad W\text{ is directed}\iff e_i=(v_{i-1},v_i)\ \forall i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hamiltonian traversals and the Eulerian graph characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Hamiltonian circuits and paths and Eulerian walks and graphs, preserving the source's alternative Eulerian convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Hamiltonian circuit in a graph $G$ is a circuit $C$ with $V(C)=V(G)$, and a Hamiltonian path is a path $P$ with $V(P)=V(G)$; $G$ is Hamiltonian if it has a Hamiltonian circuit. An Eulerian walk traverses every edge of $G$ exactly once, and $G$ is Eulerian if it has a closed Eulerian walk. If $G=(V,E)$ has no isolated vertices, then $G$ is Eulerian if and only if $G$ is connected and every vertex has even degree. Under an alternative convention, the term Eulerian may mean only that every vertex has even degree, without requiring connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hamiltonian circuit or path contains every vertex, and a graph is Hamiltonian when it has a Hamiltonian circuit. An Eulerian walk traverses every edge exactly once, and an Eulerian graph has a closed Eulerian walk. A graph without isolated vertices is Eulerian exactly when it is connected and all its vertex degrees are even. Some contexts instead use Eulerian merely to mean that all degrees are even.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ has no isolated vertices for the Eulerian equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is Eulerian}\iff G\text{ is connected and }\deg_G(v)\text{ is even for every }v\in V

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Walks, reachability, disjoint path systems, and circuit reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected, directed, and mixed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A walk is an alternating vertex-edge sequence \((v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) with each edge joining consecutive vertices; in a directed walk each \(e_i\) is directed from \(v_{i-1}\) to \(v_i\), and in a mixed-graph forward walk each \(e_i\) is either undirected or directed forward. Its length is \(k\), it is closed iff \(v_0=v_k\), and \(v_k\) is reachable from \(v_0\). Distance is the minimum length of an \(st\)-path. A \(k\)-braid is a set of \(k\) edge-disjoint \(st\)-walks; a directed braid is acyclic when its union contains no directed circuit. A \(k\)-bundle is a set of \(k\) \(st\)-paths pairwise disjoint except possibly at \(s,t\). A walk is edge-simple when its edges are distinct and simple when its defining members are distinct; an edge-simple walk using every edge is Eulerian, and if closed is an Euler tour. A circuit or path is Hamiltonian when it contains every vertex. If a nonclosed forward walk repeats a vertex and the intervening subsequence is a circuit, deleting that circuit yields another walk with the same endpoints; repeated circuit deletion terminates in a path between those endpoints, though the resulting path may depend on the deletion order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Walks may repeat vertices and edges, while directed and mixed forward walks must respect arc orientation. Reachability, length, distance, closed walks, edge-simple and simple walks, braids, bundles, Euler walks and tours, and Hamilton paths and circuits are defined. Removing repeated circuit segments from a nonclosed forward walk preserves its endpoints and eventually produces a path, potentially depending on the reduction order.
assumptions_latex: W=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\text{ is a valid walk of the stated graph type}
v_0\ne v_k\text{ for the circuit-reduction assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Maximal circuit reduction of }W\text{ yields a }v_0v_k\text{-path}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,\partial)\) be a finite loopless undirected multigraph with \(\partial:E\to\binom{V}{2}\). A path of length \(k\ge 0\) is a walk \(P=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) satisfying \(\partial(e_i)=\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\), with the vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\) pairwise distinct. Consequently, its edges are also distinct. A path system is any specified family \(\mathcal P\) of paths in \(G\), possibly restricted by prescribed endpoint pairs or other stated predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path system in a finite loopless undirected multigraph is a family of walks with no repeated vertices, possibly restricted by endpoints or other explicit conditions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the extract's interdependent definitions with its Euler-cycle and spanning-tree characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A path is specified by nodes \((n_1,\ldots,n_k)\), \(k\ge2\), together with \(k-1\) arcs, the \(i\)-th being either \((n_i,n_{i+1})\) (forward) or \((n_{i+1},n_i)\) (backward); write \(P^+\) and \(P^-\) for these arc sets. It is forward or backward when all its arcs have the corresponding orientation. A cycle has \(n_1=n_k\); a path is simple when it repeats no arc or node except possibly its coincident endpoints, and a Hamiltonian cycle is a simple forward cycle containing every node. Unless orientation is fixed, the node sequence alone need not determine the path. A graph is acyclic if it has no simple cycle, connected if every ordered node pair is joined by a path, and strongly connected if every ordered pair is joined by a forward path. If a connected graph has even degree at every node, it has an Euler cycle traversing every arc exactly once. A subgraph \(\mathcal G'=(\mathcal N',\mathcal A')\) satisfies \(\mathcal N'\subseteq\mathcal N\) and \(\mathcal A'\subseteq\mathcal A\); a tree is connected and acyclic, and a subgraph spanning all \(N\) nodes is a spanning tree if and only if it is connected and has \(N-1\) arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed-graph path consists of both a node sequence and compatible forward or backward arcs; without a fixed orientation, its arcs may not be determined by the nodes alone. The extract defines cycles, simplicity, Hamiltonian cycles, acyclicity, connectivity, strong connectivity, subgraphs, trees, and spanning trees. It also states that a connected even-degree graph has an Euler cycle, and that a spanning subgraph is a tree exactly when it is connected and has N−1 arcs.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal G\text{ connected and }\deg(i)\text{ even for every }i\quad\text{for the Euler-cycle assertion}
\mathcal G'\text{ spans all }N\text{ nodes}\quad\text{for the spanning-tree characterization}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\mathcal G\text{ connected and all degrees even}\bigr)\Rightarrow\mathcal G\text{ has an Euler cycle},\qquad \mathcal G'\text{ spanning tree}\iff\bigl(\mathcal G'\text{ connected and }|\mathcal A'|=N-1\bigr).

knowledge_statements.title: Trail Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected-graph definition, allowing open and closed trails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A trail of length \(m\ge 0\) is an alternating sequence \(T=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_m,v_m)\) such that each edge \(e_i\) has endpoints \(v_{i-1}\) and \(v_i\), and the edges \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) are pairwise distinct. Vertices may repeat. The trail is closed when \(v_0=v_m\), and open otherwise. A trail system is an indexed family \(\mathcal T=(T_j)_{j\in J}\) of trails in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trail is a walk with no repeated edge; vertices may repeat. A trail system is an indexed family of such trails in one finite graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T=(T_j)_{j\in J}\) is a trail system exactly when every \(T_j\) is a trail in \(G\).

notation.meaning: A trail represented by its alternating vertex-edge sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple cycles in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A cycle is a closed trail \(C=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_m,v_m)\) with \(m\ge 3\), \(v_m=v_0\), and pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\). Thus its edges are also pairwise distinct. A cycle system is an indexed family \(\mathcal C=(C_j)_{j\in J}\) of cycles of \(G\); no disjointness between different members is implied unless imposed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle is a closed trail of length at least three with no repeated vertex except the common start and end. A cycle system is an indexed family of cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C=(C_j)_{j\in J}\) is a cycle system exactly when every \(C_j\) is a cycle of \(G\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut vertices and the small-graph boundary of 2-connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loopless undirected graphs, including parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) be loopless. A vertex v is a cut vertex if deleting v increases the number of connected components. If |V|\ge 3, then G is 2-connected if and only if it has no cut vertex. A graph on two vertices joined by at least two parallel edges is also 2-connected, whereas the graph consisting of two vertices and one edge is not 2-connected despite having no cut vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a loopless graph, a cut vertex is one whose deletion increases the number of components. For graphs with at least three vertices, having no cut vertex is equivalent to 2-connectivity. Two vertices joined by at least two parallel edges form a 2-connected graph, but a single edge on two vertices does not, even though it has no cut vertex.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected loopless graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |V|\ge 3\implies\bigl(G\text{ is 2-connected}\iff G\text{ has no cut vertex}\bigr),\quad m_G(u,v)\ge 2\implies G[\{u,v\}]\text{ is 2-connected}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the extract's convention of calling edges or directed edges arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph $G=(N,A)$ consists of a finite node set $N$ and a set $A$ of unordered node pairs; a digraph is defined similarly with ordered pairs. A loop is an arc $(i,i)$. A network is a graph or digraph endowed with additional node or arc data. Under the convention that an undirected graph has no loops or parallel arcs, $m\le n(n-1)/2$; for a loopless digraph permitting both opposite orientations, $m\le n(n-1)$, where $n=|N|$ and $m=|A|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph has nodes and unordered node pairs as arcs, whereas a digraph uses ordered pairs. An arc from a node to itself is a loop, and a graph with additional numerical or other node or arc data is a network. A loopless simple undirected graph has at most n(n−1)/2 arcs, while a loopless digraph allowing both orientations has at most n(n−1) arcs.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the undirected bound, there are no loops or parallel arcs.}
\text{For the directed bound, loops are excluded and both }(i,j)\text{ and }(j,i)\text{ may occur.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m\le \frac{n(n-1)}2\ \text{in the undirected case},\qquad m\le n(n-1)\ \text{in the directed case}.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected edge cuts and their capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. For \(S\subseteq V\), the edge cut induced by \(S\) is \(\delta_G(S)=\{uv\in E: u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}\). It is proper when \(\varnothing\ne S\ne V\). If \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) assigns edge capacities, the cut capacity is \(c(\delta_G(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}c(e)\). The sets \(S\) and \(V\setminus S\) induce the same undirected cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph cut consists of edges with one endpoint in a vertex set and the other outside it; its capacity is the sum of their capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(c:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\) when cut capacities are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_G(S)=\delta_G(V\setminus S)\), with capacity \(\sum_{e\in\delta_G(S)}c(e)\).

notation.meaning: The undirected edge boundary of vertex set \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgraphs, deletion, induced subgraphs, and spanning subgraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard containment and deletion operations for finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(H\) is a subgraph of \(G\) if \(V(H)\subseteq V(G)\), \(E(H)\subseteq E(G)\), and every edge of \(H\) has the same endpoints in \(H\) as in \(G\). For \(A\subseteq E(G)\), \(G\setminus A\) has vertex set \(V(G)\) and edge set \(E(G)\setminus A\). For \(B\subseteq V(G)\), \(G\setminus B=G[V(G)\setminus B]\) is obtained by deleting the vertices in \(B\) and every edge incident with them. A subgraph \(H\) is spanning if \(V(H)=V(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgraph retains selected vertices and edges while preserving every retained edge's endpoints. Edge deletion keeps all vertices; vertex deletion also removes incident edges and yields the subgraph induced by the remaining vertices. A subgraph is spanning when it retains every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\subseteq G\iff V(H)\subseteq V(G),\ E(H)\subseteq E(G)\text{ and endpoints are preserved};\qquad H\text{ is spanning}\iff V(H)=V(G).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simultaneous Degree- and Size-Bounded Connectivity Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines two separately feasible augmentations—one satisfying degree bounds and one satisfying an edge-count bound—while retaining prescribed pairwise edge connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph, let \(g:V\to\mathbb Z_+\), and let \(r(u,v)\) prescribe a connectivity requirement for every pair \(\{u,v\}\subseteq V\). If there exists a graph \(H=(V,F)\) such that \(d_H(v)\le g(v)\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(\lambda_{G+H}(u,v)\ge r(u,v)\) for every pair \(\{u,v\}\), and there exists a graph \(H'\) with at most \(\gamma\) edges such that \(\lambda_{G+H'}(u,v)\ge r(u,v)\) for every pair \(\{u,v\}\), then there exists a graph \(K\) satisfying all three conditions simultaneously: \(d_K(v)\le g(v)\) for every \(v\in V\), \(|E(K)|\le\gamma\), and \(\lambda_{G+K}(u,v)\ge r(u,v)\) for every pair \(\{u,v\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a connected undirected graph, if the prescribed pairwise edge-connectivity requirements can be met by some augmentation obeying all vertex-degree bounds and can also be met by some augmentation having at most gamma edges, then one augmentation exists that meets the connectivity requirements, all degree bounds, and the edge-count bound simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K:\ |E(K)|\le\gamma,\quad \forall v\in V\ d_K(v)\le g(v),\quad \forall\{u,v\}\subseteq V\ \lambda_{G+K}(u,v)\ge r(u,v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected cuts, separating edge sets, and bridges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The empty edge set is always a cut. It is representable by a nonempty proper shore, and hence is a nontrivial cut, exactly when the graph is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $G=(V,E)$ and $U\subseteq V$, let $\delta_G(U)$ be the set of edges joining $U$ to $V\setminus U$, and let $d_G(U)=|\delta_G(U)|$. A cut is an edge set $F=\delta_G(U)$; it is nontrivial when $\varnothing
eq U
eq V$. For all $T,U\subseteq V$, $\delta(T)	riangle\delta(U)=\delta(T	riangle U)$, so the cuts are closed under symmetric difference. If $s\in U$ and $t
otin U$, then $\delta(U)$ is an $s$-$t$ cut; it is an $S$-$T$ cut when $S\subseteq U$ and $T\subseteq V\setminus U$. An edge set is $s$-$t$ disconnecting when it meets every $s$-$t$ path. Every $s$-$t$ cut is $s$-$t$ disconnecting, and every inclusionwise minimal $s$-$t$ disconnecting edge set is an $s$-$t$ cut. An edge $e$ is a bridge iff $\{e\}$ is a cut, and $G$ is bridgeless iff it has no bridge. For $U,W\subseteq V$, $E[U,W]$ is the family of edges having one end in $U$ and the other in $W$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut is the edge boundary of a vertex subset. Cuts include the empty set and are closed under symmetric difference. Every terminal cut separates its terminals, while every inclusion-minimal terminal-separating edge set is a terminal cut. A bridge is an edge whose singleton is a cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(T)\triangle\delta(U)=\delta(T\triangle U),\qquad \delta(U)\text{ an }s\text{-}t\text{ cut}\Rightarrow\delta(U)\text{ meets every }s\text{-}t\text{ path},\qquad F\text{ inclusionwise minimal }s\text{-}t\text{ disconnecting}\Rightarrow F\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ cut}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasibility and the minimum-total-capacity objective for symmetric pairwise connectivity demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $V$ be a finite ground set, let $E^*$ be the edges of the complete undirected graph on $V$, and let $r:V\times V\to\mathbb{R}_+$ be symmetric. A capacity function $g:E^*\to\mathbb{R}_+$ is $r$-feasible if $\lambda_g(u,v)\ge r(u,v)$ for every distinct $u,v\in V$, where $\lambda_g(u,v)$ is the minimum $g$-capacity of a cut separating $u$ and $v$. Equivalently, every pair admits a flow of value at least $r(u,v)$. The synthesis problem minimizes $\sum_{e\in E^*}g(e)$ over all $r$-feasible $g$. Define $R(v):=\max_{x\in V\setminus\{v\}}r(v,x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given symmetric nonnegative demands between every pair of vertices, a capacity assignment on the complete undirected graph is feasible when every pairwise minimum cut has at least the corresponding demand. Equivalently, every pair supports that much maximum flow. The synthesis problem minimizes total assigned capacity, and R(v) is the largest demand incident with v.
assumptions_latex: $V$ is finite and $E^*$ is the edge set of the complete undirected graph on $V$
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{e\in E^*}g(e):\lambda_g(u,v)\ge r(u,v)\ \forall u\ne v\right\},\qquad R(v)=\max_{x\ne v}r(v,x).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G_1 and G_2 each have an edge labelled p. A graph obtained by identifying the two edges p and then deleting the identified edge is a 2-sum of G_1 and G_2. For this operation, if p is a loop in either G_1 or G_2, it must be a loop in both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph two-sum is formed by identifying the designated edge p of two graphs and deleting the identified edge. If p is a loop in one graph, it must also be a loop in the other.
assumptions_latex: p\in E(G_1)\cap E(G_2)\text{ is the designated edge}
p\text{ is a loop of }G_1\iff p\text{ is a loop of }G_2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_1\oplus_2G_2\text{ is obtained by identifying the two copies of }p\text{ and deleting the resulting edge.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut-Multiset Characterization of Conservative Weighted Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source-established definition of conservativeness and permits repeated cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,\phi)$ be a weighted graph. Then $(G,\phi)$ is conservative if and only if there exists a multiset $\mathcal C$ of cuts such that each cut contains exactly one negative-weight edge, each edge $e$ with $\phi(e)\ge 0$ occurs in at most $2\phi(e)$ cuts of $\mathcal C$, and each edge $e$ with $\phi(e)<0$ occurs in exactly $-2\phi(e)$ cuts of $\mathcal C$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted graph is conservative exactly when there is a possibly repeated collection of cuts, each containing exactly one negative-weight edge, with the stated weight-dependent incidence multiplicities for nonnegative and negative edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G,\phi)\text{ is conservative}\iff \exists\,\mathcal C\text{ satisfying the stated cut-incidence conditions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected graph cut and its shores
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines cuts as undirected edge boundaries and distinguishes trivial from nontrivial cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(X\subseteq V\), the cut \(\Delta_G(X)\) is the set of edges with one endpoint in \(X\) and the other in \(V\setminus X\). The sets \(X\) and \(V\setminus X\) are its shores. The cut is trivial iff \(X=\varnothing\) or \(V\setminus X=\varnothing\), and otherwise it is nontrivial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut determined by a vertex set consists of the edges joining that set to its complement. The two vertex sets are the shores; the cut is trivial exactly when one shore is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_G(X)=\{uv\in E: |\{u,v\}\cap X|=1\},\quad \Delta_G(X)\text{ is nontrivial iff }\varnothing\ne X\ne V.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity definitions for joins and cuts relative to an even vertex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and let \(T\subseteq V\) satisfy \(|T|\) even. An edge set \(F\subseteq E\) is a \(T\)-join if
\[
T=\{v\in V:\deg_{(V,F)}(v)\text{ is odd}\}.
\]
A \(T\)-cut is an edge set \(\delta(W)\) for some \(W\subseteq V\) such that \(|T\cap W|\) is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an even-cardinality vertex set T, a T-join is an edge set whose odd-degree vertices are exactly T. A T-cut is a graph cut whose defining shore contains an odd number of vertices from T.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a }T\text{-join}\iff T=\{v:\deg_{(V,F)}(v)\text{ is odd}\};\quad \delta(W)\text{ is a }T\text{-cut}\iff |T\cap W|\text{ is odd}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tree representation of a set system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a set family from the oriented shores of edge-deletion cuts in a directed tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $T$ be a digraph whose underlying undirected graph is a tree, let $U$ be finite, and let $\varphi:U\to V(T)$. For each arc $e=(x,y)\in E(T)$, set $S_e:=\{s\in U:\varphi(s)\text{ lies in the component of }T-e\text{ containing }y\}$, and let $\mathcal F:=\{S_e:e\in E(T)\}$. Then $(T,\varphi)$ is called a tree representation of $(U,\mathcal F)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map the elements of a finite ground set to the vertices of an oriented tree. Each oriented edge represents the elements mapped to the component on its head side after that edge is deleted. When these sets form the family, the tree and map constitute a tree representation of the set system.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a digraph whose underlying undirected graph is a tree}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F=\left\{\left\{s\in U:\varphi(s)\in\operatorname{comp}_{y}(T-e)\right\}:e=(x,y)\in E(T)\right\}\Rightarrow (T,\varphi)\text{ is a tree representation of }(U,\mathcal F).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge contraction, set contraction, and graph minors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines contraction operations and minor terminology for undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ and $e=uv\in E$. The contraction $G/e$ is obtained by deleting $e$ and identifying $u$ and $v$; for $F\subseteq E$, $G/F$ contracts every edge in $F$, and the image of $v\in V$ is the vertex to which $v$ is contracted. A graph $H$ is a minor of $G$ if it can be obtained by edge deletions, edge contractions, and vertex deletions; it is proper when $H\ne G$, and an $H$-minor of $G$ is a minor of $G$ isomorphic to $H$. For $S\subseteq V$, $G/S$ identifies all vertices of $S$ as one vertex, deletes edges contained in $S$, and replaces each edge $uv$ with $u\in S$, $v\notin S$ by $Sv$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting an edge deletes it and identifies its endpoints; contracting an edge set contracts all its edges. A graph minor is obtained through edge deletions, edge contractions, and vertex deletions, and it is proper when it differs from the original graph. Contracting a vertex set identifies all its vertices, removes internal edges, and redirects boundary edges to the new contracted vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\preceq G\iff H\text{ is obtainable from }G\text{ by vertex deletions, edge deletions, and edge contractions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut criteria for connectivity and rooted reachability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected connectivity and directed reachability from a prescribed root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph \(G\), \(G\) is connected if and only if \(\delta(X)
eq\varnothing\) for every \(\varnothing
eq X\subset V(G)\). For a digraph \(G\) and \(r\in V(G)\), every \(v\in V(G)\) is reachable from \(r\) if and only if \(\delta^+(X)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric dual of a plane graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes parallel dual edges, primal bridges represented by dual loops, and connectedness of the constructed dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a plane graph with at least one edge. Place one vertex \(v_F\) in each face \(F\). For every primal edge \(e\) incident with two faces \(F,F'\), add a simple dual edge \(e'\) from \(v_F\) to \(v_{F'}\) that crosses \(e\) and no other primal edge; distinct dual edges intersect only at common endpoints. If \(e\) is incident with only one face \(F\), add at \(v_F\) a loop \(e'\) crossing \(e\) and no other primal or dual edge. The resulting plane graph \(G^*\) is the geometric dual of \(G\), and \(G^*\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a plane graph with at least one edge, its geometric dual has one vertex per face and one crossing dual edge per primal edge. Edges separating two faces join the corresponding dual vertices, while an edge incident with only one face produces a dual loop. The dual edges otherwise do not cross, and the resulting dual graph is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^*\text{ is the connected plane graph obtained by the stated face-vertex and edge-crossing construction.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines subdivision and graph homeomorphism and states its topological characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph $G$ is a subdivision of $H$ if it is obtained by replacing each edge of $H$ by a path of length at least one, equivalently by repeatedly subdividing an edge $uv$ with a new vertex $w$ and edges $uw,wv$. Graphs $G$ and $G'$ are homeomorphic if some graph $H$ has both as subdivisions. If $|G|$ denotes the topological space obtained by realizing vertices as points and edges as curves meeting only at common endpoints, then $G$ and $H$ are homeomorphic graphs if and only if $|G|$ and $|H|$ are homeomorphic topological spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subdivision replaces graph edges by paths of positive length. Two graphs are homeomorphic when both subdivide a common graph. Equivalently, their standard topological realizations are homeomorphic spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ and }H\text{ are homeomorphic graphs}\iff |G|\cong |H|\text{ as topological spaces}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex cuts, connectivity, and k-connected graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines graph vertex-connectivity with explicit connected, complete, and disconnected cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set X\subseteq V(G) is a vertex cut if G-X has more connected components than G; if X=\{v\}, then v is a cut-vertex. Define
\[
\kappa(G)=\begin{cases}
\min\{|X|:X\text{ is a vertex cut of }G\},&G\text{ is connected and has two distinct nonadjacent vertices},\\
|V(G)|-1,&G\text{ is connected and has no two distinct nonadjacent vertices},\\
0,&G\text{ is disconnected}.
\end{cases}
\]
For k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}, G is k-connected exactly when \kappa(G)\ge k. Consequently, a graph with at least two vertices is 1-connected if and only if it is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex cut is a vertex set whose deletion increases the number of connected components; a one-vertex cut is a cut-vertex. For a connected noncomplete graph, vertex-connectivity is the minimum size of a vertex cut. For a connected graph with no distinct nonadjacent vertices it is the number of vertices minus one, and for a disconnected graph it is zero. A graph is k-connected when its connectivity is at least k; with at least two vertices, it is 1-connected exactly when it is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is }k\text{-connected}\iff \kappa(G)\ge k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A three-set lower bound for the unweighted cut-size function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph G=(U,E) and A,B,C\subseteq U,

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for undirected graphs and digraphs, including directed, terminal, rooted, and underlying-undirected cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In an undirected graph \(G\), a cut is \(\delta(X)\) for some \(\varnothing
eq X\subset V(G)\). In a digraph, \(\delta^+(X)\) is a directed cut when \(\varnothing
eq X\subset V(G)\) and \(\delta^-(X)=\varnothing\). An edge set \(F\subseteq E(G)\) separates \(s\) and \(t\) if \(t\) is reachable from \(s\) in \(G\) but not in \((V(G),E(G)\setminus F)\). An undirected \(s\)-\(t\) cut is \(\delta(X)\) with \(s\in X\), \(t
otin X\); a directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut is \(\delta^+(X)\) under the same condition. An \(r\)-cut in a digraph is \(\delta^+(X)\) with \(r\in X\). An undirected cut in a digraph is \(\delta(X)\) in its underlying undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected cut is the edge boundary of a nonempty proper vertex set. A directed cut is an outgoing boundary with no entering arc. An edge set separates s from t when deleting it destroys previously existing s-to-t reachability. Terminal cuts place s inside and t outside the defining set; an r-cut is an outgoing boundary of a set containing r. A digraph also has undirected cuts obtained from its underlying undirected graph.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an undirected graph or digraph as specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Cuts, directed cuts, separating sets, }s\text{-}t\text{ cuts, }r\text{-cuts, and underlying-undirected cuts are defined as stated.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degrees, connectivity, and elementary undirected graph classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consolidates the related foundational definitions in the extract, including loops and bi-set degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\subseteq V\), \(d_G(X)\) is the number of edges joining \(X\) to \(V\setminus X\). The vertex degree \(d_G(v)\) counts incident loops twice, so it equals \(d_G(\{v\})\) plus twice the number of loops at \(v\). The graph is connected iff \(d_G(X)>0\) for every nonempty proper \(X\subset V\); its components are the maximal induced subgraphs not separated by a zero-degree set. An edge covers a bi-set \((X_O,X_I)\) when one endpoint lies in \(X_I\) and the other outside \(X_O\), and the number of covering edges is its degree. Isolated vertices, leaves, and \(r\)-regular graphs have degrees \(0\), \(1\), and uniformly \(r\), respectively. A matching has all degrees at most one and is perfect when all are one. A circuit is connected and 2-regular, while a path is simple, connected, has maximum degree two, and has a vertex of degree less than two; every nontrivial path has exactly two degree-one endpoints. A graph is Eulerian iff every vertex degree is even. A bipartite graph has a partition \(V=S\dot\cup T\) with every edge joining the two classes; it is complete bipartite when every \(st\), \(s\in S,t\in T\), is an edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The boundary degree of a vertex set counts edges crossing to its complement, while vertex degree counts loops twice. Connectivity means every nonempty proper vertex set has positive boundary degree, and components are maximal induced pieces not separated by a zero boundary. The extract also defines bi-set degree, isolated vertices, leaves, regular graphs, matchings, circuits, paths, Eulerian graphs, and bipartite and complete bipartite graphs through their degree or incidence properties.
assumptions_latex: (X_O,X_I)\text{ is a bi-set with }X_I\subseteq X_O\subseteq V.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The degree, connectivity, component, and elementary graph-class notions have the stated characterizations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted graph and digraph cut-function identities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here the displayed symbols denote the weighted cut, internal-edge, external-edge, in-cut, out-cut, and net-flow set functions and their corresponding cross terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For all vertex subsets X,Y, an undirected graph satisfies
\[d_z(X)+d_z(Y)=d_z(X\cap Y)+d_z(X\cup Y)+2d_z(X,Y),\]
\[d_z(X)+d_z(Y)=d_z(X\setminus Y)+d_z(Y\setminus X)+2\bar d_z(X,Y),\]
\[i_z(X)+i_z(Y)=i_z(X\cap Y)+i_z(X\cup Y)-d_z(X,Y),\]
\[e_z(X)+e_z(Y)=e_z(X\cap Y)+e_z(X\cup Y)+d_z(X,Y).\]
A digraph satisfies
\[\varrho_z(X)+\varrho_z(Y)=\varrho_z(X\cap Y)+\varrho_z(X\cup Y)+d_z(X,Y),\]
\[\delta_z(X)+\delta_z(Y)=\delta_z(X\cap Y)+\delta_z(X\cup Y)+d_z(X,Y),\]
\[\varrho_z(X)+\varrho_z(Y)=\varrho_z(X\setminus Y)+\varrho_z(Y\setminus X)+\bar d_z(X,Y)+\varrho_z(X\cap Y)-\delta_z(X\cap Y),\]
and
\[\Psi_z(X)+\Psi_z(Y)=\Psi_z(X\cap Y)+\Psi_z(X\cup Y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every pair of vertex subsets, weighted graph and digraph cut-related set functions obey the stated intersection–union and set-difference identities, including the appropriate cross-edge correction terms.
assumptions_latex: z\text{ is an edge or arc weighting on the relevant graph or digraph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The eight displayed cut-function identities hold.}

knowledge_statements.title: Cocycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary cut-space definition for finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), identify an edge set with its incidence vector in \(\mathbb F_2^E\). The cocycle space is \(\mathcal B^*(G)=\{\delta_G(S):S\subseteq V\}\), where addition is symmetric difference. Equivalently, \(F\subseteq E\) is a cocycle precisely when every cycle of \(G\) meets \(F\) in an even number of edges. A nonempty inclusion-minimal cocycle is a bond. Distinct vertex sets may represent the same cocycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cocycles are graph cuts viewed as vectors over the binary field; equivalently, they meet every cycle evenly. Minimal nonempty cocycles are bonds.
assumptions_latex: Edge-set addition is symmetric difference, equivalently addition in \(\mathbb F_2^E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\in\mathcal B^*(G)\) if and only if \(|F\cap E(C)|\equiv 0\pmod 2\) for every cycle \(C\) of \(G\).

notation.meaning: The binary cocycle or cut space of the graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separating sets, cocycles, cutsets, and source–sink cutsets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-separation definitions, with arc orientations ignored when the input is a digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(N,A) be a graph, or a digraph viewed without arc orientations. A set C\subseteq A is a separating set if (N,A\setminus C) has more connected components than G; an inclusion-minimal separating set is a cocycle. For every cocycle C, there is a partition N=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T such that C consists exactly of the arcs with one endpoint in S and the other in T, and G-C contains no s\text{--}t path for s\in S and t\in T. A separating set consisting of all arcs crossing such a partition is a cutset. A cutset need not be a cocycle because it need not be minimal. It is an (s,t)-cutset when s\in S and t\in T.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ignoring arc orientations in a digraph, a separating set is an arc set whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and a cocycle is an inclusion-minimal separating set. Every cocycle is exactly the crossing set of some vertex bipartition, and its deletion leaves no path between opposite sides. A separating crossing set is a cutset, which need not be minimal; it is an (s,t)-cutset when s and t are on the designated opposite sides.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a graph, or a digraph whose arc orientations are ignored.}
N=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\text{ when a partition-induced crossing set is considered.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is a cocycle precisely when it is an inclusion-minimal separating set; every cocycle equals the crossing set of some bipartition, whereas a cutset need not be minimal.}

knowledge_statements.title: Bisets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biset notation and the associated undirected edge boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A biset on a finite ground set \(V\) is an ordered pair \(\mathbb X=(X_O,X_I)\) with \(X_I\subseteq X_O\subseteq V\). The sets \(X_I\), \(X_O\), and \(X_O\setminus X_I\) are its inner part, outer part, and boundary. Its co-biset is \(\overline{\mathbb X}=(V\setminus X_I,V\setminus X_O)\). In an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the biset cut is \(\delta_G(\mathbb X)=\{uv\in E:u\in X_I,\ v\in V\setminus X_O\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biset consists of nested inner and outer vertex sets. Its graph boundary contains edges from the inner set to vertices outside the outer set.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is undirected when the biset cut is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_G(\mathbb X)=E_G(X_I,V\setminus X_O)\), and \(X_O\setminus X_I\) is the biset boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cut Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entering and leaving cuts in finite directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph and \(S\subseteq V\). The leaving cut and entering cut of \(S\) are \(\delta_D^+(S)=\{uv\in A:u\in S,\ v\in V\setminus S\}\) and \(\delta_D^-(S)=\{uv\in A:u\in V\setminus S,\ v\in S\}\), respectively. They satisfy \(\delta_D^+(S)=\delta_D^-(V\setminus S)\). For arc capacities \(c:A\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), their capacities are obtained by summing \(c(a)\) over their arcs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_D^+(S)=\delta_D^-(V\setminus S)\) and \(\delta_D^-(S)=\delta_D^+(V\setminus S)\).
