knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-max theorem for packing directed in-cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The demand function is subject to the restricted supermodularity condition given in the preceding extracted item.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph such that \(V=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}T\) and \(A\) consists of all arcs from \(S\) to \(T\). Let \(g:\mathcal P(V)\to\mathbb Z_+\) satisfy \[\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U)\cap\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(W)\neq\varnothing,\quad g(U)>0,\quad g(W)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ g(U)+g(W)\leq g(U\cap W)+g(U\cup W),\] and suppose \(g(U)=0\) whenever \(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U)=\varnothing\). Then \[\min\left\{x(A):x:A\to\mathbb Z_+,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\geq g(U)\ \text{for every }U\subseteq V\right\}=\max\left\{\sum_{U\in\mathcal B}g(U):\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U)\ \text{are pairwise disjoint for }U\in\mathcal B\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the digraph containing every arc from S to T, the minimum total nonnegative integral arc multiplicity covering all directed in-cut demands equals the maximum total demand over a family of pairwise disjoint entering cuts, provided the demand function satisfies the stated restricted supermodularity and vanishes on sets with empty entering cut.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ consists of all arcs from }S\text{ to }T
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\substack{x:A\to\mathbb Z_+\\x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\geq g(U)\ \forall U\subseteq V}}x(A)=\max_{\substack{\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal P(V)\\\{\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U):U\in\mathcal B\}\text{ pairwise disjoint}}}\sum_{U\in\mathcal B}g(U)

knowledge_statements.title: Connected Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical vertex partition of a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. Define \(u\sim v\) when a path in \(G\) joins \(u\) to \(v\), including the length-zero path when \(u=v\). This is an equivalence relation on \(V\). Its equivalence classes are the connected components of \(G\); equivalently, each component is an inclusion-maximal vertex set \(C\subseteq V\) for which the induced subgraph \(G[C]\) is connected. The components form a unique partition of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices belong to the same connected component exactly when a path joins them. The components uniquely partition the graph's vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=C_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_k\), where each \(G[C_i]\) is connected and no edge joins distinct classes.

notation.meaning: The subgraph induced by vertex set \(C\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-pairs characterizations of edge- and vertex-connectivity for undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G\) with at least two vertices, \(G\) is \(k\)-edge-connected if and only if every pair of distinct vertices \(s,t\in V(G)\) is joined by \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths. For an undirected graph \(G\) with more than \(k\) vertices, \(G\) is \(k\)-connected if and only if every pair of distinct vertices \(s,t\in V(G)\) is joined by \(k\) pairwise internally disjoint \(s\)-\(t\) paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected graph with at least two vertices is k-edge-connected exactly when every distinct vertex pair has k edge-disjoint connecting paths. If it has more than k vertices, it is k-connected exactly when every distinct vertex pair has k internally disjoint connecting paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}G\text{ is }k\text{-edge-connected}&\iff\forall s\ne t\in V(G),\ \exists\ k\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths},\\G\text{ is }k\text{-connected}&\iff\forall s\ne t\in V(G),\ \exists\ k\text{ pairwise internally disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives separate characterizations for digraphs having at most k vertices and those having at least k+1 vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\). If \(|V|\ge k+1\), then \(D\) is \(k\)-connected if and only if, for every integer \(j\) with \(0\le j\le k-1\), deleting any \(j\) vertices leaves a strongly connected digraph.

For a digraph with at least k+1 vertices, it is equivalent to remaining strongly connected after deletion of any j vertices for every j from 0 through k−1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic tau-critical graphs and elementary reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract combines the definition of a basic tau-critical graph with component and degree-two reduction properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a \tau-critical graph G has connected components G_1,\ldots,G_k, then every G_i is \tau-critical and \tau(G)=\sum_{i=1}^k\tau(G_i). If a connected graph G\neq K_3 has a degree-two vertex and G' is obtained by contracting its two incident edges, then G is \tau-critical if and only if G' is \tau-critical, and \tau(G')=\tau(G)-1. A connected \tau-critical graph with minimum degree at least 3 is called basic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The connected components of a tau-critical graph are tau-critical and their cover numbers add. For a connected graph other than K3, contracting the two edges incident with a degree-two vertex preserves tau-criticality and decreases tau by one. A connected tau-critical graph of minimum degree at least three is basic.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a }\tau\text{-critical graph with components }G_1,\ldots,G_k
\text{For the contraction statement, }G\text{ is connected},\ G\neq K_3,\ \deg_G(v)=2
G'\text{ is obtained by contracting the two edges incident with }v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ear Decomposition and Proper Ear Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines ears for either directed or undirected graphs and states the additional conditions for properness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a directed or undirected graph. An ear decomposition of \(G\) is a sequence \(r,P_1,\ldots,P_k\) such that \(G=(\{r\},\varnothing)+P_1+\cdots+P_k\) and, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(P_i\) is either a path whose endpoints are exactly its vertices in \(\{r\}\cup\bigcup_{j<i}V(P_j)\), or a circuit having exactly one vertex in that set. The graphs \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) are the ears. The decomposition is proper if \(k\ge 1\), \(P_1\) is a circuit of length at least three, and every \(P_i\) for \(i\ge 2\) is a path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ear decomposition builds a directed or undirected graph from a root by successively adding ears. Each ear is either a path meeting the previously built graph exactly at its endpoints or a circuit meeting it at exactly one vertex. It is proper when there is at least one ear, the first is a circuit of length at least three, and all later ears are paths.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a directed or undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r,P_1,\ldots,P_k\text{ is an ear decomposition under the stated attachment conditions, and it is proper exactly under the additional stated restrictions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph blocks and blocks of a graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines graph blocks and maximal block subgraphs, with the loopless cut-vertex characterization and the stated size-dependent consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(H\) is a block if it is connected and its cycle matroid \(M(H)\) is connected. If \(H\) is loopless, then \(H\) is a block if and only if it is connected and has no cut-vertex. Consequently, a block with at least three vertices is 2-connected. A block of a graph \(G\) is a subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) that is a block and is maximal with this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block is a connected graph whose cycle matroid is connected. For a loopless graph, this is equivalent to being connected with no cut-vertex; a block with at least three vertices is therefore 2-connected. A block of a given graph is a maximal subgraph having the block property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is a block}\iff\bigl(H\text{ is connected and }M(H)\text{ is connected}\bigr);\quad H\text{ loopless}\Rightarrow\left(H\text{ is a block}\iff H\text{ is connected and has no cut-vertex}\right).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic undirected-graph definitions, with the induced connectivity convention for digraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected graph \(G\) is connected iff every pair \(v,w\in V(G)\) is joined by a \(v\)-\(w\) path; a digraph is connected iff its underlying undirected graph is connected. Connected components are maximal connected subgraphs, and \(X\subseteq V(G)\) is connected iff \(G[X]\) is connected. A vertex \(v\) is an articulation vertex iff \(G-v\) has more components than \(G\), and an edge \(e\) is a bridge iff \(G-e\) has more components than \(G\). An undirected graph without a circuit is a forest; a connected forest is a tree. A tree vertex of degree at most one is a leaf, and a star is a tree with at most one nonleaf vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is connected when every two vertices are joined by a path; a digraph is connected when its underlying undirected graph is. Components are maximal connected subgraphs, and a vertex set is connected when it induces a connected subgraph. Removing an articulation vertex or bridge increases the number of components. A circuit-free undirected graph is a forest, a connected forest is a tree, a degree-at-most-one tree vertex is a leaf, and a star has at most one nonleaf vertex.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a graph; forest, tree, leaf, and star refer to undirected graphs.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated connectivity, separation, forest, tree, leaf, and star definitions hold.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic connectivity terminology for an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An $(s,t)$-path is a sequence of consecutive arcs $(s,i_1),(i_1,i_2),\ldots,(i_k,t)$; it has no repeated nodes when $s,i_1,\ldots,i_k,t$ are distinct. It is open if $s\ne t$ and closed if $s=t$. A cycle is a nonempty $(s,s)$-path in which no node other than $s$ is repeated; in an ordinary graph it has at least three arcs. A graph is acyclic if it has no cycle. Nodes $i,j$ are connected when an $(i,j)$-path exists, and $G$ is connected when every pair of nodes is connected. A component is a maximal connected subgraph. Thus $G$ is connected iff it has exactly one component, and the components uniquely partition the nodes and arcs of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path is a sequence of consecutive arcs, with a path without repeated nodes having distinct vertices. Paths may be open or closed; a cycle is a nonempty closed path with no repeated vertex other than its endpoint, and an ordinary-graph cycle has at least three arcs. Connectedness is existence of paths, while components are maximal connected subgraphs. A graph is connected exactly when it has one component, and its components uniquely partition its nodes and arcs.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an undirected graph; the three-arc lower bound assumes an ordinary graph without parallel edges or loops.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is connected}\iff G\text{ has exactly one component, and the components partition }V(G)\text{ and }E(G).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and well-definedness property for the 3-blocks of a 2-connected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a 2-connected graph. For a $2$-vertex cutset $\{x,y\}$, write $G=G'_1\cup G'_2$, where $G'_1,G'_2$ are connected, neither is $K_2$, and $V(G'_1)\cap V(G'_2)=\{x,y\}$. Replace the two sides by $G_i=G'_i+xy$ and repeat on any resulting piece that is not $3$-connected. The terminal $3$-connected graphs and triangles, possibly with parallel edges, are the $3$-blocks of $G$. Their list is independent of the choices of $2$-vertex cutsets, up to edge multiplicities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a 2-connected graph, repeatedly split at a two-vertex cutset and add an edge between the two cut vertices on each side. The terminal 3-connected pieces and triangles are its 3-blocks. The resulting list does not depend on the order of splits, apart from parallel-edge multiplicities.
assumptions_latex: \{x,y\}\text{ is a }2\text{-vertex cutset whenever a split is performed}
G'_1,G'_2\text{ are connected, are not }K_2,\text{ and }V(G'_1)\cap V(G'_2)=\{x,y\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ decomposes into }3\text{-connected graphs and triangles whose list is unique up to edge multiplicities.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong and weak connectivity and components of a digraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the component partition and arc-membership characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A digraph $D=(V,A)$ is strongly connected if every ordered pair $u,v\in V$ is joined by a directed $u$-$v$ path, and weakly connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected. A strong component is a maximal nonempty strongly connected subgraph; a weak component is a component of the underlying undirected graph. Strong components are induced subgraphs and their vertex sets partition $V$. An arc $(u,v)$ belongs to a strong component if and only if $D$ contains a directed path from $v$ to $u$. Equivalently, strong components are the equivalence classes of $u\sim v$ defined by mutual directed reachability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A digraph is strongly connected when every vertex can reach every other vertex by a directed path, and weakly connected when its underlying undirected graph is connected. Its strong components are maximal nonempty strongly connected induced subgraphs whose vertex sets partition the vertices. An arc from u to v lies in a strong component exactly when v can reach u. Strong components are precisely the classes of mutual reachability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The strong components are induced, partition }V,\text{ and are the equivalence classes of mutual reachability; }(u,v)\in A\text{ lies in one iff }v\leadsto u.

knowledge_statements.title: Biconnected Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal two-vertex-connected subgraphs; bridges and isolated vertices are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A biconnected block is an inclusion-maximal vertex set \(B\subseteq V\), with \(|B|\ge3\), such that \(G[B]\) is connected and remains connected after deletion of any one vertex of \(B\). Equivalently, every two distinct vertices of \(B\) are joined in \(G[B]\) by two internally vertex-disjoint paths. Distinct biconnected blocks may intersect only at articulation vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A biconnected block is a maximal induced subgraph of at least three vertices that stays connected after any single vertex is removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(v\in B\), the graph \(G[B\setminus\{v\}]\) is connected, and no proper superset of \(B\) has this property.

notation.meaning: The vertex set of a biconnected block.
The subgraph induced by the block's vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical mutual-reachability partition of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Define \(u\sim_D v\) when both a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\) and a directed path from \(v\) to \(u\) exist. This is an equivalence relation on \(V\). Its equivalence classes are the strongly connected components of \(D\), equivalently the inclusion-maximal vertex sets inducing strongly connected subgraphs. Contracting each strong component to one vertex produces an acyclic directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vertices share a strong component exactly when each is reachable from the other. These components partition the vertices, and their contraction is acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equivalence classes of \(\sim_D\) uniquely partition \(V\), and the component-contraction digraph is acyclic.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact formula for every digraph that is not strongly connected.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator-Based Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition induced by deleting a vertex separator from an undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected finite undirected graph and let \(S\subsetneq V\) be a vertex separator, so \(G-S\) has connected-component vertex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) with \(k\ge2\). Then \(V=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_k\), no edge joins \(C_i\) to \(C_j\) for \(i\ne j\), and \(G\) is represented by the pieces \(G[S\cup C_i]\), whose pairwise vertex intersections are exactly \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a vertex separator yields components with no edges between them; adjoining the separator to each component gives overlapping decomposition pieces.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subsetneq V\) and \(G-S\) has at least two connected components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=\bigcup_{i=1}^kG[S\cup C_i]\), with \((S\cup C_i)\cap(S\cup C_j)=S\) for \(i\ne j\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-flow computation of set-to-node arc connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the definition of set-to-node connectivity with the stated labeling procedure and terminal cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq N\) and \(k\in N\setminus S\), let \(\alpha[S,k]\) be the minimum cardinality of an arc set whose deletion separates \(k\) from every node in \(S\). Permit augmentations to begin at any node of \(S\) but to end only at \(k\). When the labeling algorithm terminates, no directed residual path exists from any node of \(S\) to \(k\); the labeled nodes define a cut having exactly \(\alpha[S,k]\) forward arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-to-node arc connectivity is the fewest arcs needed to separate an outside node k from every node of S. A maximum-flow labeling procedure with S as the possible starts and k as the sole endpoint computes it, and the terminal labeled set supplies a minimum separating cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha[S,k]=|\delta^+(R)|,\qquad \text{and no terminal residual directed path runs from }S\text{ to }k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The algorithm grows a set from a minimum-degree node and solves set-to-node maximum-flow subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a minimum-degree node \(p\), initialize \(S=\{p\}\), \(\alpha^*=\deg(p)\), and the cut \([\{p\},N\setminus\{p\}]\). While \(\operatorname{nonneighbor}(S)\neq\varnothing\), choose \(k\in\operatorname{nonneighbor}(S)\), compute \(\alpha[S,k]\) and a corresponding disconnecting cut using the maximum-flow labeling algorithm, update the incumbent when this value is smaller, and add \(k\) to \(S\). Upon termination, \(\alpha^*=\alpha(G)\), and the incumbent is a minimum disconnecting cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a minimum-degree node. Repeatedly select a nonneighbor of the growing set, solve the corresponding set-to-node minimum-cut problem by maximum flow, retain any improved cut, and add the selected node to the set. The final incumbent value and cut are globally minimum.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a connected undirected network}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha^*=\min\left\{\deg(p),\alpha[S_t,k_t]\text{ over all iterations }t\right\}=\alpha(G)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected arc, node, and pairwise connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a connected undirected network, using arcs as the removable edge objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A disconnecting set is a set of arcs whose deletion disconnects the network. The arc connectivity \(\alpha(G)\) is the minimum cardinality of a disconnecting set. Node connectivity is the minimum number of nodes whose deletion disconnects the network. For distinct nodes \(i,j\), \(\alpha[i,j]\) is the minimum number of arcs whose deletion separates \(i\) and \(j\), and \(\alpha(G)=\min_{i\ne j}\alpha[i,j]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc connectivity is the smallest number of arcs whose removal disconnects a connected undirected network. Node connectivity is defined analogously by deleting nodes. Pairwise arc connectivity is the fewest arcs needed to separate two distinct nodes, and global arc connectivity is the minimum pairwise value.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(G)=\min\{|D|:D\subseteq A,\ G-D\text{ is disconnected}\}=\min_{i,j\in N,\ i\ne j}\alpha[i,j]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bound involving \(m\) uses the source's arc-count convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct nodes \(i,j\), \(\alpha[i,j]=\alpha[j,i]\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(u,v\in V\) be distinct. Define the local edge-connectivity \(\lambda_G(u,v)\) as the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths. If \(u\) and \(v\) are nonadjacent, define the local vertex-connectivity \(\kappa_G(u,v)\) as the maximum number of pairwise internally vertex-disjoint \(u\)-\(v\) paths. Then \(\lambda_G(u,v)\) equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are disconnected in \(G-F\). When \(u\) and \(v\) are nonadjacent, \(\kappa_G(u,v)\) equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(S\subseteq V\setminus\{u,v\}\) such that \(u\) and \(v\) are disconnected in \(G-S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two distinct vertices of a finite undirected graph, the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths equals the minimum number of edges whose deletion separates them. If the vertices are nonadjacent, the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths equals the minimum number of other vertices whose deletion separates them.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected global edge-connectivity, expressed uniformly over all nontrivial cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph with \(|V|\ge 2\). For \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta_G(S)\) be the set of edges having exactly one endpoint in \(S\). The global edge-connectivity of \(G\) is
\[
\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}|\delta_G(S)|.
\]
For an integer \(k\ge 1\), the graph is globally \(k\)-edge-connected precisely when \(\lambda(G)\ge k\), equivalently when deleting any set of fewer than \(k\) edges leaves \(G\) connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global edge-connectivity is the smallest size of a nontrivial edge cut; it is at least k exactly when fewer than k edge deletions cannot disconnect the graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is globally \(k\)-edge-connected if and only if \(\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}|\delta_G(S)|\ge k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rooted Connectivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected rooted edge-connectivity from one distinguished vertex to every other vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected multigraph, let \(r\in V\), and let \(k\ge 1\). The rooted graph \((G,r)\) is rooted \(k\)-edge-connected if
\[
|\delta_G(S)|\ge k\qquad\text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(v\in V\setminus\{r\}\), there exist at least \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint paths joining \(r\) to \(v\). Thus every vertex remains reachable from the root after deletion of fewer than \(k\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted graph is k-edge-connected when every cut separating the root from any vertex has at least k edges, equivalently when k edge-disjoint root-to-vertex paths exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G,r)\) is rooted \(k\)-edge-connected if and only if every \(r\)-to-\(v\) edge cut has size at least \(k\).

notation.meaning: Edges with exactly one endpoint in S.

Then \(D\) is rooted \((k,\ell)\)-hybrid-connected if and only if, for every integer \(j\) with \(0\le j\le k-1\) and every \(X\subseteq V\setminus\{r_0\}\) with \(|X|=j\), the digraph \(D-X\) is rooted \(\ell(k-j)\)-edge-connected with root \(r_0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Connectivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard weak, unilateral, and strong connectivity classes for finite directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. It is weakly connected when the undirected graph obtained by forgetting arc orientations is connected. It is unilaterally connected when, for every distinct \(u,v\in V\), either a directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) path or a directed \(v\)-to-\(u\) path exists. It is strongly connected when both such directed paths exist for every ordered pair. Consequently,
\[
\text{strong connectivity}\Longrightarrow\text{unilateral connectivity}\Longrightarrow\text{weak connectivity}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed graphs admit nested weak, unilateral, and strong connectivity regimes according to whether reachability exists after ignoring orientation, in one direction, or in both directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every strongly connected digraph is unilaterally connected, and every unilaterally connected digraph is weakly connected.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected bipartite graphs and their odd-cycle characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is bipartite if there are disjoint sets \(X,Y\subseteq V\) such that \(V=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}Y\) and every edge has one endpoint in \(X\) and the other in \(Y\). Equivalently, there is a map \(c:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(uv\in E\). A finite undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is bipartite when its vertices split into two classes and every edge crosses between them; equivalently, the graph has no odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is bipartite if and only if \(G\) contains no odd cycle.

notation.meaning: Disjoint union of the two vertex classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bipartite graphs, records their even-circuit characterization, and defines complete bipartite graphs, stars, and claws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, the following are equivalent: $\chi(G)\le 2$; there is a partition $V=U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W$ such that every edge has one endpoint in $U$ and the other in $W$; and every circuit of $G$ has even length. The sets $U$ and $W$ are called colour classes and need not be unique. A complete bipartite graph is a simple graph whose vertex set has such a partition and whose edges are exactly the pairs $\{u,w\}$ with $u\in U$ and $w\in W$. If $|U|=m$ and $|W|=n$, it is denoted $K_{m,n}$. The graphs $K_{1,n}$ are stars and, when $n\ge 3$, are also called claws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is bipartite exactly when its vertices can be partitioned into two color classes so that every edge joins the classes; equivalently, every circuit has even length. The complete bipartite graph with class sizes m and n is denoted K_m,n. The graphs K_1,n are stars and, for n at least 3, are also called claws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is bipartite}\iff \chi(G)\le 2\iff \text{every circuit of }G\text{ has even length}

knowledge_statements.title: Eulerian Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connected finite undirected multigraphs characterized by Euler tours and even degrees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) with at least one edge is Eulerian if it has a closed trail containing every edge exactly once. Such a trail is an Euler tour. The graph \(G\) is Eulerian if and only if all vertices incident with edges belong to one connected component and
\[
\deg_G(v)\equiv 0\pmod 2
\]
for every \(v\in V\). Loops contribute two to the degree, so the characterization also applies to multigraphs with loops.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An Eulerian graph has a closed trail using every edge once; this occurs exactly when its nonisolated part is connected and every vertex has even degree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected multigraph with at least one edge.
Each loop contributes two to its incident vertex's degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has an Euler tour if and only if its nonisolated vertices are connected and every vertex has even degree.

notation.meaning: Degree of v in G, counting each loop twice.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The graph need not be connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An orientation \(D=(V,A)\) of an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) is Eulerian if \(\deg_A^{\mathrm{in}}(v)=\deg_A^{\mathrm{out}}(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). The graph \(G\) has an Eulerian orientation if and only if \(\deg_G(v)\) is even for every \(v\in V\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is Eulerian}\iff \forall v\in V,\ \deg_A^{\mathrm{in}}(v)=\deg_A^{\mathrm{out}}(v),\qquad G\text{ has an Eulerian orientation}\iff \forall v\in V,\ \deg_G(v)\text{ is even.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the alternate convention under which each weak component may be treated as Eulerian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph $D=(V,A)$, a Hamiltonian circuit is a directed circuit $C$ with $V(C)=V$, and a Hamiltonian path is a directed path $P$ with $V(P)=V$; $D$ is Hamiltonian iff it has a Hamiltonian circuit. A directed walk is Eulerian if it traverses every arc of $D$ exactly once, and $D$ is Eulerian if it has a closed Eulerian directed walk. Moreover, $D$ is Eulerian iff it is weakly connected and $\deg^{\mathrm{in}}(v)=\deg^{\mathrm{out}}(v)$ for every $v\in V$. An Eulerian orientation of an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ is an orientation satisfying $\deg_A^{\mathrm{in}}(v)=\deg_A^{\mathrm{out}}(v)$ for every $v\in V$, and such an orientation exists iff every vertex of $G$ has even degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hamiltonian circuit or path visits every vertex of a digraph. An Eulerian directed walk uses every arc exactly once, and a digraph is Eulerian when such a walk is closed. A digraph is Eulerian exactly when it is weakly connected and every vertex has equal indegree and outdegree. An undirected graph has a balanced Eulerian orientation exactly when all its vertex degrees are even.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an undirected graph when Eulerian orientations are considered}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ is Eulerian}\iff D\text{ is weakly connected and }\deg^{\mathrm{in}}(v)=\deg^{\mathrm{out}}(v)\ \forall v;\qquad G\text{ has an Eulerian orientation}\iff \deg_G(v)\text{ is even }\forall v.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph with \(n\ge 3\) vertices, no loops, and no multiple edges. Number its vertices so that \(d_1\le d_2\le\cdots\le d_n\). If, for every \(k\) with \(1\le k\le n/2\), \(d_k\le k\Rightarrow d_{n-k}\ge n-k\), then \(G\) is Hamiltonian.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut and cycle parity laws linking Eulerian and bipartite graph structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. For every \(S\subseteq V\) and every subgraph \(H\) in which all vertex degrees are even,
\[
|E(H)\cap\delta_G(S)|\equiv 0\pmod 2.
\]
Thus every Eulerian subgraph crosses every cut an even number of times. Dually, a vertex two-coloring exists exactly when every cycle has even length. These two tests expose the cut-side and cycle-side parity constraints underlying Eulerian and bipartite graph regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eulerian subgraphs meet every cut evenly, while bipartite graphs have only even cycles; these are the fundamental cut-side and cycle-side parity tests.
assumptions_latex: Every vertex of \(H\) has even degree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E(H)\cap\delta_G(S)|\) is even for every \(S\subseteq V\), and \(G\) is bipartite exactly when all its cycles are even.

notation.meaning: Cut consisting of edges with exactly one endpoint in S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar embeddings, planar graphs, and faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation of a graph in the plane without crossings and the face decomposition induced by a fixed embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A planar embedding of a graph \(G\) consists of an injective map \(\psi:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}^2\) and, for every edge \(e=\{x,y\}\), a polygonal arc \(J_e\) with endpoints \(\psi(x)\) and \(\psi(y)\), such that \[\bigl(J_e\setminus\{\psi(x),\psi(y)\}\bigr)\cap\left(\{\psi(v):v\in V(G)\}\cup\bigcup_{e'\in E(G)\setminus\{e\}}J_{e'}\right)=\varnothing.\] A graph is planar if it has a planar embedding. For a fixed planar embedding \(\Phi=(\psi,(J_e)_{e\in E(G)})\), its faces are the open connected regions of \[\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\left(\{\psi(v):v\in V(G)\}\cup\bigcup_{e\in E(G)}J_e\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar embedding maps distinct vertices to distinct points and represents edges by polygonal arcs whose interiors meet no embedded vertex or other edge arc. A graph is planar if such an embedding exists. The faces of a fixed embedding are the open connected regions left after removing its vertices and edge arcs from the plane.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is planar}\iff G\text{ has a planar embedding, and the faces of }\Phi\text{ are the open connected regions of its complement.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rectilinear layouts and their existence criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and existence boundary for rectilinear realization of a prescribed plane embedding, together with the associated bend-minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed plane embedding of $G$, a rectilinear layout is a plane embedding having the same boundary circuits and the same external-face boundary circuit, with every edge represented by a polygonal chain of horizontal and vertical segments. Assuming that $G$ is connected, has at least three vertices, and has no cut vertex, such a layout exists if and only if $\Delta(G)\le 4$. The associated optimization problem is to minimize the total number of bends.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectilinear layout preserves the boundary circuits and external-face boundary of a given plane embedding while drawing every edge with horizontal and vertical segments. Under the stated connectivity assumptions, it exists exactly when the graph has maximum degree at most four. The associated problem minimizes the total number of bends.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orientation Parity Representation for Klein-Bottle Graph Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines curve orientation type and gives an edge-parity representation for embedded graph circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A closed curve \(C\) on the Klein bottle is orientation-preserving exactly when traversing \(C\) leaves the meanings of left and right unchanged, equivalently when \(C\) traverses the two cross-caps an even total number of times; it is orientation-reversing exactly when that number is odd. Consequently, for every graph \(G=(V,E)\) embedded in the Klein bottle, there exists \(R\subseteq E\) such that a circuit of \(G\) is orientation-reversing if and only if it traverses edges of \(R\) an odd number of times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed Klein-bottle curve preserves orientation exactly when it crosses the cross-caps an even number of times and reverses orientation exactly when it does so an odd number of times. Thus every embedded graph admits a distinguished edge subset whose traversal parity detects orientation-reversing circuits.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a closed curve on the Klein bottle}
G=(V,E)\text{ is embedded in the Klein bottle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists R\subseteq E\ \forall\text{ circuits }Q\text{ of }G:\ Q\text{ is orientation-reversing}\iff |E(Q)\cap R|\equiv 1\pmod 2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces, Boundaries, and Adjacency in a Planar Embedding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These notions depend on the chosen planar embedding; different embeddings can have different face sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed planar embedding of \(G=(N,A)\), a face is a connected region of the plane separated from the embedded nodes and arcs. The boundary of a face consists of its incident enclosing arcs and is generally represented by a boundary walk. Each arc is incident to at most two faces. Distinct faces \(f\) and \(f'\) are adjacent if and only if their boundaries share an arc; contact only at a node does not make them adjacent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a fixed planar drawing, faces are the connected regions left between the embedded nodes and arcs. Each arc borders at most two faces, and two faces are adjacent only when they share a boundary arc, not merely a node.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ has a fixed planar embedding}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\in A\text{ is incident to at most two faces, and }f\sim f'\iff \partial f\cap\partial f'\text{ contains an arc}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric decomposition exact on matched boundary pairs and on pairs incident with a third distinguished face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) be a bipartite planar graph, and let F_1,F_2,F_3 be three faces of G, with F_1 and F_2 bounded. Then there exist K_{2,3}-metrics \mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k such that \operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\geq\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_j(u,v) for all u,v\in V, with equality if u=s_i and v=t_i for some i, or if both u and v are incident with F_3.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar Embeddings, Plane Graphs, and Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines planar embeddings, planar and plane graphs, and the faces determined by a plane graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A planar embedding of a graph \(G\) represents distinct vertices by distinct points of \(\mathbb R^2\) and each edge by a simple curve joining its ends and meeting no other vertex, with every intersection of two edge-curves being an end of both edges. A graph is planar if it has a planar embedding, and a plane graph is a graph together with a chosen planar embedding. The faces of a plane graph are the equivalence classes of points outside its vertices and edges under connection by a simple curve lying entirely outside the graph. Every plane graph has exactly one unbounded face, called the infinite face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar embedding draws a graph in the plane without edge crossings except at common endpoints. A planar graph admits such an embedding, while a plane graph includes a chosen embedding. Its faces are the curve-connected regions outside the drawing, exactly one of which is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is planar}\iff G\text{ has a planar embedding},\qquad \text{every plane graph has exactly one unbounded face}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph \(G=(V,E)\) is planar if it has an embedding in the plane that maps distinct vertices to distinct points and each edge \(uv\) to a simple curve joining the images of \(u\) and \(v\), with curves for distinct edges disjoint except at common endpoints. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jordan curves, polygonal objects, and connected plane regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of the plane-topological objects used to construct planar embeddings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simple Jordan curve is the image of a continuous injective map \(\varphi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2\), with endpoints \(\varphi(0)\) and \(\varphi(1)\). A closed Jordan curve is the image of a continuous map \(\varphi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2\) such that \(\varphi(0)=\varphi(1)\) and \(\varphi(\tau)\ne\varphi(\tau')\) whenever \(0\le \tau<\tau'<1\). A polygonal arc is a simple Jordan curve that is the union of finitely many line segments, and a polygon is a closed Jordan curve that is the union of finitely many line segments. If \(J\) is a finite union of line segments and \(R=\mathbb{R}^2\setminus J\), the connected regions of \(R\) are the equivalence classes under \(x\sim y\) exactly when \(x\) and \(y\) can be joined by a polygonal arc contained in \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple Jordan curve is the injective continuous image of an interval, while a closed Jordan curve closes its endpoints and is otherwise injective. Polygonal arcs and polygons are the corresponding objects made from finitely many line segments. For the complement of a finite union of segments, connected regions are the classes of points joinable within the complement by polygonal arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\sim y\iff\text{there is a polygonal arc in }\mathbb{R}^2\setminus J\text{ joining }x\text{ and }y.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar embeddings, faces, and Euler's formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Plane-embedding terminology, face incidence, and the Euler relation for connected plane graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An embedding of a graph \(G\) in a topological space \(S\) is a continuous injection of \(|G|\) into \(S\). The graph \(G\) is planar if it embeds in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). For a fixed plane embedding, the components of \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus |G|\) are the faces of \(G\). A vertex or edge is incident with a face when it is contained in the face boundary, and two faces are adjacent when they are incident with a common edge. There is a unique unbounded face, whose boundary is the outer boundary of \(G\). If \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and \(\mathcal F\) is its face collection, then \(|V|+|\mathcal F|=|E|+2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar graph admits an embedding in the plane. A fixed plane embedding determines its faces, incidences, adjacencies, and unique unbounded face. Every connected plane graph satisfies Euler's vertex-edge-face formula.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ has a fixed embedding in }\mathbb{R}^2\text{ for the face terminology}
G=(V,E)\text{ is connected for Euler's formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |V|+|\mathcal F|=|E|+2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence and uniqueness of planar embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions using facial boundary walks, with a conditional facial-edge-set characterization and sphere terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a connected planar graph, and let G_1 and G_2 be planar embeddings of G. The embeddings G_1 and G_2 are equivalent if every walk obtained by traversing the boundary of a face of G_1 can also be obtained by traversing the boundary of a face of G_2. If G is 2-connected and loopless, then G_1 and G_2 are equivalent if and only if every edge set bounding a face of G_1 also bounds a face of G_2. The graph G is uniquely embeddable in the plane if every two planar embeddings of G are equivalent; it is also called uniquely embeddable on the sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two planar embeddings of a connected planar graph are equivalent when every facial boundary walk of the first is also a facial boundary walk of the second. For a 2-connected loopless graph, this is equivalent to preservation of every facial edge set. The graph is uniquely embeddable when every two planar embeddings are equivalent; the same terminology is used for the sphere.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected planar graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}G_1\sim G_2&\iff\text{ every facial boundary walk of }G_1\text{ is facial in }G_2,\\ G\text{ 2-connected and loopless}&\Longrightarrow\bigl(G_1\sim G_2\iff\text{ every facial edge set of }G_1\text{ is facial in }G_2\bigr),\\ G\text{ uniquely embeddable}&\iff\text{ every two planar embeddings of }G\text{ are equivalent.}\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotation-system representation of cellular embeddings of connected graphs in the oriented sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a finite connected graph with dart set \(D\). Let \(\alpha\) be the fixed-point-free involution reversing each dart, and let \(\sigma\) be a permutation whose cycles give the cyclic order of darts incident with each vertex. The pair \((\sigma,\alpha)\) is a combinatorial embedding. Its facial boundary walks are the cycles of \(\sigma\alpha\). It represents a cellular embedding in the oriented sphere precisely when
\[
|V(G)|-|E(G)|+c(\sigma\alpha)=2,
\]
where \(c(\sigma\alpha)\) is the number of facial cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotation system records the cyclic edge order at each vertex. Face tracing and Euler's formula determine when it represents a cellular embedding in the oriented sphere.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) contains the two oppositely oriented darts of every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\sigma,\alpha)\) represents an oriented spherical embedding if and only if \(|V(G)|-|E(G)|+c(\sigma\alpha)=2\).

notation.meaning: Involution pairing the two darts of each edge.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crossing-free topological realizations of finite graphs in a surface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph and let \(\Sigma\) be a surface. A topological embedding \(\varphi\) assigns distinct points of \(\Sigma\) to the vertices and assigns to each edge \(uv\in E\) a simple arc with endpoints \(\varphi(u)\) and \(\varphi(v)\). The interior of every edge arc must avoid all vertex images, and interiors of distinct edge arcs must be disjoint. The connected components of
\[
\Sigma\setminus\varphi(G)
\]
are the faces; the embedding is cellular when every face is homeomorphic to an open disk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological embedding maps vertices to distinct surface points and edges to noncrossing arcs. Its complementary regions are faces, and it is cellular when every face is a disk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi\) is a graph embedding exactly when edge arcs intersect only at images of their common endpoints.

notation.meaning: Topological realization of G in the surface.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar graphs, plane graphs, and geometric duals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines crossing-free embeddings, faces, and geometric duals, including loops, parallel edges, embedding dependence, and directed-dual orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph $G$ is planar if it has a drawing in the plane in which edge curves meet only at common endpoints and pass through no nonincident vertex. A fixed such drawing is a plane graph, and the connected regions of its complement are its faces, including the unbounded exterior face. For a plane graph $G$, its geometric dual $G^*$ has one vertex in each face and, for every primal edge $e$, a dual edge $e^*$ crossing only $e$ and joining the vertices of the two incident faces; $G^*$ may contain loops or parallel edges. The underlying dual graph or multigraph can depend on the chosen plane embedding. For a plane digraph, $e^*$ is oriented by placing its arrowhead at the end that would first meet the arrowhead of $e$ when $e^*$ is rotated clockwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A planar graph admits a crossing-free drawing, while a plane graph is a particular such drawing and has defined faces. Its geometric dual places a vertex in each face and a dual edge across every primal edge; loops and parallel edges may result, and the abstract dual can depend on the embedding. Dual arcs of a plane digraph receive the specified clockwise orientation.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a graph; for the dual construction, a fixed plane embedding of }G\text{ is given.}
\text{For the directed orientation rule, }G\text{ is a plane digraph.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^*\text{ is the geometric dual determined by the chosen plane embedding of }G.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedding Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientation-preserving equivalence for labeled connected graph embeddings in the sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) be embeddings of the same finite connected labeled graph \(G\) in the oriented sphere. They are orientation-preservingly equivalent if an orientation-preserving homeomorphism \(h\) of the sphere satisfies \(h\circ\varphi_1=\varphi_2\) on every vertex and edge of \(G\). This holds if and only if \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) induce the same cyclic order of incident darts at every vertex. Allowing an orientation-reversing homeomorphism simultaneously reverses all cyclic orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two oriented spherical embeddings of a labeled connected graph are equivalent exactly when their cyclic orders agree at every vertex; mirror equivalence reverses all orders simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite connected labeled graph.
\(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) embed \(G\) in the oriented sphere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) are orientation-preservingly equivalent if and only if their vertex rotation systems coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Planar Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric duality for a fixed connected plane graph, including cycle–bond correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a finite connected plane graph. Its geometric dual \(G^*\) has one vertex for each face of \(G\) and, for every edge \(e\in E(G)\), one dual edge \(e^*\) crossing \(e\) and joining the faces incident with its two sides. The correspondence \(e\leftrightarrow e^*\) is a bijection. For every \(F\subseteq E(G)\), \(F\) is the edge set of a cycle minimal under inclusion if and only if
\[
F^*=\{e^*:e\in F\}
\]
is a bond of \(G^*\). Moreover, \((G^*)^*\) is naturally isomorphic to \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a connected plane graph exchanges faces with vertices and exchanges inclusion-minimal cycles with inclusion-minimal cuts under the edge correspondence.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite connected graph with a fixed plane embedding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a cycle of \(G\) if and only if \(F^*\) is a bond of \(G^*\), and \((G^*)^*\cong G\).

notation.meaning: Geometric dual of the fixed plane graph G.
Dual edge corresponding to the primal edge e.
Set of dual edges corresponding to F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual of a Connected Plane Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual construction and basic correspondences for a fixed planar embedding; exact cycle-cut statements require distinguishing bonds from arbitrary cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a connected plane network. Its dual \(G^*=(N^*,A^*)\) has one node \(f^*\) for each face \(f\) of \(G\) and one dual arc for each primal arc. A primal arc incident to distinct faces \(f_1,f_2\) gives a dual arc joining \(f_1^*\) and \(f_2^*\); an arc incident twice to one face gives a dual loop. Thus \(|N^*|=f(G)\), \(|A^*|=|A|\), \(f(G^*)=|N|\), and \((G^*)^*\cong G\) as embedded networks. Under the standard edge correspondence, dual cycles correspond to primal bonds; a general primal cut may correspond to a union of dual cycles rather than one cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar dual places a node in every primal face and assigns one dual arc to every primal arc. Nodes and faces exchange, arc counts agree, and dualizing twice recovers the embedded primal network. Simple cycle correspondence is properly with minimal cuts; arbitrary cuts can yield unions of dual cycles.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is connected and has a fixed planar embedding}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |N^*|=f(G),\quad |A^*|=|A|,\quad f(G^*)=|N|,\quad (G^*)^*\cong G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed planar duality and the circuit–cut correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The directed dual depends on a fixed planar embedding. Weak connectivity is required for the stated double-dual isomorphism, but the extracted circuit–cut equivalence is stated independently of that condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D$ be a planar digraph with a fixed planar embedding. For each arc $a=(u,v)$, orient its dual edge $a^*$ from the face lying to the left of $a$ when traversed from $u$ to $v$ toward the face lying to its right; the resulting digraph is $D^*$. If $D$ is weakly connected, then $D^{**}\cong D^{-1}$. Moreover, a set $C$ of arcs is a directed circuit in $D$ if and only if $\{a^*:a\in C\}$ is an inclusionwise minimal directed cut in $D^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a fixed planar embedding, each dual edge is directed from the left face of its primal arc to the right face. If the digraph is weakly connected, taking this directed dual twice produces the arc-reversed digraph. Directed circuits correspond exactly to inclusionwise minimal directed cuts in the dual.
assumptions_latex: D\text{ is a planar digraph with a fixed planar embedding}
D\text{ is weakly connected for the assertion }D^{**}\cong D^{-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ weakly connected}\implies D^{**}\cong D^{-1};\qquad C\text{ is a directed circuit in }D\iff \{a^*:a\in C\}\text{ is an inclusionwise minimal directed cut in }D^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer cut-cone characterization for planar graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes nonnegative integral combinations of cut incidence vectors by circuit parity and circuit inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a planar graph and let \(p:E\to\mathbb Z_+\). Then \(p\) is a nonnegative integer sum of incidence vectors of cuts of \(G\) if and only if \(p(C)\) is even for every circuit \(C\) of \(G\), and \(p(e)\le p(C\setminus\{e\})\) for every circuit \(C\) of \(G\) and every \(e\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative integer edge vector of a planar graph is an integer sum of cut incidence vectors exactly when every circuit has even total weight and no circuit edge has more weight than the other edges of that circuit combined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\in\operatorname{intcone}\{\chi^D:D\text{ is a cut of }G\}\iff\left[\forall C\text{ circuit},\ p(C)\equiv0\pmod 2\right]\land\left[\forall C\text{ circuit},\ \forall e\in C,\ p(e)\le p(C\setminus\{e\})\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Planar Dual and Standard Dual Embedding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for directed or undirected embedded planar graphs, allowing loops.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a directed or undirected graph, possibly with loops, and let \(\Phi=(\psi,(J_e)_{e\in E(G)})\) be a planar embedding. The planar dual \(G^*\) has the faces of \(\Phi\) as vertices and an edge \(e^*\) for each \(e\in E(G)\), joining the faces adjacent to \(J_e\); if \(J_e\) is adjacent to only one face, then \(e^*\) is a loop. If \(e=(v,w)\) is directed, orient \(e^*=(F_1,F_2)\) so that \(F_1\) is to the right when \(J_e\) is traversed from \(\psi(v)\) to \(\psi(w)\). Moreover, \(G^*\) has a standard planar embedding in which each dual vertex lies in its corresponding face, \(J_{e^*}\) avoids all primal vertices and every \(J_f\) with \(f\ne e\), and \(|J_{e^*}\cap J_e|=1\); if \(e^*\) is a loop, the face bounded by \(J_{e^*}\) contains exactly one endpoint of \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The planar dual of a fixed embedding has one vertex per face and one dual edge per primal edge, joining its incident faces; an edge incident with only one face produces a dual loop. Directed dual edges are oriented with the right-hand face first. The dual admits a standard planar embedding in which corresponding primal and dual edges cross exactly once, no other primal feature is crossed, and each dual loop bounds a face containing exactly one endpoint of its primal edge.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is directed or undirected and may contain loops}
\Phi=(\psi,(J_e)_{e\in E(G)})\text{ is a planar embedding of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^*\text{ is defined by facial incidence, with the stated directed orientation when applicable, and admits the stated standard planar embedding.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the planar dual relative to a fixed crossing-free embedding, including face vertices, the outer face, and primal–dual edge correspondence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abstract Graph Duality and Planarity Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric circuit–minimal-cut definition of abstract duals, its relation to planar duals, and Whitney's existence characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) and \(G'\) be graphs. The graph \(G'\) is an abstract dual of \(G\) if there is a bijection \(\chi:E(G)\to E(G')\) such that, for every \(F\subseteq E(G)\), \(F\) is the edge set of a circuit in \(G\) if and only if \(\chi(F)\) is a minimal cut in \(G'\), and \(F\) is a minimal cut in \(G\) if and only if \(\chi(F)\) is the edge set of a circuit in \(G'\). Every planar dual is an abstract dual, but not every abstract dual is a planar dual. A graph admits an abstract dual if and only if it is planar.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abstract dual is connected to the original graph by an edge bijection that exchanges circuits and minimal cuts in both directions. Every geometric planar dual is an abstract dual, but the converse need not hold. A graph has an abstract dual exactly when it is planar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G'\text{ is an abstract dual of }G\iff\chi\text{ exchanges circuit edge sets and minimal cuts in both directions};\qquad G\text{ admits an abstract dual}\iff G\text{ is planar}.

The graph \(G^*\) is planar, and if \(G\) is connected then \((G^*)^*\cong G\). For every \(C\subseteq E\), \(C\) is a circuit in \(G\) if and only if \(C^*=\{e^*:e\in C\}\) is an inclusionwise minimal nonempty cut in \(G^*\). Moreover, \(C\) is a spanning tree in \(G\) if and only if \(\{e^*:e\in E\setminus C\}\) is a spanning tree in \(G^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a plane graph has one vertex per face and one dual edge per primal edge. It is planar; for connected graphs, dualizing twice recovers the original graph up to isomorphism. Primal circuits correspond to minimal nonempty dual cuts, and complementary dual edges of a primal spanning tree form a dual spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is an embedded planar graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^*\text{ is planar},\quad (G^*)^*\cong G\text{ when }G\text{ is connected},\quad C\text{ is a circuit in }G\iff C^*\text{ is an inclusionwise minimal nonempty cut in }G^*,\quad C\text{ is a spanning tree in }G\iff (E\setminus C)^*\text{ is a spanning tree in }G^*

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed graph $G=(V,A)$ is acyclic if and only if its vertices admit a numbering $v:V\to\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $v(i)<v(j)$ for every arc $(i,j)\in A$. knowledge_statements.title: Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected trees and their standard acyclicity, path, and edge-count characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite undirected graph \(T=(V,E)\) is a tree if it is connected and contains no cycle. For \(|V|\ge 1\), the following conditions are equivalent: \(T\) is a tree; every pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one simple path; \(T\) is connected and \(|E|=|V|-1\); and \(T\) is acyclic and \(|E|=|V|-1\). Consequently, deleting any edge of a tree disconnects it, while adding an edge between two existing vertices creates exactly one cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree is a connected acyclic graph, equivalently a graph with a unique path between each vertex pair or a connected graph with one fewer edge than vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is a tree if and only if it is connected and \(|E|=|V|-1\), equivalently if every vertex pair has a unique simple path.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the root, parent relation, predecessor encoding, and reflexive ancestor-descendant convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rooted tree is a tree \(T\) with a distinguished node \(r\). For each \(i\ne r\), the unique path from \(i\) to \(r\) determines a unique predecessor \(\operatorname{pred}(i)\), the neighbor of \(i\) on that path. Consequently, \(E(T)=\{\{i,\operatorname{pred}(i)\}:i\in V(T)\setminus\{r\}\}\). The descendants of a node include the node itself and all nodes reachable through successive child relations; the node is an ancestor of each of its descendants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rooted tree is a tree with a distinguished root. Every nonroot node has a unique parent, namely its next neighbor on the path to the root, and these parent links encode all tree edges. Descendant and ancestor relations include the node itself.
assumptions_latex: r\in V(T)\text{ is the distinguished root}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i\in V(T)\setminus\{r\}\ \exists!\operatorname{pred}(i),\qquad E(T)=\{\{i,\operatorname{pred}(i)\}:i\ne r\}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) is a forest if the spanning subgraph \((V,F)\) contains no cycle. Equivalently, each connected component of \((V,F)\) is a tree. Consequently, \(|F|=|V|-c((V,F))\). More generally, every \(W\subseteq V\) satisfies \(|F[W]|\leq |W|-1\) when \(W\neq\varnothing\), where \(F[W]\) denotes the edges of \(F\) with both endpoints in \(W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forest is an acyclic spanning subgraph; its components are trees, and its edge count equals its vertex count minus its number of components.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient conditions for covering a partitionable mixed graph by k matching forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E,A)$ be a mixed graph partitionable into $R$ and $S$. Then $E\cup A$ can be covered by $k$ matching forests if and only if (i) $|\delta^{\mathrm{head}}(v)|\le k$ for every $v\in V$, and (ii) $|A[U]|\le k(|U|-1)$ for every nonempty subset $U$ of $R$ or of $S$.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An arc set \(B\subseteq A\) is a spanning out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) if \(\delta_B^-(r)=0\), \(\delta_B^-(v)=1\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{r\}\), and every vertex is reachable from \(r\) in \((V,B)\). These conditions imply \(|B|=|V|-1\), the underlying undirected graph is a tree, and the directed path from \(r\) to each \(v\in V\) is unique. Reversing every arc defines the corresponding in-arborescence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An out-arborescence is a rooted directed spanning tree whose arcs give every nonroot vertex one incoming arc and a unique path from the root.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the outward-orientation convention and records the path and minimal-reachability characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph. An arborescence is a set \(A'\subseteq A\) whose arcs form a spanning tree and enter every vertex at most once. Exactly one vertex \(r\) is not entered; it is the root, and \(A'\) is an \(r\)-arborescence. It has \(|V|-1\) arcs and contains a unique directed \((r,v)\)-path for every \(v\in V\). Equivalently, \(r\)-arborescences are the inclusionwise minimal arc sets containing a directed \((r,v)\)-path for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arborescence is a directed spanning tree with at most one entering arc at each vertex. Its unique vertex with no entering arc is the root. It has one fewer arc than vertices, has a unique directed path from the root to each vertex, and is inclusionwise minimal among arc sets providing all such paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A'\text{ is an }r\text{-arborescence}\iff A'\text{ is inclusionwise minimal among arc sets containing an }(r,v)\text{-dipath for every }v\in V,\quad |A'|=|V|-1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual covering variables for a weighted branching problem in a digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph with arc weights $w$. A pair $(\pi,y)$, where $\pi:V\to\mathbb R_+$ and $y:2^V\to\mathbb R_+$, is a covering if every arc $uv\in A$ satisfies $$w(uv)\le \pi(v)+\sum_{\{Z:\,u,v\in Z\subseteq V\}}y(Z).$$ Its value is $$\sum_{v\in V}\pi(v)+\sum_{Z\subseteq V}(|Z|-1)y(Z).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering for the maximum-weight branching problem assigns nonnegative values to vertices and vertex subsets so that each arc's weight is bounded by the value at its head plus the values of all subsets containing both endpoints. Its value is the sum of vertex values plus each subset value multiplied by one less than the subset's cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\pi,y)\text{ is a covering}\iff \forall uv\in A,\quad w(uv)\le\pi(v)+\sum_{Z:\,u,v\in Z\subseteq V}y(Z),\qquad \operatorname{val}(\pi,y)=\sum_{v\in V}\pi(v)+\sum_{Z\subseteq V}(|Z|-1)y(Z)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut characterization for packing reachability-spanning arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An existence characterization for edge-disjoint arborescences rooted at a possibly non-distinct family of vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed graph and let \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\in V\), with repetitions allowed. For each \(i\), let \(S_i\) be the set of vertices reachable from \(r_i\). There exist pairwise edge-disjoint \(r_i\)-arborescences \(A_i\) spanning \(S_i\), for \(i=1,\ldots,k\), if and only if, for every \(Z\subseteq V\), \[\varrho_D(Z)\ge p_1(Z),\] where \(p_1(Z)=\left|\{i: S_i\cap Z\ne\varnothing\text{ and }r_i\notin Z\}\right|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a directed graph and a possibly repeated list of roots, let Si contain all vertices reachable from root ri. Pairwise edge-disjoint ri-arborescences spanning their respective Si exist exactly when every vertex subset Z has at least as many entering edges as there are reachability sets Si that meet Z while their roots lie outside Z.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\exists\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint }r_i\text{-arborescences }A_i\text{ spanning }S_i\ (i=1,\ldots,k)\right]\iff\left[\forall Z\subseteq V,\ \varrho_D(Z)\ge p_1(Z)\right]

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected vertex-spanning forests and trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spanning forest of \(G\) is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) for which \((V,F)\) is acyclic, so isolated vertices remain represented. It is component-spanning if, for every connected component \(W\) of \(G\), the graph \((W,F[W])\) is connected. Equivalently, a component-spanning forest is an inclusion-maximal forest in \(G\). If \(G\) is connected, such an \(F\) is a spanning tree; if \(G\) is not connected, no spanning tree exists, but component-spanning forests do.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning forest includes every vertex; a maximal one spans each original component by a tree and becomes a spanning tree when the graph is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A component-spanning forest has exactly \(|V|-c(G)\) edges; when \(G\) is connected, it is a spanning tree.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matching in \(G\) is a set \(M\subseteq E\) such that no two distinct edges of \(M\) share an endpoint, equivalently \(|M\cap\delta(v)|\leq 1\) for every \(v\in V\). A vertex in \(V(M)\) is matched, and every other vertex is exposed. The matching is perfect if \(V(M)=V\), and it is maximum if its cardinality is largest among all matchings of \(G\). A maximal matching need only be inclusion-maximal and need not be maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is a set of pairwise endpoint-disjoint edges. It is perfect when every vertex is matched and maximum when its cardinality is largest.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise Binding-Number Lower Bound for Matching Number
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A three-regime lower bound on maximum matching cardinality for binding number at most four thirds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a graph with \(p\) vertices and \(\operatorname{bind}(G)=c\). Then
\[
\nu(G)\ge
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{pc}{c+1},&0\le c\le \dfrac12,\\
\dfrac p3,&\dfrac12\le c\le 1,\\
\dfrac{p(3c-2)}{3c}-\dfrac{2(c-1)}c,&1\le c\le \dfrac43.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a p-vertex graph with binding number c, the matching number is at least pc/(c+1) when c is between 0 and 1/2, at least p/3 when c is between 1/2 and 1, and at least p(3c-2)/(3c)-2(c-1)/c when c is between 1 and 4/3.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nu(G)\ge \begin{cases}\frac{pc}{c+1},&0\le c\le \frac12,\\ \frac p3,&\frac12\le c\le 1,\\ \frac{p(3c-2)}{3c}-\frac{2(c-1)}c,&1\le c\le \frac43.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected integral degree-constrained spanning factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An edge set \(F\subseteq E\) is a \((g,f)\)-factor of \(G\) if \(g(v)\leq\deg_F(v)\leq f(v)\) for every \(v\in V\). When \(g=f=b\), it is a \(b\)-factor; when \(b(v)=k\) for all vertices, it is a \(k\)-factor. Thus a perfect matching is a \(1\)-factor, while an ordinary matching is a spanning subgraph satisfying only the upper bounds \(\deg_F(v)\leq 1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-constrained factor is a spanning subgraph whose degree at each vertex lies between prescribed integral lower and upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A one-to-one assignment is a bijection \(\pi:I\to J\). It corresponds to the perfect matching \(M_\pi=\{(i,\pi(i)):i\in I\}\) of \(K_{I,J}\), and to the binary matrix \(x\) defined by \(x_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(j=\pi(i)\). Conversely, every binary matrix satisfying \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\) for all \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\) for all \(j\in J\) determines a unique assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced assignment is equivalently a bijection, a perfect bipartite matching, or a binary matrix with one entry in every row and column.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clique-inequality relaxation of the stable-set polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong fractional stable sets and records the relaxation's integer-hull, bound, and antiblocking properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \[P(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:x_v\ge0\ (v\in V),\ x(C)\le1\text{ for every clique }C\}.\] The integer points of \(P(G)\) are exactly the incidence vectors of stable sets, so \(P_{\mathrm{stable}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}(P(G)\cap\mathbb Z^V)\). Vectors in \(P(G)\) are strong fractional stable sets, and \(\alpha^{**}(G)=\max\{x(V):x\in P(G)\}\) satisfies \(\alpha(G)\le\alpha^{**}(G)\le\alpha^*(G)\). Moreover, \(P(G)=A(P_{\mathrm{clique}}(G))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The clique-inequality relaxation consists of nonnegative vertex vectors whose total on every clique is at most one. Its integer points are precisely stable-set incidence vectors, so the stable-set polytope is its integer hull. Its optimum, the strong fractional stability number, lies between the stability number and the ordinary fractional stability number. The relaxation is the antiblocking polyhedron of the clique polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{stable}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}(P(G)\cap\mathbb Z^V),\qquad \alpha(G)\le\alpha^{**}(G)\le\alpha^*(G),\qquad P(G)=A(P_{\mathrm{clique}}(G)).

The clique number is \(\omega(G)=\max\{|K|:K\subseteq V,\ \binom{K}{2}\subseteq E\}\). A maximum clique attains \(\omega(G)\); a maximal clique is merely inclusion-maximal. The empty set and every singleton are cliques under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clique is a vertex subset whose distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. Maximum and maximal cliques need not coincide.

A connected graph \(C\) on \(n\) vertices is a \emph{clique tree} if its maximal cliques can be partitioned into handles \(H_1,\ldots,H_r\) and teeth \(T_1,\ldots,T_s\) such that: (i) \(T_i\cap T_j=\varnothing\) for \(i
e j\); (ii) \(H_i\cap H_j=\varnothing\) for \(i
e j\); (iii) every tooth \(T_j\) has \(2\le |T_j|\le n-2\) and contains a vertex belonging to no handle; (iv) every handle intersects an odd number, at least three, of the teeth; and (v) whenever \(H_i\cap T_j
e\varnothing\), the graph \(C-(H_i\cap T_j)\) is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clique tree is a connected n-vertex graph whose maximal cliques split into pairwise disjoint handles and pairwise disjoint teeth. Each tooth has between 2 and n−2 vertices and includes a vertex in no handle; each handle meets an odd number of teeth, at least three; and deleting any nonempty handle–tooth intersection disconnects the graph.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph without loops.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper \(k\)-coloring exists exactly when \(V\) can be partitioned into at most \(k\) stable sets.

notation.meaning: A vertex-coloring map using colors 1 through k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper vertex colorings of finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper \(k\)-coloring of \(G\) is a map \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) satisfying \(c(u)\neq c(v)\) for every edge \(uv\in E\). Each color class \(c^{-1}(i)\) is therefore a stable set, and the nonempty color classes partition \(V\). Conversely, any partition of \(V\) into at most \(k\) stable sets defines a proper \(k\)-coloring. The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the least \(k\) for which such a coloring exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper coloring assigns different colors to adjacent vertices, equivalently partitioning the vertex set into stable color classes. The chromatic number is the minimum colors needed.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Colorings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalence between proper colorings and partitions into stable sets is correct and fits the container, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Complementation Relations
children.top_down_role: Correspondences among stable sets, cliques, and colorings under graph complementation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\), \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\), and \(\chi(G)=\theta(\overline G)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of cliques partitioning V in H.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement dualities for stable sets, cliques, and colorings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq V\), \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if \(S\) is a clique in \(\overline G\). Hence \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\) and \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\). Moreover, a proper coloring of \(G\) partitions \(V\) into stable sets of \(G\), equivalently into cliques of \(\overline G\). Therefore \(\chi(G)=\theta(\overline G)\), where \(\theta(H)\) is the minimum number of cliques in a vertex partition of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph complementation exchanges stable sets with cliques and turns proper colorings into clique partitions of the complement.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementation Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complementation identities are correct with \(\theta\) explicitly defined as a clique-partition number, and duality is an appropriate content kind. No supporting source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set cover of \(U\) by \(\mathcal A\) is a subfamily \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal A\) such that \(\bigcup_{A\in\mathcal C}A=U\). With incidence matrix \(M_{uA}=1\) when \(u\in A\) and \(M_{uA}=0\) otherwise, covers correspond exactly to binary vectors \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal A}\) satisfying \(Mx\geq\mathbf 1\). A disjoint packing is a subfamily \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal F\) such that \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) for all distinct \(A,B\in\mathcal P\). Let \mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n) and \mathcal B=(B_1,\ldots,B_m) be families of sets. Let I',I''\subseteq[n] and J',J''\subseteq[m]. knowledge_statements.scope_note: A complete linear description of the convex hull of complete systems of distinct representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) be a family of subsets of \(S\), and let \(A_I:=\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\). The transversal polytope is determined by
\[
0\le x_s\le1\quad(s\in S),\qquad x(A_I)\ge |I|\quad(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}),\qquad x(S)=n,

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Write A_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i and B_J=\bigcup_{j\in J}B_j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Min–Max Formula for Minimum-Weight Transversals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a function \(y:S\to\mathbb Z_+\), write \(y(S)=\sum_{s\in S}y(s)\); transversal weight is the sum of selected-element weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) be a family of subsets of \(S\) having a transversal, and let \(w:S\to\mathbb Z\). Then
\[\min_{T\text{ transversal of }\mathcal A}\sum_{s\in T}w(s)=\max_{y:S\to\mathbb Z_+}\left[y(S)+\sum_{i=1}^n\min_{s\in A_i}\bigl(w(s)-y(s)\bigr)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a set family admitting a system of distinct representatives and integer element weights, the minimum transversal weight equals the stated maximum over nonnegative integer functions on the ground set.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) is a family of subsets of a set \(S\).
For the maximization, \(y:S\to\mathbb Z_+\) and \(y(S):=\sum_{s\in S}y(s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \min_{T\text{ transversal}}\sum_{s\in T}w(s)=\max_{y:S\to\mathbb Z_+}\left(y(S)+\sum_{i=1}^n\min_{s\in A_i}(w(s)-y(s))\right).\)
