knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\text{ is a vertex of }P\iff \{v\}\text{ is a face of }P\iff v\text{ is an extreme point of }P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies vertices with zero-dimensional faces and extreme points of a convex polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex polyhedron. A point \(v\in P\) is a vertex of \(P\) when the singleton \(\{v\}\) is a face of \(P\). Equivalently, \(v\) is an extreme point: whenever \(x,y\in P\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and \(v=\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\), one has \(x=y=v\). Thus a vertex is precisely a zero-dimensional nonempty face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is a zero-dimensional face, equivalently a point that is not a nontrivial convex combination of two points of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertices

source_witnesses.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63

children.title: Face Lattices
children.top_down_role: Global containment organization of polyhedral faces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\) is a bounded lattice with \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\) and \(F\vee G=\bigcap\{H\in\mathcal{F}(P):F\cup G\subseteq H\}\).

notation.meaning: set of all faces of \(P\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\)
meet and join in the inclusion order

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the empty face and the whole polyhedron as the least and greatest lattice elements.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) contain every face of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\), ordered by inclusion. Then \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\) is a bounded lattice. For faces \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), their meet is \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), and their join is the smallest face containing both, given by \(F\vee G=\bigcap\{H\in\mathcal{F}(P):F\cup G\subseteq H\}\). The least element is \(\varnothing\), and the greatest element is \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces ordered by inclusion form a bounded lattice: intersection is meet, and the smallest face containing two faces is their join.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Lattices

source_witnesses.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces of a Face Are Exactly the Contained Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral closure under taking faces and inheritance of the face-containment structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron and let \(F\) be a face of \(P\). Then \(F\) is a polyhedron. Moreover, for every \(F'\subseteq F\), \[F'\text{ is a face of }P\iff F'\text{ is a face of }F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a polyhedron is itself a polyhedron. A subset of that face is a face of the original polyhedron exactly when it is a face of the face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a polyhedron},\qquad \bigl(F'\text{ is a face of }P\bigr)\iff\bigl(F'\text{ is a face of }F\bigr).

children.title: Face Incidence Structure
children.top_down_role: Local incidence relationships among faces of different dimensions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is incident with }G\iff F\subseteq G\text{ or }G\subseteq F\), with cover incidence characterized by no intermediate face.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses incidence as comparability under face inclusion and distinguishes immediate incidence by the cover relation.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For faces \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), the faces are incident when they are comparable in the face order, that is, when \(F\subseteq G\) or \(G\subseteq F\). If \(F\subsetneq G\), then \(F\) is immediately incident with \(G\) when no face \(H\in\mathcal{F}(P)\) satisfies \(F\subsetneq H\subsetneq G\). The incidence structure is therefore the inclusion poset of faces; its Hasse diagram records precisely these immediate incidences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two faces are incident when one contains the other. Immediate incidence means that no third face lies strictly between them in the inclusion order.
knowledge_statements.title: Face Incidence Structure

children.title: Minimal Polyhedral Description Criteria
children.top_down_role: Descriptional issues governing full dimension, implied constraints, and irredundancy.

children.title: Polyhedral Dimension
children.top_down_role: Affine dimensional structure of polyhedra and their descriptions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(P)=\dim(\operatorname{aff}(P))=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-P)\).

notation.meaning: set of pairwise differences of points of \(P\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines intrinsic dimension, independent of the dimension of the chosen ambient representation.

source_refs.locator: Hulls, Independence, Dimension p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its dimension is the dimension of its affine hull: \(\dim(P):=\dim(\operatorname{aff}(P))\). Equivalently, for any \(x_0\in P\), one has \(\dim(P)=\dim\operatorname{span}\{x-x_0:x\in P\}=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-P)\). The polyhedron is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) exactly when \(\dim(P)=n\), equivalently when \(\operatorname{aff}(P)=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron's dimension is the dimension of its affine hull, equivalently the linear span of all differences between its points.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Dimension

source_witnesses.locator: Hulls, Independence, Dimension p. 3

children.title: Redundant Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraints implied by the remainder of a linear description.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for }i\in I\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\text{ is redundant}\iff P_{-k}\subseteq\{x:a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\}\iff P_{-k}=P\).

notation.meaning: polyhedron defined by the full inequality system

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy is defined relative to a particular finite inequality description, not solely to the represented polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\), and fix \(k\in I\). Define \(P_{-k}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\setminus\{k\}\}\). The inequality \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\) is redundant in this description exactly when deleting it does not enlarge the feasible set, equivalently when \(P_{-k}=P\), or when every \(x\in P_{-k}\) already satisfies \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is redundant when removing it leaves the represented feasible set unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Constraints

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

children.title: Irredundant Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Linear descriptions without removable constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for }i\in I\}\) is a finite inequality description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\leq b\text{ is irredundant}\iff \forall k\in I\ \exists x^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ a_i^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}\leq b_i\ (i\neq k),\ a_k^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}>b_k\).

notation.meaning: witness that inequality \(k\) cannot be deleted

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes irredundancy by a deletion witness for every inequality in a finite system.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite description \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\) is irredundant when none of its inequalities is redundant. Equivalently, for every \(k\in I\), there exists a deletion witness \(x^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}\leq b_i\) for every \(i\in I\setminus\{k\}\), while \(a_k^{\mathsf T}x^{(k)}>b_k\). Hence deleting any single inequality strictly enlarges the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality description is irredundant exactly when each inequality has a point satisfying all the others but violating that inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Irredundant Descriptions

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144

children.title: Description Minimality Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural standards for comparing the economy of linear descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\) is a finite inequality description with \(a_i\neq 0\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\leq b\text{ is irredundant}\iff \forall i\in I,\ F_i=\{x\in P:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\text{ is a facet and distinct indices define distinct facets}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to full-dimensional polyhedra; lower-dimensional descriptions additionally require equations for the affine hull.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3. Polyhedral Descriptions p. 144
5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and full-dimensional, and let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\), where \(I\) is finite and \(a_i\neq 0\) for every \(i\in I\). This description is irredundant exactly when every equality set \(F_i=\{x\in P:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\) is a facet of \(P\) and distinct indices define distinct facets. Consequently, after positive rescaling of inequalities is identified, a minimal inequality description contains exactly one supporting inequality for each facet of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional polyhedron, a description is minimal exactly when it contains one essential supporting inequality for each facet and no duplicates.
knowledge_statements.title: Description Minimality Criteria

children.title: Vertex Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Local edge incidence among polyhedral vertices.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron and \(u,v\) are distinct vertices of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\text{ and }v\text{ are adjacent}\iff \operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\text{ is a one-dimensional face of }P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines adjacency through edges, the one-dimensional bounded faces of a polyhedron.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) and \(v\) be distinct vertices of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). The vertices are adjacent when the segment \(\operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\), called an edge. Equivalently, there is a supporting hyperplane of \(P\) whose intersection with \(P\) is exactly \(\operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\). Vertex adjacency is symmetric and supplies the edge relation used in the one-skeleton of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct vertices are adjacent when the segment joining them is an edge, meaning a one-dimensional face of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Adjacency

Distinct vertices $\widehat x,\widehat y\in F_1$ are adjacent if and only if there exists a cost vector $\widehat d$ such that $\widehat x$ is the uniquely optimal vertex and $\widehat y$ is a second-best vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct vertices of the associated LP region are adjacent exactly when some cost vector makes the first vertex uniquely optimal and the second a second-best vertex.

children.title: Polyhedral Skeletons
children.top_down_role: Graphs formed by polyhedral vertices and edges.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)=(V(P),E(P))\), where \(\{u,v\}\in E(P)\iff \operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\text{ is a one-dimensional face of }P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the combinatorial one-skeleton, not the geometric union of embedded vertices and edges.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63
0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The one-skeleton of a polyhedron \(P\) is the undirected graph \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)=(V(P),E(P))\). Its node set \(V(P)\) is the set of vertices of \(P\), and \(\{u,v\}\in E(P)\) exactly when \(u\neq v\) and \(\operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\). Thus the abstract edges of the skeleton correspond bijectively to the bounded one-dimensional faces of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-skeleton is the graph whose nodes are polyhedral vertices and whose edges join precisely the adjacent vertex pairs.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Skeletons

children.title: Graph Diameters
children.top_down_role: Global distance structure within polyhedral skeletons.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph with \(V\neq\varnothing\).
\(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\).
\(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron whose one-skeleton is nonempty and connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diam}(G)=\max_{u,v\in V}d_G(u,v)\); hence \(\operatorname{diam}(P)=\operatorname{diam}(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures unweighted shortest-path length in a finite abstract one-skeleton; it is not Euclidean diameter.

source_refs.locator: 0.2 Graph Theory p. 16

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V\neq\varnothing\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum number of edges in any path joining \(u\) and \(v\). The graph diameter is \(\operatorname{diam}(G):=\max\{d_G(u,v):u,v\in V\}\). For a polyhedron \(P\) whose one-skeleton is nonempty and connected, its combinatorial diameter is \(\operatorname{diam}(P):=\operatorname{diam}(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\), the largest minimum number of edge pivots needed to travel between two vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diameter of a finite connected graph is the greatest shortest-path distance between two nodes; a polyhedron's combinatorial diameter is the diameter of its nonempty connected one-skeleton.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Diameters

children.title: Skeleton Connectivity
children.top_down_role: Connectivity structure of the vertex-edge graph of a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\geq d\), equivalently deletion of fewer than \(d\) vertices leaves the skeleton connected.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States Balinski's theorem for bounded polyhedra; the supplied inventory lacks a reliable exact theorem locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a \(d\)-dimensional polytope with \(d\geq 1\). Then its one-skeleton \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)\) is \(d\)-vertex-connected: for every set \(S\) of fewer than \(d\) vertices, the graph obtained from \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)\) by deleting \(S\) and all incident edges remains connected. Equivalently, the vertex connectivity satisfies \(\kappa(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P))\geq d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balinski's theorem says that the graph of a d-dimensional polytope remains connected after deletion of any fewer than d vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Skeleton Connectivity

children.title: Linear Programming Duality Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Dual representations and alternative systems underlying feasibility and optimality certificates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standard inequality-form LP and its dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The primal and dual formulations together with basic feasible- and optimal-solution terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), the primal LP is \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\}\), with feasible region \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), and its dual is \(\min\{y^Tb:y\ge0,\ y^TA=c^T\}\). A primal-feasible point attaining the maximum is optimal. Moreover, \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\}=-\max\{-c^Tx:Ax\le b\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard inequality-form primal maximizes c-transpose x subject to Ax at most b, while its dual minimizes y-transpose b subject to nonnegative y and y-transpose A equal to c-transpose. A feasible primal point satisfies the constraints and is optimal if it attains the maximum. Minimization can be converted to maximization by negating the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{P}=\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\},\qquad \mathrm{D}=\min\{y^Tb:y\ge0,\ y^TA=c^T\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Totally unimodular dual-support criterion for box-TDI
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient box-TDI criterion based on the support of an optimal dual solution for every finite linear objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Suppose that for every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), whenever \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\}\) is finite, it has an optimal dual solution \(y\in\mathbb R_+^m\) such that the rows \(A_i\) with \(y_i>0\) form a totally unimodular submatrix of \(A\). Then \(Ax\le b\) is box-TDI.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every finite linear optimization problem over the system has an optimal nonnegative dual solution whose positively supported constraint rows form a totally unimodular submatrix, then the system is box-TDI.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear programs and their solution regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines inequality-form linear programming, feasible and optimal solutions, and the feasible-bounded, infeasible, and unbounded regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the linear program \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\}\) seeks an \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) maximizing \(c^\top x\). A vector \(x\) is feasible if \(Ax\le b\), and it is optimal if it is feasible and attains the maximum. Writing \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), the program is infeasible when \(P=\varnothing\), and unbounded when \(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\,\exists x\in P\) such that \(c^\top x>\alpha\). If it is neither infeasible nor unbounded, it has an optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality-form linear program maximizes a linear objective over the vectors satisfying its linear inequalities. Such a vector is feasible, and a feasible vector attaining the maximum is optimal. The program is infeasible if its feasible set is empty and unbounded if feasible objective values exceed every real threshold. Otherwise, an optimal solution exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\varnothing\;\lor\;\bigl(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\,\exists x\in P:c^\top x>\alpha\bigr)\;\lor\;\bigl(\exists z\in P:c^\top z=\max_{x\in P}c^\top x\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the canonical primal linear program is
\[
\sup\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}.
\]
Its feasible region is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). The value is \(p^*=\sup_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), with \(p^*=-\infty\) when \(P=\varnothing\) and \(p^*=+\infty\) when the objective is unbounded above on \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical primal LP maximizes a linear objective over nonnegative variables satisfying componentwise upper-bound constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian dual of bounded minimum-cost flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the arcwise representation and common-price-shift invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimum-cost flow problem with arc costs a_{ij}, bounds b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}, node supplies s_i, and conservation multipliers p_i, define L(x,p)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}(a_{ij}+p_j-p_i)x_{ij}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal N}s_ip_i. Then q(p)=\min_{b\le x\le c}L(x,p)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}q_{ij}(p_i-p_j)+\sum_i s_ip_i, where q_{ij}=(a_{ij}+p_j-p_i)b_{ij} if p_i\le a_{ij}+p_j and q_{ij}=(a_{ij}+p_j-p_i)c_{ij} otherwise. The dual problem is \max_{p\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal N}}q(p). The function q is piecewise linear; if \sum_i s_i=0, then q(p+\alpha\mathbf 1)=q(p) for every \alpha\in\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing flow conservation with unrestricted node prices gives an arc-separable Lagrangian dual. Each arc is minimized at a capacity bound according to its reduced-cost sign. The dual maximizes the resulting piecewise-linear function, which is invariant under a common price shift when total supply is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(p)=\min_{b\le x\le c}L(x,p)\text{ is arc-separable and piecewise linear; the dual is }\max_p q(p);\ q(p+\alpha\mathbf1)=q(p)\text{ if }\sum_i s_i=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian Dual of a Separable Convex-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the node-price dual and records its arcwise decomposition, concavity, effective domain, and compact-domain attainment condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal problem minimizing \(\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}f_{ij}(x_{ij})\) subject to flow conservation and \(x_{ij}\in X_{ij}\), introduce unrestricted node prices \(p\). Then
\[L(x,p)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}\bigl(f_{ij}(x_{ij})-(p_i-p_j)x_{ij}\bigr)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal N}s_ip_i,\]
and
\[q(p)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,p)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}q_{ij}(p_i-p_j)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal N}s_ip_i,\quad q_{ij}(t)=\inf_{x_{ij}\in X_{ij}}\{f_{ij}(x_{ij})-tx_{ij}\}.\]
The dual problem is \(\sup_{p\in\mathbb R^{\mathcal N}}q(p)\), equivalently \(\sup_{p\in Q}q(p)\) with \(Q=\{p:q(p)>-\infty\}\). Each \(q_{ij}\) is concave. If every \(X_{ij}\) is compact and every \(f_{ij}\) is closed, each arc infimum is attained and \(q\) is real-valued everywhere; without compactness, \(q_{ij}\) may equal \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node prices yield an unrestricted Lagrangian dual whose dual cost separates by arcs. Each arc dual cost is concave, and dual feasibility means that the total dual cost is greater than minus infinity. Compact arc domains with closed costs guarantee attainment and finite arc dual values; without compactness, minus-infinite values may occur.
assumptions_latex: \text{The primal constraints include nodewise flow conservation.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(p)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}q_{ij}(p_i-p_j)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal N}s_ip_i,\quad \sup_p q(p)=\sup_{p\in Q}q(p),\quad Q=\{p:q(p)>-\infty\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimum Dual Solutions for Oracle-Described Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of general, basic, oracle-inequality, and standard optimum dual solutions when no fixed explicit constraint system determines the dual variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P\neq\varnothing$ be a polyhedron given by a strong separation oracle, and suppose $v=\max\{c^Tx:x\in P\}$ exists. An optimum dual solution is a finite collection of valid inequalities $a_i^Tx\leq\alpha_i$ for $P$ and multipliers $\lambda_i>0$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i a_i=c$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\alpha_i=v$. It is basic if $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ are linearly independent. It is an optimum dual solution with oracle inequalities if the selected normals are outputs of the strong separation oracle, and an optimum standard dual solution if the selected inequalities belong to a standard representation of $P$, with each equation treated as two inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty oracle-described polyhedron whose objective maximum exists, an optimum dual solution is a finite positive combination of valid inequalities whose combined normal equals the objective and whose combined right-hand side equals the optimum value. It is basic when the selected normals are linearly independent; oracle and standard variants restrict which valid inequalities may be selected.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a nonempty polyhedron given by a strong separation oracle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i a_i=c,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\alpha_i=v;\qquad \text{basic}\iff a_1,\ldots,a_k\text{ are linearly independent, with oracle and standard variants determined by the permitted inequalities.}

knowledge_statements.title: Standard-Form Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-corresponding reductions among equality, inequality, sign-restricted, and free-variable finite-dimensional LP forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A free variable \(x_j\in\mathbb{R}\) may be replaced by \(x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-\), where \(x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0\). An inequality \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) may be replaced by \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+s_i=b_i\), where \(s_i\ge0\); an inequality in the opposite direction may first be multiplied by \(-1\). An equality may be replaced by the two corresponding opposite inequalities. These transformations preserve feasibility and objective values under the natural correspondence of solutions. A minimization problem with objective \(f(x)\) may be represented as a maximization problem with objective \(-f(x)\); the feasible set is unchanged and the objective values are negated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free variables, inequalities, and equalities can be converted by variable splitting, slack variables, sign reversal, and paired inequalities while preserving corresponding objective values. Changing minimization to maximization negates, rather than preserves, objective values.
assumptions_latex: All variables and constraints are finite-dimensional and real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constraint and variable transformations preserve corresponding feasible objective values, while replacing minimization of \(f\) by maximization of \(-f\) negates those values.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative parts replacing a free variable.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the canonical pair, each primal row \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) determines a nonnegative dual variable \(y_i\), while each nonnegative primal variable \(x_j\) determines the dual inequality \((A^{\mathsf T}y)_j\ge c_j\). Thus transposition exchanges rows and columns, maximization with upper-bound constraints becomes minimization with lower-bound constraints, and primal and dual slacks are \(b-Ax\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y-c\). Applying the same correspondence to the dual recovers the primal after canonical sign identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualization exchanges constraints and variables, transposes the coefficient matrix, reverses optimization direction and inequalities, and is involutive in canonical form.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Duality for Separable Convex-Cost Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States equality of extended primal and dual values when either side is feasible, including the infeasibility consequences of unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the primal separable convex-cost flow problem is feasible or its dual is feasible, then their optimal values are equal in the extended-real sense. In particular, if the primal is feasible and unbounded below, then the dual is infeasible and both values equal \(-\infty\); if the dual is feasible and unbounded above, then the primal is infeasible and both values equal \(+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural correspondence between finite-dimensional primal and dual linear programs under consistent sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a linear-programming primal–dual pair, each primal constraint corresponds to a dual variable and each primal variable corresponds to a dual constraint. A primal inequality constraint corresponds to a sign-restricted dual variable, while a primal equality corresponds to an unrestricted dual variable; analogously, the sign restriction on a primal variable determines whether its dual constraint is an inequality or equality. The coefficient matrices are transposes up to the adopted sign convention, the roles of \(b\) and \(c\) are exchanged, and dualization is reflexive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal constraints correspond to dual variables, and primal variables correspond to dual constraints. Equality and sign restrictions determine the corresponding unrestricted variables and equality constraints. The coefficient matrix is transposed, the right-hand-side and objective vectors exchange roles, and the dual of the dual is the primal.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual use mutually consistent objective, inequality, and sign conventions
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dual}(\operatorname{dual}(P))=P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the greedy primal vector and associated dual vector constructed for the polymatroid linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the polymatroid primal program $\max\{cx:x\ge0,\ \widetilde x(Z)\le b(Z)\ \forall Z\subseteq S\}$ and its dual $\min\{\sum_{Z\subseteq S}y(Z)b(Z):y\ge0,\ \sum_{Z\subseteq S}y(Z)\chi_Z\ge c\}$, the greedy vector $x_{\mathrm{alg}}$ is primal-optimal and the constructed vector $y^*$ is dual-optimal. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polymatroid greedy construction and its associated dual solution are respectively optimal for the primal and dual linear programs, and the polymatroid constraint system is totally dual integral.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for a feasible primal–dual pair in the nonnegative inequality formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{u^{\mathsf T}b:u^{\mathsf T}A\le c^{\mathsf T},\ u\ge0\}\). A feasible pair \((\bar x,\bar u)\) is primal–dual optimal if and only if \(\bar x_j\bigl(c_j-(\bar u^{\mathsf T}A)_j\bigr)=0\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,n\), and \(\bar u_i\bigl((A\bar x)_i-b_i\bigr)=0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Equivalently, \(\bar x_j>0\Rightarrow(\bar u^{\mathsf T}A)_j=c_j\) and \(\bar u_i>0\Rightarrow(A\bar x)_i=b_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal–dual pair is optimal exactly when every positive primal variable has a tight dual constraint and every positive dual variable has a tight primal constraint.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar u\ge0\) and \(\bar u^{\mathsf T}A\le c^{\mathsf T}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\bar x,\bar u)\text{ is primal--dual optimal}\iff\forall j,\ \bar x_j\bigl(c_j-(\bar u^{\mathsf T}A)_j\bigr)=0\ \land\ \forall i,\ \bar u_i\bigl((A\bar x)_i-b_i\bigr)=0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality equivalence for a primal with unrestricted variables and its nonnegative dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\) and \(\min\{yb:yA=c,\ y\ge0\}\). If \(x\) and \(y\) are feasible, then the following are equivalent: \(x\) and \(y\) are both optimal; \(cx=yb\); and \(y(b-Ax)=0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(x,y\text{ are optimal}\bigr)\iff(cx=yb)\iff\bigl(y(b-Ax)=0\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain of the Linear-Programming Objective-Coefficient Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General linear-programming sensitivity result concerning variation of the objective vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\} be nonempty and define g(c)=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\} whenever the optimum is finite. Then \operatorname{dom}g=\{c\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R_+^m,\ A^\top y=c\}. Consequently, \operatorname{dom}g is describable by finitely many linear inequalities and is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty linear-programming feasible region, the objective vectors yielding a finite maximum are exactly those representable as A transpose times a nonnegative vector. This domain is a polyhedral convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}g=\{c:\exists y\ge0,\ A^\top y=c\}\text{ is a convex polyhedron.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Optimum with Linearly Independent Positive Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of an attaining dual solution whose positive support indexes linearly independent constraint rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual pair
\[
\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\},\qquad \min\{y^\top b:y\ge\mathbf 0,\ y^\top A=c^\top\},
\]
if the optimum value is finite, then the dual minimum is attained by a vector \(y^*\ge\mathbf 0\) such that the rows \(A_{i\bullet}\) with \(y_i^*>0\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite LP optimum, there is an optimal dual solution whose positive components correspond to linearly independent rows of the constraint matrix.
assumptions_latex: \text{The optimum value of the stated primal-dual LP pair is finite.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y^*\in\arg\min\{y^\top b:y\ge\mathbf 0,\ y^\top A=c^\top\}\text{ such that }\{A_{i\bullet}:y_i^*>0\}\text{ is linearly independent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weight splitting for an intersection-structured linear program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the component polyhedra, their intersection problem, an objective-weight splitting, and the associated component problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each $k\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$, let $\mathcal P_k=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}^k x_j\le b_i^k\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m(k)\}$, and let $(P)$ be $\max\{c^\top x:x\in\bigcap_{k=1}^p\mathcal P_k\}$. Vectors $c^1,\ldots,c^p\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfying $c=\sum_{k=1}^p c^k$ form a weight splitting of $c$. The associated component problem is $(P_k):\max\{(c^k)^\top x:x\in\mathcal P_k\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given component polyhedra whose intersection is the feasible region of a linear program, a weight splitting decomposes the objective vector into one vector per component, with each vector defining a component linear program.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c=\sum_{k=1}^p c^k\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (c^1,\ldots,c^p)\text{ is a weight splitting of }c,\qquad (P_k)=\max_{x\in\mathcal P_k}(c^k)^\top x.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following holds for a primal-dual LP pair (P,D): (i) both possess optimal solutions x^* and w^* with c^{\top}x^*=(w^*)^{\top}b; (ii) P is unbounded above and D is infeasible, or D is unbounded below and P is infeasible; (iii) both P and D are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one outcome occurs: both problems attain equal optimal values; one is unbounded and the other infeasible; or both are infeasible.
assumptions_latex: (P,D)\text{ is a primal-dual pair of linear programs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ExactlyOne}\!\left[\begin{array}{l}\exists x^*,w^*:\ x^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(P),\ w^*\in\operatorname{Opt}(D),\ c^{\top}x^*=(w^*)^{\top}b;\\ (P\text{ unbounded above}\wedge D\text{ infeasible})\vee(D\text{ unbounded below}\wedge P\text{ infeasible});\\ P\text{ infeasible}\wedge D\text{ infeasible}\end{array}\right]

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak duality for the canonical finite-dimensional linear-programming pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(x\ge0\) and \(Ax\le b\), and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfies \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\), then \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\). Consequently, when both feasible regions are nonempty, their extended optimal values satisfy \(p^*\le d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every dual feasible value upper-bounds every primal feasible value, so the primal optimal value cannot exceed the dual optimal value when both feasible regions are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\), and hence \(p^*\le d^*\) whenever both feasible regions are nonempty.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-halfspace interpretation of feasible dual multipliers and supporting-hyperplane interpretation of zero-gap primal-dual pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b,\ x\ge0\}\). Every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\) defines a valid containing halfspace \(P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\}\). If \(x^*\in P\) and a dual-feasible \(y^*\) satisfy \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=b^{\mathsf T}y^*\), then \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y^*\}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(P\) at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible multiplier defines a halfspace containing the primal polyhedron. Equality at a primal feasible point makes its boundary a supporting hyperplane there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^{\mathsf T}x\le b^{\mathsf T}y\}\); equality at \(x^*\in P\) yields a supporting hyperplane at \(x^*\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form Farkas infeasibility certificate for a nonnegative linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), a Farkas certificate of infeasibility is a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that
\[
A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.
\]
Indeed, the displayed inequalities are directly checkable from \(A\), \(b\), and \(y\). Farkas' alternative states that such a certificate exists if and only if no vector \(x\ge0\) satisfies \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infeasibility of a nonnegative equality system is certified by a multiplier nonnegative on every column but negative on the right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility alternative for equality systems with componentwise nonnegative primal variables and an unrestricted certificate vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), has a solution if and only if no \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfies \(A^Ty\ge0\) and \(b^Ty<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative vector x satisfying Ax = b exists exactly when there is no unrestricted vector y whose products with all columns of A are nonnegative while its product with b is strictly negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0)\iff\neg(\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ A^Ty\ge0,\ b^Ty<0).

Then \(b\in C\) if and only if no homogeneous halfspace contains \(C\) while excluding \(b\). Likewise, for a polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^k\), \(b\in P\) if and only if no halfspace contains \(P\) while excluding \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point belongs to a generated cone, respectively a polytope, exactly when it cannot be separated from that set by a homogeneous halfspace, respectively an arbitrary halfspace, containing the set.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^k\text{ is a generated cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
b\in C\iff
exists H	ext{ homogeneous halfspace}:C\subseteq H,\ b
otin H;\qquad b\in P\iff
exists H	ext{ halfspace}:P\subseteq H,\ b
otin H.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Ax\le b\) be feasible, and suppose \(c^\top x\le\delta\) for every \(x\) satisfying \(Ax\le b\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda\ge0,\ \exists\delta'\le\delta:\ \lambda^\top A=c^\top\land\lambda^\top b=\delta'

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible:
\[
\text{(I)}\quad Ax=b,\quad x\ge0,
\]
\[
\text{(II)}\quad A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.
\]
Thus feasibility of the first system excludes every witness for the second, while infeasibility of the first guarantees at least one witness satisfying the second.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic incompatibility of the two systems in the equality-form Farkas alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(x\ge0\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), and suppose \(y\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\). Then
\[
b^{\mathsf T}y=(Ax)^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0.
\]
Consequently the additional strict inequality \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) cannot hold. Hence the feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\) and its Farkas alternative system are mutually exclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible nonnegative solution forces every column-nonnegative multiplier to evaluate the right-hand side nonnegatively, excluding a negative certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\ge0\), \(Ax\le b\), \(y\ge0\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\). The feasible pair \((x,y)\) is primal-dual optimal if and only if
\[
y_i(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)=0\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m,
\]
and
\[
x_j((A^{\mathsf T}y)_j-c_j)=0\quad\text{for every }j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Equivalently, every positive variable has a tight corresponding constraint and every positive multiplier has a tight primal constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal-dual pair is optimal exactly when each variable or multiplier is complementary to its corresponding nonnegative slack.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\) be feasible for \((P)=\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\}\), and let \(v\) be feasible for \((D)=\min\{y^Tb:y^TA=c^T,\ y\ge0\}\). Then \(u\) and \(v\) are optimal for their respective programs if and only if \(v_i(b_i-A_i u)=0\) for every \(i\), equivalently \(v_i>0\Rightarrow A_i u=b_i\), or \(A_i u<b_i\Rightarrow v_i=0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u,v\text{ are optimal}\iff \forall i,\ v_i(b_i-A_i u)=0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes optimality when commodity-specific arc upper bounds are infinite, while shared arc capacities remain present.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume $u_{ij}^k=+\infty$ for every $(i,j)\in A$ and $k=1,\ldots,K$. Commodity flows $y$ are optimal if and only if they are feasible and there exist arc prices $w_{ij}\ge 0$ and unrestricted node potentials $\pi^k(i)$ such that
\[
w_{ij}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^K y_{ij}^{\ell}-u_{ij}\right)=0
\quad\forall(i,j)\in A,
\]
\[
c_{ij}^{\pi,k}\ge0,
\qquad
c_{ij}^{\pi,k}y_{ij}^k=0
\quad\forall(i,j)\in A, k=1,ldots,K.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With all commodity-specific arc upper bounds infinite, a multicommodity flow is optimal exactly when it is feasible and admits nonnegative shared arc prices and unrestricted commodity-specific node potentials such that shared-capacity slack is complementary to price, every reduced cost is nonnegative, and positive commodity flow can occur only on zero-reduced-cost arcs.
assumptions_latex: y\text{ is governed by the feasibility constraints of the stated multicommodity-flow problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\text{ is optimal}\iff y\text{ is feasible and }\exists\,w\ge0,\pi:\;w_{ij}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^K y_{ij}^{\ell}-u_{ij}\right)=0,\;c_{ij}^{\pi,k}\ge0,\;c_{ij}^{\pi,k}y_{ij}^k=0\quad\forall(i,j),k.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). A primal-dual optimality certificate is a pair \((x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(x\ge0\), \(Ax\le b\), \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge c\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\). With \(v:=c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\), the certificate establishes that \(x\) and \(y\) are optimal and that \(p^*=d^*=v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual feasible points with equal objective values jointly certify their optimality and the common optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(v:=c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\), the pair \((x,y)\) certifies \(p^*=d^*=v\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent optimality, improving-direction, and complementary primal–dual certificate conditions for the mixed linear description (4.1).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*=(x_0^*,x_1^*)\in R\), where \(R\) is given by (4.1), and suppose \(\{cx:x\in R\}\) is bounded above. Then the following are equivalent: (i) \(cx^*\ge cx\) for every \(x\in R\); (ii) no direction \(z=(z_0,z_1)\) satisfies \(cz>0\), \(Pz_0+Az_1=0\), \(Q_{x^*}^{=}z_0+B_{x^*}^{=}z_1\le0\), and \(x_1^*(j)=0\Rightarrow z_1(j)\ge0\); (iii) there is a dual solution \(y^*=(y_0^*,y_1^*)\) such that \(x_1^*(j)>0\Rightarrow y_0^*a_j+y_1^*b_j=c_1(j)\) and \(y_1^*(i)>0\Rightarrow {}_iqx_0^*+{}_ibx_1^*=b_1(i)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is optimal exactly when it has no feasible improving active-set direction, equivalently when it can be paired with a dual feasible solution satisfying complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is optimal}\iff\text{no improving direction satisfying (4.6) exists}\iff\exists y^*\text{ dual feasible with the stated complementary-slackness implications}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient reduced-cost certificate for a minimization problem with nonbasic variables fixed at lower or upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar x\) be a bounded-variable basic feasible solution and write the objective in canonical form as \(z(x)=z_0+\sum_{j\in\mathbf L}c_j^\pi x_j+\sum_{j\in\mathbf U}c_j^\pi x_j\). If \(c_j^\pi\ge0\) for every \(j\in\mathbf L\) and \(c_j^\pi\le0\) for every \(j\in\mathbf U\), then every feasible \(x\) satisfies \(z(x)\ge z_0+\sum_{j\in\mathbf U}c_j^\pi u_j\). The basic feasible solution \(\bar x\), for which \(\bar x_{\mathbf L}=0\) and \(\bar x_{\mathbf U}=u_{\mathbf U}\), attains this bound and is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a minimization problem, nonnegative reduced costs at lower bounds and nonpositive reduced costs at upper bounds give a lower bound on every feasible objective value. The current bounded-variable basic feasible solution attains that bound and is therefore optimal.
assumptions_latex: \bar x\text{ is a feasible bounded-variable basic solution with nonbasic partition }(\mathbf L,\mathbf U)
c_j^\pi\ge0\ \forall j\in\mathbf L,\qquad c_j^\pi\le0\ \forall j\in\mathbf U
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z(x)\ge z_0+\sum_{j\in\mathbf U}c_j^\pi u_j=z(\bar x)\quad\forall x\text{ feasible},\qquad \bar x\text{ is optimal}

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Certificate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pair-specific degeneracy through failure of strict complementarity in standard-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible primal-dual pair \((x,y)\), let \(s=c-A^Ty\geq0\). The pair is an optimality certificate when \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts=0\), equivalently when \(x_i s_i=0\) for every \(i\). Call this certificate pair-degenerate when \(D_0(x,y)=\{i:x_i=s_i=0\}\) is nonempty. Equivalently, it is pair-degenerate when it fails strict complementarity, which requires \(x_i+s_i>0\) for every \(i\). Pair-degeneracy does not by itself imply nonoptimality or nonuniqueness of the primal or dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal primal-dual certificate is pair-degenerate when some primal variable and its complementary dual slack are both zero, equivalently when that pair is not strictly complementary.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are feasible for \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\leq c\}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate is pair-degenerate exactly when \(D_0(x,y)\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Indices simultaneously zero on both complementary sides.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear program \(\inf\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\) is unbounded below if and only if there exists a recession direction \(d\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d\geq0\), and \(c^Td<0\). Given any \(x^0\in P\), the ray \(x^0+td\) is feasible for every \(t\geq0\), and its objective value is \(c^Tx^0+t c^Td\). Thus \((x^0,d)\) is an exactly verifiable unboundedness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible standard-form minimization problem is unbounded exactly when it has a feasible recession direction with strictly negative objective slope.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal basic-solution degeneracy in equality-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) contain \(r\) indices such that the columns of \(A_B\) are linearly independent. A basic feasible solution associated with \(B\) has \(x_j=0\) for \(j\notin B\), while \(x_B\) is the unique nonnegative vector satisfying \(A_Bx_B=b\). It is degenerate when at least one component of \(x_B\) is zero. Equivalently, a basic feasible solution \(x\) is degenerate exactly when \(|\{i:x_i>0\}|<r\). Degeneracy does not imply infeasibility or failure of optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible solution is degenerate when at least one basic variable is zero, equivalently when fewer than the rank of the constraint matrix many variables are positive.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is degenerate}\iff |\{i:x_i>0\}|<r\).

notation.meaning: An index set of r linearly independent columns used as a basis.
The submatrix formed by the basis columns.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \((P)\) and \((D)\) are both feasible, both attain finite optima and their optimal values are equal. If \((P)\) is feasible while \((D)\) is infeasible, then \((P)\) is unbounded below. If \((D)\) is feasible while \((P)\) is infeasible, then \((D)\) is unbounded above. Both programs may be infeasible. Weak duality excludes primal unboundedness when the dual is feasible and excludes dual unboundedness when the primal is feasible. Hence a positive finite duality gap is not a failure regime for this linear-programming model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional primal-dual LP pair, feasible problems have equal attained optima; all remaining failures reduce to the permitted infeasible or unbounded status combinations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unimodular invariance of Gomory–Chvátal closure and integer hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States preservation of polyhedrality and equivariance of the closure and integer hull under unimodular linear transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron, let \(U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) be unimodular, and define \(f(P):=\{Ux:x\in P\}\). Then \(f(P)\) is a polyhedron. If \(P\) is rational, then \[(f(P))'=f(P')\qquad\text{and}\qquad (f(P))_I=f(P_I).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unimodular linear image of a polyhedron is polyhedral. For a rational polyhedron, both Gomory–Chvátal closure and integer hull commute with the unimodular transformation.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is rational for the closure and integer-hull identities}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(P)\text{ is a polyhedron};\qquad (f(P))'=f(P'),\quad (f(P))_I=f(P_I)\text{ when }P\text{ is rational}.

children.title: Encoding Length of Rational Data
children.top_down_role: Size measures for rational vectors, matrices, inequalities, and objective data.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Length of Rational Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit additive binary-size convention for rational scalar, vector, matrix, and linear-program data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a reduced rational number \(p/q\), define \(\lambda(p/q)=1+\lceil\log_2(|p|+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(q+1)\rceil\), where the initial bit accommodates the sign. For \(v\in\mathbb{Q}^k\), define \(\lambda(v)=k+\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda(v_i)\). For \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), define \(\lambda(A)=m+n+mn+\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda(A_{ij})\). For rational linear-program data \((A,b,c)\), define its total encoding length by \(L=\lambda(A)+\lambda(b)+\lambda(c)\). Inequality systems are encoded analogously by including the coefficient arrays, right-hand sides, dimensions, and objective data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under this explicit convention, rational input size is the sum of the binary lengths of reduced numerators, positive denominators, signs, dimensions, and all entries of the matrix, right-hand side, and objective vector.
assumptions_latex: Every rational number is written uniquely as \(p/q\), where \(p\in\mathbb{Z}\), \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The input size of \((A,b,c)\) is \(L=\lambda(A)+\lambda(b)+\lambda(c)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Encoding Size of Rational Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines encoding sizes for integers, reduced rational numbers, rational vectors, and rational matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\in\mathbb Z\), define \(\operatorname{size}(n):=1+\lceil\log(|n|+1)\rceil\). For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb Q^n\), define \(\operatorname{size}(x):=n+\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{size}(x_i)\). For \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), define \(\operatorname{size}(A):=mn+\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{size}(a_{ij})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary encoding size is defined componentwise: an integer uses 1 plus the ceiling of the logarithm of one plus its absolute value; a reduced rational uses the combined sizes of its numerator and denominator; a vector or matrix uses the sum of its entry sizes plus its number of entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}(n)=1+\lceil\log(|n|+1)\rceil,\quad \operatorname{size}(r)=\operatorname{size}(p)+\operatorname{size}(q),\quad \operatorname{size}(x)=n+\sum_i\operatorname{size}(x_i),\quad \operatorname{size}(A)=mn+\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{size}(a_{ij})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Encoding Length of Integer and Rational Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-size conventions for integers, reduced rationals, rational arrays, linear inequalities, systems, tuples, and linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $\langle n\rangle:=1+\left\lceil\log_2(|n|+1)\right\rceil$. If $r=p/q\in\mathbb Q$ is in its unique reduced representation with $q>0$, define $\langle r\rangle:=\langle p\rangle+\langle q\rangle$. The encoding length of a rational vector or matrix is the sum of its entry lengths; the encoding length of $a^Tx\le b$ is $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle$; and the lengths of systems and tuples are obtained by summation. In particular, $\max\{c^Tx:Ax\le b\}$ has encoding length $\langle A,b,c\rangle$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer is encoded in binary with a sign bit, and a rational is encoded through its coprime numerator and positive denominator. The lengths of rational arrays, inequalities, systems, tuples, and linear programs are the sums of the lengths of their numerical data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle n\rangle=1+\left\lceil\log_2(|n|+1)\right\rceil,\qquad \langle r\rangle=\langle p\rangle+\langle q\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet Complexity, Vertex Complexity, and Well-Described Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the exceptional conventions for the full space and empty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron and let \(\varphi,v\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). The polyhedron \(P\) has facet-complexity at most \(\varphi\) if it is the solution set of a rational inequality system in which every inequality has encoding length at most \(\varphi\); when \(P=\mathbb R^n\), additionally require \(\varphi\ge n+1\). It has vertex-complexity at most \(v\) if finite sets \(V,E\subseteq\mathbb Q^n\) exist such that \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(E)\) and every vector in \(V\cup E\) has encoding length at most \(v\); when \(P=\varnothing\), additionally require \(v\ge n\). A well-described polyhedron is a triple \((P;n,\varphi)\) with facet-complexity at most \(\varphi\), and its encoding length is \(\langle P\rangle=\varphi+n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facet-complexity bounds the encoding length of every inequality in some rational description of the polyhedron. Vertex-complexity bounds the encoding length of every vector in some finite convex-hull-plus-conical-hull representation. The full-space and empty-set cases obey the stated lower-bound conventions. A well-described polyhedron records its dimension and facet-complexity bound and has encoding length equal to their sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle P\rangle=\varphi+n\text{ for a well-described polyhedron }(P;n,\varphi),\text{ with facet- and vertex-complexity as defined above.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Small-Encoding Optimal LP Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives encoding bounds independent of the objective-data size and a sharper special-case bound for a signed unit right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\). If \(\max\{c^{\top}x:Ax\leq b\}\) has an optimal solution, then it has an optimal solution \(x\) satisfying \[\operatorname{size}(x)\leq4n\bigl(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b)\bigr),\] and every component of \(x\) has size at most \(4(\operatorname{size}(A)+\operatorname{size}(b))\). If additionally \(b=e_i\) or \(b=-e_i\) for some unit vector \(e_i\), then there are a nonsingular submatrix \(A'\) of \(A\) and an optimal solution \(x\) such that \[\operatorname{size}(x)\leq4n\operatorname{size}(A').\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever a rational linear program attains its optimum, it has an optimum whose total and componentwise encoding sizes are bounded by the encoding sizes of the constraint matrix and right-hand side. For a signed unit right-hand side, an optimum can instead be bounded using a nonsingular submatrix of the constraint matrix.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb Q^m,\quad c\in\mathbb Q^n

In reduced form, every numerator and denominator of \(v_j\) is bounded in absolute value by \(n^{n/2}2^{n\ell}\). Consequently, each coordinate has encoding length \(O(n(\ell+\log n))\), and \(\lambda(v)=O(n^2(\ell+\log n))\). Clearing denominators first gives a polynomial bound in the total encoding length for rational descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vertex is determined by independent tight inequalities, and determinant bounds make its rational encoding polynomial in the dimension and coefficient bit size.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Encoding Size

children.title: Strong Polyhedral Problems

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}\) is a rational polyhedron and all queries are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong problems require exact membership, exact separating inequalities, and exact optimal values or status certificates.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong separation, given \(y\), must decide exactly whether \(y\in P\); if not, it returns rational \((a,\beta)\) such that \(a^Tx\leq\beta<a^Ty\) for every \(x\in P\). Strong optimization, given \(c\), must return an exact maximizer of \(c^Tx\) over \(P\) and its exact rational value when finite and attained, or correctly report infeasibility or unboundedness with the corresponding exact certificate. No geometric or objective tolerance is part of either specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polyhedral problems demand exact membership and separation, or an exact optimizer and value, with exact certificates for infeasibility or unboundedness.

children.title: Exact–Approximate Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Representation and precision conditions separating the two problem regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact–Approximate Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational-gap boundary separating tolerance answers from recoverable exact polyhedral answers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Distinct reduced rational numbers with denominators at most \(Q\) differ by at least \(1/Q^2\). Therefore, if an approximation \(\widehat z\) to such a rational value \(z\) satisfies \(|\widehat z-z|<1/(2Q^2)\), then \(z\) is the unique rational with reduced denominator at most \(Q\) in that error interval and can be recovered by rational reconstruction. Without a known encoding or denominator bound, no fixed positive tolerance ensures exact recovery: for any \(\varepsilon>0\), choose a rational \(\delta\) with \(0<\delta<\varepsilon\). The intervals \(P_0=[0,1]\) and \(P_\delta=[0,1+\delta]\) admit a common \(\varepsilon\)-accurate maximization answer for objective \(c=1\), although their exact optimal values are \(1\) and \(1+\delta\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation determines an exact rational answer when its error is strictly below half a known denominator-dependent gap; without such a bound, arbitrarily close polyhedra can have different exact optima.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and the exact rational value \(z\) has reduced denominator at most \(Q\).
\(\widehat z\) is an approximation to \(z\), and weak answers use a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact recovery is guaranteed when \(|\widehat z-z|<1/(2Q^2)\); without a known size bound, fixed-tolerance weak information does not determine exact answers.

notation.meaning: Known upper bound on the reduced denominator of the exact rational value.
Approximation to the exact rational value z.

knowledge_statements.title: Precision Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient absolute accuracy for exact membership decisions on integer inequality systems at rational query points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). If \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) satisfies \(qy\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), then every slack \(s_i=b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}y\) belongs to \(q^{-1}\mathbb{Z}\). For approximations satisfying \(|\widetilde{s}_i-s_i|<1/(2q)\), one has \(s_i>0\) when \(\widetilde{s}_i>1/(2q)\), \(s_i<0\) when \(\widetilde{s}_i<-1/(2q)\), and \(s_i=0\) when \(|\widetilde{s}_i|<1/(2q)\). These alternatives decide exactly whether \(y\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer inequality system and a rational query with common denominator q, slack approximations with absolute error below 1/(2q) determine every slack sign, including zero, and therefore decide exact membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The approximations determine every slack sign and decide exactly whether \(y\in P\).

notation.meaning: slack of inequality i at the query point
a common denominator of the query coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Radius Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An explicit outer-radius estimate for bounded polyhedra described by bounded integer data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(H\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\), with \(|A_{ij}|\le H\) and \(|b_i|\le H\) for all indices. If \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is nonempty and bounded, then every \(x\in P\) satisfies \(\|x\|_2\le\sqrt n\,n!H^n\). Equivalently, \(P\subseteq B(0,\sqrt n\,n!H^n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty bounded polyhedron in n dimensions whose integral inequality data have magnitude at most H lies in the Euclidean ball centered at zero with radius √n n! H^n.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}\), \(|A_{ij}|\le H\), and \(|b_i|\le H\) for all indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P\subseteq B\!\left(0,\sqrt n\,n!H^n\right).\]

children.top_down_role: Dependence of oracle behavior on geometric conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz sensitivity of linear optimization values to Hausdorff perturbations of compact feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty compact sets and let \(d_H(K,L)\le\delta\) under the Euclidean metric, where \(\delta\ge0\). Define \(h_K(c)=\max_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(h_L(c)=\max_{x\in L}c^{\mathsf T}x\). For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(|h_K(c)-h_L(c)|\le\|c\|_2\delta\). In particular, if \(\|c\|_2=1\), then \(|h_K(c)-h_L(c)|\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving a nonempty compact feasible set by Hausdorff distance at most δ changes any linear optimum by at most the objective norm times δ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|h_K(c)-h_L(c)|\le \|c\|_2\delta\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]

notation.meaning: support functions of K and L

children.title: Tolerance Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where rounding or separation tolerances obscure the intended conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional family showing that tolerance comparable to geometric feature size cannot preserve exact decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(K_\varepsilon=[0,\varepsilon]\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(y_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon\). Then \(y_\varepsilon\notin K_\varepsilon\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(y_\varepsilon,K_\varepsilon)=\varepsilon\). Under a weak-membership convention that permits an IN response whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\), the exterior query \(y_\varepsilon\) may receive IN for every \(\delta\ge\varepsilon\). For the objective \(c=1\), its candidate value \(c y_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon\) exceeds the exact optimum \(h_{K_\varepsilon}(c)=\varepsilon\) by \(\varepsilon\). Thus weak acceptance at this tolerance cannot certify exact membership or exact-feasible optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When tolerance is at least the width of a small interval, weak membership may accept an exterior point whose objective value exceeds the interval's true optimum by that width.
assumptions_latex: The weak-membership convention permits IN when \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak acceptance at tolerance \(\delta\ge\varepsilon\) need not certify exact membership or an exactly feasible optimizer over \(K_\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Point Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership oracle for a specified convex or polyhedral feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a fixed set represented implicitly. An exact point-membership oracle accepts a query \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and returns YES precisely when \(y\in K\), and NO precisely when \(y\notin K\). When \(K=P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) is explicitly represented, the predicate is equivalent to \(a_i^{\mathsf T}y\le b_i\) for every row \(i\). The oracle's output is exact: no tolerance band around the boundary is left unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point-membership oracle decides exactly whether a rational query belongs to the fixed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns YES if and only if \(y\in K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\), let \((K;n,R,r,a_0)\) be a centered convex body given by a weak membership oracle, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and supplied by an evaluation oracle such that, for every \(x\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and \(\delta>0\), it returns \(t\in\mathbb{Q}\) satisfying \(|f(x)-t|\le\delta\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the parameter dependence that prevents an oracle-polynomial weak-separation algorithm in the bit length of \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), rational \(0<\delta,\beta<1\), and a centered convex body \((K;n,R,r,a)\) supplied by a weak membership oracle, an algorithm either asserts \(y\in S(K,\delta)\) or returns \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that, for every \(x\in K\), \[c^Tx\le c^Ty+(\delta+\beta\lVert x-y\rVert)\lVert c\rVert.\] Its running time is oracle-polynomial in \(\lceil1/\beta\rceil,\langle K\rangle,\langle y\rangle,\langle\delta\rangle\). Consequently, this bound does not yield an oracle-polynomial weak-separation algorithm in the encoding length \(\langle\beta\rangle\); such an algorithm would follow if the dependence were polynomial in \(\langle\beta\rangle\) instead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak membership access yields either approximate membership of the query point or a nonzero approximate separating vector. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle reduction with explicit rationality, interior-point, and encoding-size hypotheses.

children.title: Inequality Validity

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validity oracle for linear inequalities over a fixed feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be fixed. An exact inequality-validity oracle receives \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\) and returns YES precisely when \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) holds for every \(x\in K\). If \(K\) is nonempty and compact, this is equivalent to \(h_K(a)=\max_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\). A NO answer asserts the existence of some \(x\in K\) with \(a^{\mathsf T}x>\beta\), although the interface need not return such a witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality-validity oracle decides whether a queried rational linear inequality holds at every point of the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns YES if and only if \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in K\).

children.title: Membership–Validity Reductions
children.top_down_role: Conditions supporting computational transfer between the two interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership–Validity Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership–validity conversion through polar duality for convex bodies containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\), and define \(K^\circ=\{z:z^{\mathsf T}x\le1\text{ for all }x\in K\}\). The bipolar theorem gives \(K=(K^\circ)^\circ\). Hence a membership query \(y\in K\) is equivalent to validity of \(y^{\mathsf T}z\le1\) over \(K^\circ\). Conversely, for \(\beta>0\), validity of \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) over \(K\) is equivalent to membership \(a/\beta\in K^\circ\). Thus exact membership and positive-right-hand-side validity reduce to one another when the polar body is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar duality converts membership in a convex body into validity over its polar, and positive-threshold validity into polar membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y\in K\iff y^{\mathsf T}z\le1\ \forall z\in K^\circ,\qquad a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\ \forall x\in K\iff a/\beta\in K^\circ.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Violated, active, satisfying, and almost-satisfying cut sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for a proper cut-requirement function and a selected edge set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\) be a proper function on \(2^{V(G)}\), let \(F\subseteq E(G)\), and let \(X\subseteq V(G)\). The set \(X\) is violated with respect to \((g,F)\) iff \(|\delta_F(X)|<g(X)\). An active set is an inclusion-minimal violated set. The set \(F\) satisfies \(g\) iff no vertex set is violated, and it almost satisfies \(g\) iff \(|\delta_F(X)|\ge g(X)-1\) for every \(X\subseteq V(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex set is violated when too few selected edges cross its cut. Active sets are inclusion-minimal violated sets. The edge set satisfies the requirement when no set is violated, and almost satisfies it when every cut misses its requirement by at most one.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ is a proper function on }2^{V(G)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is violated}\iff |\delta_F(X)|<g(X);\quad F\text{ satisfies }g\iff \nexists X:\ |\delta_F(X)|<g(X);\quad F\text{ almost satisfies }g\iff \forall X\subseteq V(G),\ |\delta_F(X)|\ge g(X)-1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uncrossing and disjointness of active sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncrossing structure when the selected edge set misses every proper-function cut requirement by at most one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\) be a proper function and let \(F\subseteq E(G)\) almost satisfy \(g\). If \(A,B\subseteq V(G)\) are violated, then either both \(A\setminus B\) and \(B\setminus A\) are violated, or both \(A\cap B\) and \(A\cup B\) are violated. Consequently, any two distinct active sets with respect to \((g,F)\) are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an edge set that almost satisfies a proper cut requirement, two violated sets uncross into either two violated differences or a violated intersection and union. Hence distinct inclusion-minimal violated sets are disjoint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact strong separation oracle for a nonempty compact convex feasible set.

children.title: Weak Separation
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-based separation for approximate geometric access.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based separation with a specified Euclidean near-membership alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\delta>0\). A \(\delta\)-weak separation oracle queried at \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) may return NEAR only when \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\). Otherwise it returns a vector \(a\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) with \(\|a\|_2=1\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}y\ge h_K(a)+\delta\), where \(h_K(a)=\sup_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x\). Thus queries farther than \(\delta\) receive a valid separating direction with margin at least \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak separation may declare a point near the set within δ; farther points receive a normalized separator with margin at least δ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns NEAR with \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\), or \(a\) with \(\|a\|_2=1\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}y\ge h_K(a)+\delta\).

children.title: Separation Precision Boundary
children.top_down_role: Geometric and encoding conditions controlling transfer between exact and weak access.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Precision Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The rational slack gap separating sufficient precision from an unavoidable weak-oracle ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). If \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) satisfies \(qy\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), then every violated row satisfies \(a_i^{\mathsf T}y-b_i\ge1/q\), and row-evaluation error strictly below \(1/(2q)\) preserves the sign of every nonzero violation. This scale is sharp up to the factor two: for \(P=(-\infty,0]\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(y=1/q\), the violation and distance to \(P\) both equal \(1/q\). Under a weak-separation convention permitting NEAR whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,P)\le\delta\), \(\delta\ge1/q\) therefore does not require a separating output for this exterior query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a rational query with common denominator q, nonzero row violations are at least 1/q, so evaluation error below 1/(2q) preserves their signs, while near-set tolerance at least 1/q can hide an exterior point.
assumptions_latex: The weak-separation convention permits NEAR when \(\operatorname{dist}(y,P)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Evaluation precision strictly below \(1/(2q)\) detects every nonzero row violation, whereas ambiguity tolerance \(\delta\ge1/q\) cannot guarantee a separating output in general.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error linear optimization with exact feasibility over a compact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and compact. Given \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), an additive \(\varepsilon\)-weak optimization oracle returns \(x_\varepsilon\in K\) such that \(c^{\mathsf T}x_\varepsilon\ge h_K(c)-\varepsilon\), where \(h_K(c)=\max_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\). This convention relaxes objective optimality by an absolute amount \(\varepsilon\) but retains exact feasibility. If objectives are normalized by \(\|c\|_2=1\), the tolerance has the same geometric scale as Euclidean perturbations of \(K\).

children.title: Separating-Witness Output

knowledge_statements.title: Separating-Witness Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation certificate for a point outside a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A separating-witness output for \(y\) is a pair \((a,\beta)\in(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) for every \(x\in K\), while \(a^{\mathsf T}y>\beta\). Positive rescaling leaves the represented halfspace unchanged, so the witness may be normalized by \(\lVert a\rVert_2=1\). The strict inequality places \(y\) outside a valid halfspace containing all of \(K\), thereby certifying \(y\notin K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separating witness is a valid inequality containing the entire convex set but strictly violated by the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((a,\beta)\) is a mathematical certificate that \(y\notin K\).

notation.meaning: normal vector of the separating inequality
right-hand side of the separating inequality

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Violation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean additive tolerance with an explicit indifference band.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(\delta\)-approximate violation detector for \(K\), where \(\delta>0\), must return \(\mathrm{ACCEPT}\) whenever \(y\in K\), and must return \(\mathrm{REJECT}\) whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\geq\delta\), where \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)=\inf_{x\in K}\lVert y-x\rVert_2\). For queries satisfying \(0<\operatorname{dist}(y,K)<\delta\), either answer is allowed. Exact violation detection is the separate regime in which every query outside \(K\) must be rejected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate detection must accept members and reject points at least delta away, but may answer arbitrarily within the intervening tolerance band; exact detection rejects every nonmember.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correct output is mandatory for \(y\in K\) and for \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\geq\delta\), while either output is permitted when \(0<\operatorname{dist}(y,K)<\delta\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from the query to the set
