knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite program data and operational semantics, including the two distinguished halting outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic one-tape Turing-machine program consists of finite alphabets \(\Sigma\subset\Gamma\), a blank symbol \(b\in\Gamma\setminus\Sigma\), a finite state set \(Q\) containing distinct states \(q_0,q_Y,q_N\), and a transition function \(\delta:(Q\setminus\{q_Y,q_N\})\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}\). On input \(x\in\Sigma^*\), the symbols of \(x\) initially occupy squares \(1,\ldots,|x|\), every other square is blank, and the machine begins in state \(q_0\) scanning square \(1\). If \(\delta(q,s)=(q',s',\Delta)\), one step writes \(s'\), moves the head by \(\Delta\), and changes the state to \(q'\). Entering \(q_Y\) or \(q_N\) halts with answer yes or no, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic one-tape Turing machine has finite input and tape alphabets, a blank symbol, finitely many states with start, yes-halt, and no-halt states, and a deterministic transition function specifying the next state, written symbol, and one-square head movement. The input is placed from square 1 onward, all other squares are blank, and execution halts with the outcome determined by which halt state is entered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta:(Q\setminus\{q_Y,q_N\})\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}\text{ determines each nonhalting computation step, while }q_Y,q_N\text{ determine the two halting outcomes.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic multitape Turing machine and problem-solving criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine structure, initialization, halting output, and total correctness for an encoded problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), a deterministic \(t\)-tape Turing machine is a tuple \(T=(X,B,E,\Phi,\Psi,\Xi)\), where \(X\) is finite, \(B,E\in X\) are the beginning and end states, and, with \(*\) denoting blank, \(\Phi:X\times\{0,1,*\}^t\to X\), \(\Psi:X\times\{0,1,*\}^t\to\{0,1,*\}^t\), and \(\Xi:X\times\{0,1,*\}^t\to\{0,1,-1\}^t\) determine the next state, symbols written, and head movements. It solves \(\Pi\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\{0,1\}^*\) if, for every input \(\sigma\), it starts in state \(B\) with \(\sigma\) on tape 1 and the other tapes blank, halts after finitely many moves in state \(E\), and leaves on tape 1 some \(\tau\) satisfying \((\sigma,\tau)\in\Pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic multitape Turing machine has finitely many states and transition functions controlling its next state, written symbols, and head movements. It solves an encoded problem only if it halts on every input and returns an admissible output on the first tape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ solves }\Pi\iff\forall\sigma\in\{0,1\}^*\;T(\sigma)\text{ halts with some }\tau\text{ such that }(\sigma,\tau)\in\Pi.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Turing-machine and certificate characterizations of NP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States polynomially bounded deterministic and nondeterministic recognition and the equivalence between nondeterministic acceptance and efficiently verifiable certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-string decision problem \(A\), \(A\in P\) if and only if some deterministic Turing machine recognizes \(A\), halts on every input, and uses at most \(p(|x|)\) steps for some fixed polynomial \(p\). Moreover, \(A\in NP\) if and only if there exist a nondeterministic Turing machine \(M\) and a fixed polynomial \(p\) such that every yes-instance \(x\) has a legal accepting computation of length at most \(p(|x|)\), whereas no no-instance has any accepting computation. The latter condition is equivalent to yes-instances, and only yes-instances, possessing polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: P is the class of finite-string decision problems recognized by deterministic Turing machines that halt on every input in polynomial time. NP is the class for which every yes-instance has a polynomial-length accepting nondeterministic computation and no no-instance has one. Equivalently, exactly the yes-instances have polynomial-length certificates checkable in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a decision problem whose instances \(x\) are finite strings.
Running-time and computation-length bounds are measured as functions of the input length \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\in NP\iff A\text{ has polynomially bounded accepting nondeterministic computations exactly on its yes-instances}\iff A\text{ has polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time};\qquad A\in P\iff A\text{ is recognized by an always-halting deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Computational Problems and Polynomial-Time Turing Computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total relational search problems, their computation by Turing machines, the functional and decision special cases, and polynomial-time computability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an alphabet \(A\), a computational problem is a pair \((X,R)\) such that \(X\subseteq A^*\), \(R\subseteq X\times A^*\), and \(\forall x\in X\,\exists y\in A^*:(x,y)\in R\). A Turing machine \(\Phi\) computes \((X,R)\) if, for every \(x\in X\), it halts and \((x,\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x))\in R\). It is polynomial-time for \((X,R)\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that \(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)\le p(\operatorname{size}(x))\) for every \(x\in X\). If every \(x\in X\) has exactly one related output, then \(R\) defines a function \(f:X\to A^*\), and \(\Phi\) computes \(f\). If \(X=A^*\) and \(f:A^*\to\{0,1\}\), then \(\Phi\) decides \(L:=\{x\in A^*:f(x)=1\}\). A function is polynomial-time computable, or a language polynomial-time decidable, if an appropriate polynomial-time Turing machine exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computational problem assigns at least one admissible output string to every input in its input language. A Turing machine computes the problem when it halts on every permitted input and returns an admissible output. Polynomial time is a uniform polynomial bound in input length. Unique admissible outputs define function computation, while Boolean functions on all strings define language decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ computes }(X,R)\iff\forall x\in X:\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)<\infty\ \land\ (x,\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x))\in R;\quad \Phi\text{ is polynomial-time for }(X,R)\iff\exists p\text{ polynomial}\ \forall x\in X:\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)\le p(\operatorname{size}(x)).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines acceptance by reaching the halting state from the standard initial configuration, the accepted language, and a polynomial bound applying only to accepted words.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) have start state \(0\), halting state \(\infty\), and blank symbol \(\mathtt{blank}\). It accepts \(w\in(\Sigma\setminus\{\mathtt{blank}\})^*\) if, starting in state \(0\) with \(w\) on the otherwise blank tape and the head scanning its first symbol, it reaches \(\infty\) after finitely many iterations; when \(w=\varepsilon\), the head initially scans a blank. If \(\Pi=\{w:T\text{ accepts }w\}\), then \(T\) solves \(\Pi\). It solves \(\Pi\) in polynomial time if there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that every accepted word \(w\) is accepted within at most \(p(\operatorname{size}(w))\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A word is accepted when the machine, started in its start state on the standard input configuration, reaches the halting state after finitely many iterations. The machine solves the language consisting exactly of its accepted words. It solves that language in polynomial time when one polynomial bounds the iterations for every accepted word. No halting or time bound is imposed on words outside the language.
assumptions_latex: \text{Initially the tape contains }w\text{ and blanks elsewhere, with the head scanning the first input symbol; for }w=\varepsilon\text{ it scans a blank}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ solves }\Pi\text{ in polynomial time}\iff\exists p\text{ polynomial }\forall w\in\Pi,\ \operatorname{time}_T(w)\le p(\operatorname{size}(w)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Turing Machine for a Computational Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a two-tape oracle machine with a special query state, relation-valued answers, and output-length-sensitive query cost; the stated answer rule applies to queries in the oracle domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $A$ be an alphabet, $\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}$, and let $(X,R)$ be a computational problem with $X\subseteq A^*$. An oracle Turing machine using $(X,R)$ is a function
\[
\Phi:\{0,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\to\{-2,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\times\{-1,0,1\}^2,
\qquad N\in\mathbb Z_+.
\]
Its computation follows the two-tape model, with accumulated time initially $0$ and transition value $-2$ designating an oracle call. At such a call, let $q\in A^k$ be the string in cells $1,\ldots,k$ of the second tape, where
\[
k=\min\{j\in\mathbb N:t_j^{(i)}=\sqcup\}-1.
\]
If $q\in X$, choose some $y\in A^*$ with $(q,y)\in R$, write $y$ in the initial cells of the second tape followed by a blank, increase accumulated time by $1+|y|$, set $n^{(i+1)}=n^{(i)}+1$, and leave the remaining configuration components unchanged. In every other case accumulated time increases by $1$. The computation ends when the state is $-1$; its accumulated time is then $\operatorname{time}(\Phi,w)$ for the machine input $w$, and output is defined as in the two-tape model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle Turing machine is a two-tape machine with a special oracle-call transition. Its query is the second-tape string preceding the first blank. When that query belongs to the oracle domain, the oracle may return any related output, writes it followed by a blank, charges one step plus the output length, and resumes at the successor of the calling state. Other steps cost one, and state -1 halts. The extract supplies an oracle-answer rule only for queries in the domain X.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an alphabet and }\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}
(X,R)\text{ is a computational problem with }X\subseteq A^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ defines a two-tape computation with oracle-call value }-2;\ q\in X\text{ permits some answer }y\text{ with }(q,y)\in R\text{ at cost }1+|y|,\text{ while other steps cost }1\text{ and state }-1\text{ halts.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bounded-error probabilistic time and its polynomial-time union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) and \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\). A PTM \(M\) decides \(L\) in time \(T(n)\) if, for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^*\), it halts within \(T(|x|)\) steps for every sequence of random choices and satisfies \(\Pr[M(x)=L(x)]\geq 2/3\), where \(L(x)=1\) iff \(x\in L\). The class \(\operatorname{BPTIME}(T(n))\) consists of languages decided by PTMs in \(O(T(n))\) time, and \(\mathbf{BPP}=\bigcup_c\operatorname{BPTIME}(n^c)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A language is decidable in bounded-error probabilistic time T when a probabilistic Turing machine always halts within the stated input-length bound, independently of its random choices, and is correct on every input with probability at least two thirds. BPTIME collects languages with the corresponding asymptotic bound, and BPP is their polynomial-time union.
assumptions_latex: \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\ M\text{ halts within }T(|x|)\text{ steps for every random-choice sequence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{BPTIME}(T(n))=\{L:\exists\text{ PTM deciding }L\text{ in }O(T(n))\text{ time with error at most }1/3\},\qquad \mathbf{BPP}=\bigcup_c\operatorname{BPTIME}(n^c)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for the stated one-tape model with a write-only guessing head.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An NDTM has the components of a deterministic one-tape Turing machine together with a guessing module and write-only head. On input \(x\in\Sigma^*\), the guessing stage arbitrarily writes any finite string in \(\Gamma^*\) to the tape and stops, or may continue forever. If it stops, the checking stage begins in state \(q_0\) and thereafter follows the deterministic transition function \(\delta:(Q\setminus\{q_Y,q_N\})\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{-1,+1\}\). A computation is accepting exactly when the checking stage enters \(q_Y\); every halting or nonhalting computation that does not enter \(q_Y\) is non-accepting.

If guessing stops, an ordinary deterministic Turing-machine computation checks the input and guess. The computation accepts exactly by halting in the yes state; all other computations are non-accepting.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A computation accepts}\iff\text{its checking stage enters }q_Y.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines additive and scale-relative accuracy of a rational approximation to a real number, including the behavior at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\rho\in\mathbb R$, $r\in\mathbb Q$, and $\varepsilon>0$. The number $r$ approximates $\rho$ with absolute error $\varepsilon$ if $|\rho-r|\le\varepsilon$, and with relative error $\varepsilon$ if $|\rho-r|\le\varepsilon|\rho|$. In particular, when $\rho=0$, the relative-error condition forces $r=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational approximation has absolute error at most epsilon when its distance from the real target is at most epsilon. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Tape Turing Machine and Its Computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a deterministic two-tape machine with integer-indexed tapes, separate heads, and halting state -1.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $A$ be an alphabet, $\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}$, and $N\in\mathbb Z_+$. A two-tape Turing machine is a function
\[
\Phi:\{0,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\to\{-1,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A^2\times\{-1,0,1\}^2.
\]
For $x\in A^*$, its computation is the finite or infinite sequence $(n^{(i)},s^{(i)},t^{(i)},\pi^{(i)},\rho^{(i)})_{i\ge0}$ initialized by $n^{(0)}=0$, $\pi^{(0)}=\rho^{(0)}=1$, the symbols of $x$ in cells $1,\ldots,|x|$ of the first tape, and blanks elsewhere on both tapes. If $n^{(i)}\ne-1$ and
\[
\Phi(n^{(i)},s^{(i)}_{\pi^{(i)}},t^{(i)}_{\rho^{(i)}})=(m,\sigma,\tau,\delta,\epsilon),
\]
then the next configuration has state $m$, writes $\sigma$ and $\tau$ in the scanned cells, leaves all other cells unchanged, and moves the heads to $\pi^{(i)}+\delta$ and $\rho^{(i)}+\epsilon$. The computation terminates upon reaching state $-1$; its time and output are defined as in the one-tape model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-tape Turing machine has finite control, two integer-indexed tapes, and an independently moving head on each tape. The input initially occupies the first tape, while the second tape is blank. Each nonhalting transition reads both scanned symbols, changes state, writes on both tapes, and moves each head by -1, 0, or 1. State -1 terminates the computation; time and output follow the one-tape conventions.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is an alphabet and }\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi\text{ together with the initialization and update rules determines a finite or infinite computation that terminates when the control state reaches }-1.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite binary word \(x\in\{0,1\}^*\).
The machine is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and transition function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic bit-complexity model for finite binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) and input \(x\in\{0,1\}^*\), the time cost \(T_M(x)\) is the number of transition steps executed before \(M\) halts. Its space cost \(S_M(x)\) is the number of distinct work-tape cells visited during that computation; read-only input cells are excluded. An algorithm has worst-case time \(T(n)\) and space \(S(n)\) when every input of length \(n\) halts within those respective bounds. Thus arithmetic on encoded integers is charged according to the bit-level transitions required, rather than as a single operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Turing cost model counts elementary transitions and visited work cells on binary inputs, so arithmetic cost depends on operand encoding length.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal machine structure, transition semantics, initial configuration, and halting convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(k\ge 1\), a deterministic \(k\)-tape Turing machine is a tuple \(M=(\Gamma,Q,\delta)\), where \(\Gamma\) is a finite alphabet containing designated symbols \(\square,\vartriangleright,0,1\), \(Q\) is a finite state set containing \(q_{\mathrm{start}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{halt}}\), and \(\delta:Q\times\Gamma^k\to Q\times\Gamma^{k-1}\times\{L,S,R\}^k\). The first tape is read-only; the remaining \(k-1\) tapes are read-write, with the last serving as output. A transition updates the state and symbols on the read-write tapes and moves each head left, right, or not at all, with a left move at a tape's left boundary leaving the head fixed. On input \(x\), all heads begin at the left ends in state \(q_{\mathrm{start}}\); the input tape contains \(\vartriangleright x\) followed by blanks, and each other tape contains \(\vartriangleright\) followed by blanks. The state \(q_{\mathrm{halt}}\) admits no further tape or state modification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic k-tape Turing machine has a finite tape alphabet, a finite state set, and a transition function that reads all k tapes, writes only on the k−1 work tapes, changes state, and moves each head left, right, or stays put. The first tape is read-only and the last work tape is the output tape. Computation begins from the designated start configuration, and the halting state permits no further modification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M=(\Gamma,Q,\delta),\qquad \delta:Q\times\Gamma^k\to Q\times\Gamma^{k-1}\times\{L,S,R\}^k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Worst-case DTM time complexity and polynomial time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures running time by transition steps and maximizes over inputs of a fixed positive length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The time used by a DTM program \(M\) on input \(x\) is the number of computation steps taken before a halt state is entered. If \(M\) halts on every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), its worst-case time-complexity function is \[T_M(n)=\max\{m:\exists x\in\Sigma^*,\ |x|=n,\text{ and the computation of }M\text{ on }x\text{ takes }m\text{ steps}\},\qquad n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}.\] The program \(M\) is polynomial-time if there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that \(T_M(n)\le p(n)\) for every \(n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The running time of a DTM on an input is its number of steps before halting. For a machine that halts on every input, its time complexity at length n is the maximum running time over all inputs of that length. It is polynomial-time when one polynomial bounds this function for every positive input length.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a DTM program with input alphabet }\Sigma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_M(n)=\max_{x\in\Sigma^*,\ |x|=n}\operatorname{time}_M(x),\qquad M\text{ is polynomial-time}\iff\exists p\text{ polynomial }\forall n\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ T_M(n)\le p(n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Running Time of a Multi-Oracle Turing Machine
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case step count parameterized by input length and polynomial oracle-answer bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle call counts as one machine step, although reading its returned string may require additional steps. For a \(k\)-oracle Turing machine \((T;\Pi_1,\ldots,\Pi_k)\), let \(\widetilde\Phi_i=\{(\sigma,\tau)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\{0,1\}^*: \operatorname{len}(\tau)\le\Phi_i(\operatorname{len}(\sigma))\}\). Its running-time function \(f:\mathbb N\times\mathrm{POL}^k\to\mathbb N\) is defined by letting \(f(n;\Phi_1,\ldots,\Phi_k)\) be the maximum number of steps over all inputs of encoding length at most \(n\) and all possible answers supplied during execution by the restricted oracle relations \(\Pi_i\cap\widetilde\Phi_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle call costs one step, while reading its answer can cost additional ordinary steps. For given input and answer-length bounds, running time is the maximum step count over all inputs within the input-length bound and all possible valid oracle answers within the specified polynomial bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(n;\Phi_1,\ldots,\Phi_k)=\max_{\substack{\operatorname{len}(u)\le n\\\text{answers from }\Pi_i\cap\widetilde\Phi_i}}\{\text{number of machine steps on }u\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Turing Machine, Computation, Time, and Output
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a deterministic one-tape Turing machine with a bi-infinite tape and its finite or infinite execution on a finite input string.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be an alphabet and \(\bar A=A\cup\{\sqcup\}\). A Turing machine is a function \(\Phi:\{0,\ldots,N\}\times\bar A\to\{-1,�\ldots,N\}\times\bar A\times\{-1,0,1\}\) for some \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\). On input \(x\in A^*\), the initial instruction is \(0\), the symbols of \(x\) occupy tape positions \(1,\ldots,\operatorname{size}(x)\), all other positions are blank, and the head is at position \(1\). Each transition changes the instruction, writes one symbol, and moves the head by \(-1\), \(0\), or \(1\). If instruction \(-1\) is reached after \(i\) transitions, then \(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x):=i\), and the output is the tape prefix in positions \(1,\ldots,k\), where \(k\) is one less than the first nonnegative tape position containing a blank. If instruction \(-1\) is never reached, then \(\operatorname{time}(\Phi,x):=\infty\) and \(\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)\) is undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic one-tape Turing machine uses the current instruction and scanned symbol to choose the next instruction, symbol to write, and a movement left, stationary, or right. The finite input begins at tape position 1 and all other positions are blank. Reaching instruction -1 defines halting time and an output given by the tape prefix before its first blank. A nonhalting computation has infinite runtime and undefined output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)<\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)\in A^*,\qquad \operatorname{time}(\Phi,x)=\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{output}(\Phi,x)\text{ is undefined}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Turing Machine and Its Step-Count Cost Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the deterministic Turing-machine components, transition rule, and step-count running-time measure, with linear programming as an illustrative encoded task.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Turing machine consists of a tape of discrete cells containing symbols from a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a read-write head that moves one cell left or right, and a finite-state controller. At each step, the current state and scanned symbol uniquely determine the next state, the symbol written, and the head movement. For a terminating computation on an encoded instance \(I\), the running time is the number of machine steps executed before termination. Illustratively, an LP instance \((A,b,c)\) may produce an encoded primal-dual solution \((x^*,\lambda^*,s^*)\) or a designated symbol indicating primal infeasibility, dual infeasibility, or both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Turing machine has a tape over a finite alphabet, a movable read-write head, and a finite-state controller. Each current-state and scanned-symbol pair uniquely determines the next state, written symbol, and one-cell movement. For a terminating computation, running time is the number of steps before termination. As an illustration, an encoded linear program may output a primal-dual solution or a symbol indicating primal or dual infeasibility, or both.
assumptions_latex: \Sigma\text{ is finite, and the controller has finitely many states.}
\text{Each current-state/scanned-symbol pair specifies exactly one state update, written symbol, and left-or-right head move.}
\text{The instance and output are encoded in the machine alphabet.}
\text{The step-count running time is stated for a computation that terminates.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(I)=\#\{\text{Turing-machine steps executed on encoded instance }I\text{ before termination}\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal simulation of encoded Turing machines with logarithmic-factor time overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a Turing machine \(\mathcal U\) such that, for every \(x,\alpha\in\{0,1\}^*\), \(\mathcal U(x,\alpha)=M_\alpha(x)\), where \(M_\alpha\) is the Turing machine encoded by \(\alpha\). Moreover, if \(M_\alpha\) halts on \(x\) within \(T\) steps, then \(\mathcal U(x,\alpha)\) halts within \(CT\log T\) steps, where \(C\) is independent of \(|x|\) and depends only on the alphabet size, number of tapes, and number of states of \(M_\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An efficient universal Turing machine simulates every encoded Turing machine on every binary input. If the simulated machine halts within T steps, the universal machine halts within C T log T steps, with C independent of the input length and dependent only on the simulated machine's alphabet size, tape count, and state count.
assumptions_latex: M_\alpha\text{ is the Turing machine encoded by }\alpha
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal U(x,\alpha)=M_\alpha(x)\quad\text{and, under the halting assumption, }\operatorname{time}_{\mathcal U}(x,\alpha)\le CT\log T.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algorithmic solvability and undecidability of the halting problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the extract's characterization of an algorithm with its central impossibility result.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm is a precise, unambiguous procedure applicable to every instance of a rigorously defined computational problem and guaranteed to terminate with the correct answer. Algorithms can be formalized by Turing machines. The halting problem asks, for an arbitrary program $P$ and input $x$, whether $P(x)$ eventually halts; no algorithm decides this question correctly for every pair $(P,x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm is a precise and unambiguous procedure that applies to every instance of a well-defined computational problem and always terminates with the correct answer; Turing machines provide a rigorous formalization. There is no algorithm that correctly determines for every program and input whether the program will eventually halt.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is an arbitrary program and }x\text{ is an arbitrary input to }P.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,H\text{ such that for every }(P,x),\ H(P,x)\text{ terminates and correctly decides whether }P(x)\text{ halts}.

children.title: Binary Encoding Length
children.top_down_role: Instance-size measurement for binary-encoded combinatorial and rational data.

assumptions_latex: Integers use signed binary notation without leading zeroes, except that zero is encoded by one bit.
A rational number is represented in reduced numerator-denominator form with positive denominator.

source_refs.locator: Encoding Length of Numbers p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\mathbb Z\), define its signed binary encoding length by \(\ell(a)=1+\lceil\log_2(|a|+1)\rceil\), where the first bit accounts for sign. If \(r=p/q\in\mathbb Q\) is represented uniquely with \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), define \(\ell(r)=\ell(p)+\ell(q)\). For a finite vector or matrix of rational entries, its encoding length is the sum of the entry lengths plus a fixed self-delimiting encoding of its dimensions. Polynomial-time bounds are measured as functions of this total length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary encoding length counts the bits for signed integers, reduced rational numerators and denominators, and the dimensions and entries of finite arrays.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines encoding-robust polynomial relationships between alternative instance measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two length functions \(L,L':D_\Pi\to\mathbb Z_{>0}\) are polynomially related if there exist polynomials \(p,p'\) such that, for every \(I\in D_\Pi\), \(L(I)\le p'(L'(I))\) and \(L'(I)\le p(L(I))\). assumptions_latex: Each rational is stored as a reduced pair \((p,q)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z_{>0}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent \(p/q\in\mathbb Q\) by coprime integers \((p,q)\) with \(q>0\). For operands \(p/q\) and \(r/s\), compute addition as \((ps+rq)/(qs)\), multiplication as \((pr)/(qs)\), and division, when \(r\ne0\), as \((ps)/(qr)\); subtraction is analogous. After each operation, divide numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor and make the denominator positive. Compare two rationals by the exact sign of \(ps-rq\). The output is therefore the canonical reduced result, while bit cost depends on the lengths of all intermediate integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact rational arithmetic stores reduced fractions, applies integer formulas, normalizes by a greatest common divisor, and compares by cross multiplication without rounding.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoding-Length Bounds for Products and Determinants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output encoding-length bounds for rational multiplication and determinants, including the sharper integral-matrix case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For all $r,s\in\mathbb Q$, $\langle rs\rangle\le\langle r\rangle+\langle s\rangle$. For every $D\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}$, $\langle\det D\rangle\le 2\langle D\rangle-n^2$. If $D\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}$, then $\langle\det D\rangle\le\langle D\rangle-n^2+1$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blum–Shub–Smale machine over a ring or field
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the machine states, direct algebraic storage, fixed update functions, register, and input-size convention described in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A BSS machine over K has tape cells containing elements of K, with only finitely many cells initially nonblank. Its states include shift states, branch states that test whether the scanned value equals a specified a\in K, and computation states that replace the scanned value a by a fixed value f(a). In the ring model f is polynomial over K; in the field model f=p/q is rational, where p,q\in K[x] and q is not the zero polynomial. The fixed function is representable using a constant number of elements of K. A register can receive the scanned value and be used in computation. Time and space are measured as functions of the number of cells occupied by the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A BSS machine stores ring or field elements directly in tape cells and has separate shift, equality-branch, and algebraic-computation states. Its fixed update is polynomial in the ring model and rational in the field model, and it may use a register containing the scanned value. Input size is the number of cells occupied by the input.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is the ring or field over which the machine operates}
\text{Only finitely many tape cells are initially nonblank}
f\in K[x]\text{ in the ring model, or }f=p/q\text{ with }p,q\in K[x]\text{ and }q\not\equiv0\text{ in the field model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{This defines an algebraic machine model whose time and space are measured against the number of input-occupied cells.}

children.title: Random-Access Machine Model
children.top_down_role: Memory-access assumptions used in combinatorial runtime analysis.

assumptions_latex: Memory consists of addressable words indexed by nonnegative integers.
The instruction set and word-cost convention are fixed independently of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is \(T_P(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{h(x)}c_t\), where \(c_t\) is the prescribed cost of instruction \(t\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General RAM framework encompassing unit-cost and length-sensitive instruction charges.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 The random access machine p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A random-access machine has finitely many registers and an unbounded array of addressable words. A fixed program \(P\) applies instructions for loading constants, copying, indirect addressing, branching, comparison, and specified arithmetic operations. Any word can be accessed by its address without scanning preceding memory. If the computation on input \(x\) halts after \(h(x)\) instructions and the cost assigned to its \(t\)-th instruction is \(c_t\), then its running time is \(T_P(x)=\sum_{t=1}^{h(x)}c_t\). A complexity claim in this model must state whether \(c_t\) is uniform or depends on operand lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A RAM directly accesses addressed words and executes a fixed instruction set; its running time sums the costs assigned to executed instructions.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Access Machine Model

children.title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Model
children.top_down_role: Operation-count analysis treating arithmetic primitives as unit-cost operations.

assumptions_latex: The computation uses a random-access machine.
Every permitted arithmetic, comparison, branch, and memory-access instruction has cost one, regardless of operand magnitude.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_P(x)=h(x)\), the number of executed machine instructions.

notation.meaning: executed instruction count on input x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost specialization of the RAM model, including arithmetic on stored words.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 The random access machine p. 39

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unit-cost arithmetic RAM model, each permitted instruction has cost \(1\), including memory access, comparison, branching, and arithmetic operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and exact division when defined. Consequently, if a program \(P\) executes \(h(x)\) instructions on input \(x\), then \(T_P(x)=h(x)\). The charge is independent of the binary lengths of operands and results. Therefore an operation-count bound in this model is not by itself a bit-complexity bound unless all encountered word lengths are also polynomially bounded in the input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-cost model charges one step per permitted RAM operation, even for large operands, so operation counts need not equal bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Cost Arithmetic Model

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2 The random access machine p. 39

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation counting and input-size conventions in the arithmetic model, contrasted with bit-level Turing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the arithmetic model, each addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, or comparison counts as one elementary operation. Input size is the number of numerical input entries, without charging for their individual encoding lengths. Bits encoding nonnumerical input are treated as numerical entries, and elementary nonnumeric updates are charged as operations. Thus standard multiplication of two $n\times n$ matrices takes $O(n^3)$ arithmetic operations, whereas its Turing-model running time also depends on the entries' encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arithmetic model treats basic arithmetic operations and comparisons as unit-cost steps and measures input size by the number of input numbers rather than their bit lengths. Encoded nonnumeric data and elementary nonnumeric actions are counted analogously.
assumptions_latex: \text{addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and comparison have unit cost}
n\in\mathbb N\text{ for the matrix-multiplication illustration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{arith}}(\text{standard }n\times n\text{ matrix multiplication})=O(n^3)

children.title: Arithmetic-Cost Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by operand size or arithmetic-cost assumptions.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm performs \(N(x)\) arithmetic or memory operations on input \(x\).
Every operand encountered has binary length at most \(B(x)\).
A corresponding bit implementation charges each operation according to operand length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unit-cost polynomiality transfers to bit polynomiality only when both \(N(x)\) and the relevant length-dependent operation costs are polynomial in \(\ell(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer criterion between arithmetic-operation counts and bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm executes \(N(x)\) abstract operations and every intermediate operand has length at most \(B(x)\). If each corresponding bit operation on operands of length at most \(B\) costs at most \(C(B)\), then the implemented running time is bounded by \(O(N(x)C(B(x)))\), up to representation-management overhead. Hence a polynomial unit-cost bound yields a polynomial bit bound when \(N(x)\), \(B(x)\), and \(C(B(x))\) are polynomial in \(\ell(x)\). Without a polynomial bound on intermediate lengths, a polynomial arithmetic-operation count may conceal superpolynomial bit cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operation-count complexity transfers to bit complexity only when intermediate numbers and the bit costs of their operations remain polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-Cost Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transfer principle is appropriately scoped and mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the stated bit-cost transfer bound or its representation-overhead qualification.

children.title: Succinct Instance Encodings
children.top_down_role: Compressed representations whose described objects may be much larger than their encodings.

assumptions_latex: A finite object \(I\) is generated by a finite binary description \(d\).
A fixed deterministic interpreter maps valid descriptions to represented instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The succinct size is \(|d|\), which can be exponentially smaller than the size of an explicit listing of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-based representation whose description may be much smaller than its expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a deterministic interpreter \(G\). A succinct encoding of an instance \(I\) is a finite binary description \(d\) satisfying \(G(d)=I\), where \(d\) specifies a circuit, formula, program, or other compact generator rather than listing all components of \(I\). The represented input size is \(|d|\), not the length of an expanded explicit encoding of \(I\). The expansion size may be exponential in \(|d|\); consequently, an algorithm polynomial in the explicit size need not be polynomial in the succinct size. The interpreter \(G\) is part of the representation class and must be fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A succinct encoding uses a fixed compact generator; complexity is measured by the description length, even when the generated explicit instance is exponentially larger.
knowledge_statements.title: Succinct Instance Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly makes the interpreter part of the representation class and says that exponential compression may occur, but no inspectable source supports this representation-sensitive complexity claim.

children.title: Oracle-Access Encodings

assumptions_latex: The instance contains an implicit object accessible through a specified oracle \(O\).
Each legal query and answer has a finite encoding under a fixed query protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle complexity records the number of calls to \(O\), together with any separately charged local computation and query lengths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box input representation with an explicit query protocol and cost convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle-access encoding specifies an instance through a black box \(O\) and a query domain. On a legal query \(q\), the algorithm receives the exact response \(O(q)\), such as a value, membership answer, separation witness, or optimization result. The oracle protocol fixes the admissible queries, response format, and cost of a call. Query complexity is the number of oracle calls; total complexity additionally charges local computation and, when required, the lengths of queries and responses. Claims made in this representation are relative to the chosen oracle and do not automatically imply complexity bounds for an explicit implementation of \(O\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle encoding exposes instance information through specified queries; complexity must distinguish oracle calls from local work and from implementing the oracle.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Access Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits oracle-access encodings and distinguishes query cost from local and implementation cost, but the broad oracle protocol conventions require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boolean satisfiability and its NP certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean expressions generated from variables by conjunction, disjunction, and negation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Boolean expressions are generated inductively from variables using \((v\land w)\), \((v\lor w)\), and \(\neg v\). An expression \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) is satisfiable if \(\exists(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)\in\{0,1\}^k\) such that \(f(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)=1\). The decision problem \(\mathrm{SAT}\) is the set of satisfiable Boolean expressions, and \(\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{NP}\) because a satisfying assignment is a polynomial-time checkable positive certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boolean expressions are built from variables using AND, OR, and NOT. An expression is satisfiable if some zero-one assignment makes it true. SAT consists of all satisfiable Boolean expressions and belongs to NP because a satisfying assignment can be checked in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathrm{SAT}\iff\exists\alpha\in\{0,1\}^k\;f(\alpha)=1,\qquad \mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{NP}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truth Assignments, Literals, Clauses, and CNF Satisfiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the elementary objects and satisfaction semantics of Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a finite set of Boolean variables. A truth assignment is a function $T:X\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}$, extended to $L:=X\mathbin{\dot\cup}\{\bar x:x\in X\}$ by assigning $\bar x$ the truth value opposite to that of $x$. The elements of $L$ are literals. A clause over $X$ is a set of literals and is satisfied by $T$ if and only if at least one of its literals is true. A family $\mathcal C$ of clauses is satisfiable if and only if some truth assignment satisfies every clause; it represents the conjunctive-normal-form formula $\bigwedge_{C\in\mathcal C}\bigvee_{\ell\in C}\ell$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite set of Boolean variables, a truth assignment assigns true or false to each variable and the opposite value to its negation. A clause is a set of literals interpreted as their disjunction. A family of clauses is satisfiable exactly when one assignment satisfies every clause, and it represents a conjunctive-normal-form formula.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is a finite set of Boolean variables.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal C\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \exists T:X\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\;\forall C\in\mathcal C\;\exists \ell\in C:\ T(\ell)=\mathrm{true}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold decisions, optimum recovery, and good characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational-valued optimization with a bound on the encoding size of the optimum; the certificate conclusion additionally assumes a min–max equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)\), where \(f:X\to\mathbb{Q}\), the associated threshold problem asks whether \(\exists x\in X\) such that \(f(x)\le r\) for a given \(r\in\mathbb{Q}\). If the encoding size of the minimum value is bounded by \(\beta\), its value can be found by binary search using \(O(\beta)\) threshold questions, so polynomial-time decision algorithms usually yield polynomial-time optimization algorithms; analogously for maximization. If \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)=\max_{y\in Y}g(y)\), then \(\min f\le r\) is certified by an \(x\in X\) with \(f(x)\le r\), whereas \(\min f>r\) is certified by a \(y\in Y\) with \(g(y)>r\). The min–max relation is a good characterization, and the problem is well-characterized, when both certificate types are polynomial-time checkable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational optimization problem has a threshold decision form. Given a bound on the encoded size of its optimum, binary search can recover the optimum using linearly many threshold questions in that bound. A min–max equality also supplies certificates for both possible threshold outcomes; it is a good characterization when those certificates are polynomial-time checkable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OptVal}\text{ can be recovered using }O(\beta)\text{ threshold questions, and the min–max equality gives checkable certificates for both threshold outcomes when their verification is polynomial-time.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial equivalence of set optimization and threshold decision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization-to-decision equivalence for integer-weighted feasible subsets, preserving the possibility of infeasibility and the stated hardness transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal F'\) be infinite families of finite sets. Given \(E\in\mathcal F\) and \(c:E\to\mathbb Z\), let \(\mathcal P\) minimize \(c(F)\) over sets \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \(F\in\mathcal F'\), or decide that no such set exists. Then \(\mathcal P\) is solvable in polynomial time if and only if the problem of deciding, for an instance \((E,c)\) and an integer \(k\), whether \(\operatorname{OPT}((E,c))\le k\) is solvable in polynomial time. If \(\mathcal P\) is NP-hard, then this threshold decision problem is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer-weighted feasible-subset optimization over families of finite sets, polynomial-time optimization is equivalent to polynomial-time threshold decision, while allowing that no feasible subset may exist. If the optimization problem is NP-hard, its threshold decision problem is also NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F,\mathcal F'\text{ are infinite families of finite sets}
\{F\subseteq E:F\in\mathcal F'\}\text{ is the feasible-set family, which may be empty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\in\mathrm P\iff\bigl[(E,c,k)\mapsto(\operatorname{OPT}((E,c))\le k)\bigr]\in\mathrm P;\qquad \mathcal P\text{ NP-hard}\Rightarrow\text{the threshold decision problem is NP-hard.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the class using logarithmically many random bits, a constant number of nonadaptive proof queries, perfect completeness, and soundness strictly below one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y)\) be a decision problem. For a polynomial \(p\), put \(m(x)=\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor\) and \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor\). Then \((X,Y)\in\operatorname{PCP}(\log n,1)\) if there exist \(k\in\mathbb N\), a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that \(f(x,r)\in\{1,\ldots,m(x)\}^k\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(r\in\{0,1\}^{\ell(x)}\), and a decision problem \((X',Y')\in P\), where \(X'=\{(x,\pi,\gamma):x\in X,\ \pi\in\{1,\ldots,m(x)\}^k,\ \gamma\in\{0,1\}^k\}\), satisfying: if \(x\in Y\), some \(c\in\{0,1\}^{m(x)}\) has \(\Pr_r[(x,f(x,r),c_{f(x,r)})\in Y']=1\); if \(x\notin Y\), every \(c\in\{0,1\}^{m(x)}\) has \(\Pr_r[(x,f(x,r),c_{f(x,r)})\in Y']<\tfrac12\). In both cases \(r\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\ell(x)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem is in PCP(log n, 1) when a polynomial-time verifier uses logarithmically many uniformly random bits to select a constant number of proof positions, accepts every yes-instance with probability one for some polynomial-length proof, and accepts any proof for a no-instance with probability strictly less than one half.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a polynomial and \(k\in\mathbb N\) is constant.
The query map \(f\) is polynomial-time computable and returns \(k\) valid proof positions.
The verifier decision problem \((X',Y')\) belongs to \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (X,Y)\in\operatorname{PCP}(\log n,1)\iff\text{the stated perfect-completeness and soundness conditions hold}.

knowledge_statements.title: Witness Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary prefix self-reduction for polynomially bounded witnesses, with explicit witness recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First query whether \(R(x)\neq\varnothing\); if not, output \(\bot\). Otherwise initialize \(u:=\epsilon\). Before extending \(u\), test whether \(u\in R(x)\), and output \(u\) if so. For each remaining position up to \(p(|x|)\), query whether a witness in \(R(x)\) has prefix \(u0\). If so, set \(u:=u0\); otherwise query whether a witness has prefix \(u1\) and set \(u:=u1\) when the answer is affirmative. After each extension, test whether \(u\in R(x)\). The initial query and at most two prefix queries per position use at most \(2p(|x|)+1\) oracle calls; witness-membership tests are performed directly by the assumed verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prefix-feasibility oracle and an efficient witness verifier recover a bounded binary witness by retaining a feasible prefix one bit at a time.
assumptions_latex: Witnesses are binary strings of length at most \(p(|x|)\).
For every prefix \(u\), the oracle decides whether some witness in \(R(x)\) begins with \(u\).
Membership \((x,u)\in R\) is decidable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(2p(|x|)+1\) prefix-feasibility oracle calls either construct a witness in \(R(x)\) or determine that \(R(x)=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The usual decision-to-search reduction requires that, for every prefix \(u\), the predicate \(R_u(x)\neq\varnothing\), where \(R_u(x)=\{y\in R(x):u\preceq y\}\), be representable by a polynomial-size instance accepted by the decision oracle. It also requires polynomially bounded witness length. children.title: Value-to-Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which value access supports recovery of an optimal object.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-to-Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimization with polynomially bounded, self-delimiting binary solution encodings and polynomial-time restriction closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Query \(v^*(x)\); if the answer is \(\bot\), output \(\bot\). Otherwise initialize \(u:=\epsilon\). If \(u\) is a complete feasible encoding with objective value \(v^*(x)\), output it. Otherwise query \(v_{u0}^*(x)\); when it equals \(v^*(x)\), set \(u:=u0\). If it does not, query \(v_{u1}^*(x)\) and set \(u:=u1\), which must preserve the optimum. After each extension, test whether \(u\) is a complete feasible encoding attaining \(v^*(x)\), and stop when it is. The initial query and at most two restricted-value queries per bit use at most \(2p(|x|)+1\) value-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact value oracle recovers an optimal self-delimiting binary solution by retaining a prefix whose restricted optimum equals the original optimum and stopping when that prefix is a complete optimal encoding.
assumptions_latex: Feasible solutions have self-delimiting binary encodings of length at most \(p(|x|)\).
Whether a string is a complete feasible encoding and its objective value are computable in polynomial time.
Prefix-restricted instances are constructible with encoding length polynomial in \(|x|+|u|\).
An exact value oracle returns the restricted optimum \(v_u^*(x)\), or \(\bot\) when no feasible solution extends \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A solution attaining \(v^*(x)\) is recovered using at most \(2p(|x|)+1\) exact value-oracle calls.

notation.meaning: Optimum among feasible solutions whose encodings extend prefix u

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Listing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes total output-polynomial time from the stronger polynomial-delay guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(x)\) be the total encoded length of all witnesses emitted on instance \(x\), and let \(T(x)\) include computation and writing time. A complete duplicate-free listing algorithm is output-polynomial if some polynomial \(q\) satisfies \(T(x)\leq q(|x|+L(x))\). It has polynomial delay if the time before the first output, between consecutive outputs, and after the last output before termination is bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\). Polynomial delay implies output-polynomial total time when every witness has polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An output-polynomial listing algorithm runs in time polynomial in the combined input and output length. A polynomial-delay algorithm also bounds, polynomially in the input length, the wait before the first output, between consecutive outputs, and between the last output and termination.
assumptions_latex: Each output witness has encoding length polynomial in \(|x|\).
Writing one output symbol costs one unit of time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The listing is output-polynomial when \(T(x)\leq q(|x|+L(x))\) for some polynomial \(q\); polynomial delay additionally bounds the initial, inter-output, and final intervals by a polynomial in \(|x|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Class P and examples of polynomial-time recognition problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines P for recognition problems, states its robustness across reasonable computational models, and lists four members of the class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(P\) consists of recognition problems solvable by polynomial-time algorithms. For reasonable models of computation, polynomial-time solvability in one such model implies polynomial-time solvability in the others. The following recognition problems belong to \(P\): deciding whether a graph is connected; deciding whether a digraph \(D=(V,A)\) contains a path from some vertex in \(S\subseteq V\) to some vertex in \(T\subseteq V\); deciding whether a graph has a matching with at least \(k\) edges; and, for a connected graph with edge costs, deciding whether it has a spanning tree of cost at most \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: P is the class of recognition problems solvable in polynomial time, a classification stable across reasonable computational models. Graph connectedness, directed path existence between designated vertex sets, matching-size threshold, and minimum-spanning-tree cost threshold are examples in P.
assumptions_latex: Problems are recognition problems represented by finite inputs.
For directed path existence, \(D=(V,A)\) is a digraph and \(S,T\subseteq V\).
For the matching problem, the input includes a graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\).
For the spanning-tree problem, \(G=(V,E)\) is connected, \(d\) is a cost function on \(E\), and \(L\) is an integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\{A: A\text{ is a recognition problem solvable in polynomial time}\},\quad\text{and the four stated recognition problems are in }P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate-verifier characterization of nondeterministic polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), \[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in\Sigma^*\;\bigl(|y|\leq p(|x|)\ \text{and}\ V(x,y)=1\bigr).\] The string \(y\) is a certificate for membership. No certificate is required to be accepted when \(x\notin L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Class NP contains decision problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-length certificates verifiable in deterministic polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Informal guess-and-check characterization, including its positive-instance running-time convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nondeterministic algorithm solves a decision problem \(\Pi\) when, for every \(I\in D_\Pi\), \(I\in Y_\Pi\) if and only if there exists a guessed structure \(S\) for which the deterministic checking stage halts with answer \(\mathrm{yes}\). It operates in polynomial time if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every \(I\in Y_\Pi\), some such guess produces \(\mathrm{yes}\) within \(p(\operatorname{Length}(I))\) time. Under reasonable encodings, \(\mathrm{NP}\) is the class of decision problems solvable by such polynomial-time nondeterministic algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondeterministic algorithm solves a decision problem exactly when every yes-instance has at least one guess accepted by its deterministic checker and no no-instance has any accepted guess. It is polynomial-time when every yes-instance has an accepting guess checked within a polynomial in the input length; NP consists of decision problems admitting such algorithms under reasonable encodings.
assumptions_latex: \Pi\text{ is a decision problem with domain }D_\Pi\text{ and yes-set }Y_\Pi.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\iff \Pi\text{ is solvable, under a reasonable encoding, by a polynomial-time nondeterministic guess-and-check algorithm.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NP and co-NP certificate properties for weak convex-body problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate definitions account for fuzzy instances by requiring certificates only when the alternative weak conclusion does not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal K\) be a class of named well-bounded convex bodies. Weak membership is in \(\mathcal{NP}\) if, whenever \(y\in S(K,-\delta)\), the assertion \(y\in S(K,\delta)\) has a certificate of length polynomial in the input encoding length; it is in co-\(\mathcal{NP}\) if, whenever \(y
otin S(K,\delta)\), the assertion \(y
otin S(K,-\delta)\) has such a certificate. Weak validity is in \(\mathcal{NP}\) if \(c^Tx<\gamma-\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in S(K,\varepsilon)\) implies that \(c^Tx\leq\gamma+\varepsilon\) for every \(x\in S(K,-\varepsilon)\) has such a certificate; it is in co-\(\mathcal{NP}\) if the existence of \(x\in S(K,-\varepsilon)\) with \(c^Tx>\gamma+\varepsilon\) implies that the existence of \(x\in S(K,\varepsilon)\) with \(c^Tx\geq\gamma-\varepsilon\) has such a certificate. Weak separation is in \(\mathcal{NP}\) if \(y
otin S(K,\delta)\) implies the existence of a polynomially encoded \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), \(\lVert cVert_\infty=1\), for which \(c^Tx\leq c^Ty+\delta\) for every \(x\in S(K,-\delta)\) has a polynomial-length certificate. Weak violation is in \(\mathcal{NP}\) if the existence of \(x\in S(K,-\varepsilon)\) with \(c^Tx>\gamma+\varepsilon\) implies the existence of \(y\in S(K,\varepsilon)\) with \(c^Ty\geq\gamma-\varepsilon\), whose approximate membership has a polynomial-length certificate. By definition, weak violation is in co-\(mathcal{NP}\) when weak validity is in \(\mathcal{NP}\), and weak separation is in co-\(\mathcal{NP}\) when weak membership is in \(\mathcal{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For named well-bounded convex bodies, weak membership, validity, separation, and violation have specialized NP and co-NP certificate definitions. Polynomial certificates are required outside the fuzzy tolerance band, where the competing weak answer is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal K\text{ is a class of named well-bounded convex bodies }(K;n,R,r).
\text{Certificate and auxiliary-output lengths are polynomial in the stated binary input encoding length.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These conditions define the stated NP and co-NP certificate properties for weak membership, validity, separation, and violation.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recognition problem P_1 is in \mathcal{NP} if there exist a certificate-checking algorithm \mathcal{AL} and a polynomial p such that every yes-instance I has a certificate \operatorname{CR}(I), and \mathcal{AL} verifies that certificate in at most p(|I|) steps. Moreover, \mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal{NP}, since a polynomial-time decision algorithm can serve as a verifier with an empty certificate.

Every problem in P is in NP, using an empty certificate and the polynomial-time decision algorithm as verifier.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes branchwise acceptance, positive-instance acceptance time, the empty-length convention, and polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an NDTM program \(M\), \(M\) accepts \(x\) if at least one computation generated by a guessed string in \(\Gamma^*\) enters \(q_Y\), and \(L_M=\{x\in\Sigma^*:M\text{ accepts }x\}\). For \(x\in L_M\), its acceptance time is the minimum number of guessing and checking steps among accepting computations. Let \(T_M(n)\) be the maximum of these acceptance times over accepted strings of length \(n\), with \(T_M(n)=1\) if no such string is accepted. The machine is polynomial-time if \(T_M(n)\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\) and every \(n\ge1\), and \(\mathrm{NP}=\{L:\exists\text{ a polynomial-time NDTM }M\text{ with }L_M=L\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NDTM accepts an input when at least one computation branch accepts. Its acceptance time is the shortest accepting-branch time, and its length-n complexity is the largest such time among accepted inputs of that length, set to one if none are accepted. NP is the class of languages recognized by polynomial-time NDTMs.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is an NDTM program over input alphabet }\Sigma\text{ and guessing alphabet }\Gamma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\in\mathrm{NP}\iff\exists M\,\exists p\text{ polynomial}:L_M=L\ \land\ \forall n\ge1,\ T_M(n)\le p(n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: P = NP Implies Polynomial-Time Certificate Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search-to-decision consequence for arbitrary NP languages and their polynomial-time verifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}\). For every language \(L\in\mathbf{NP}\), if a polynomial \(p\) and polynomial-time Turing machine \(M\) satisfy \(x\in L\iff \exists u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\;M(x,u)=1\), then there exists a polynomial-time Turing machine \(B\) such that, for every \(x\in L\), \(B(x)\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) and \(M(x,B(x))=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If P equals NP, then for every NP language and every polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifier characterizing it, a certificate can be constructed in polynomial time for each positive instance.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in L\iff \exists u\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\;M(x,u)=1\), where \(p\) is a polynomial and \(M\) runs in polynomial time
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\) a polynomial-time Turing machine \(B\) such that \(\forall x\in L\), \(B(x)\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}\) and \(M(x,B(x))=1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate-verifier definition using certificates of the source's prescribed polynomial length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(\mathcal P=(X,Y)\) belongs to \(NP\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a decision problem \(\mathcal P'=(X',Y')\in P\), where \[X'=\{x\#c:x\in X,\ c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor}\},\] such that \[Y=\{y\in X:\text{there exists }c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(y))\rfloor}\text{ with }y\#c\in Y'\}.\] Here \(x\#c\) denotes concatenation of \(x\), the symbol \(\#\), and \(c\). A string \(c\) satisfying \(y\#c\in Y'\) is a certificate for \(y\), and an algorithm for \(\mathcal P'\) is a certificate-checking algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem (X,Y) belongs to NP if a polynomial fixes a certificate length and there is a decision problem in P that checks the concatenation of an instance, a separator, and such a certificate. An instance is a yes-instance exactly when at least one certificate of that prescribed length is accepted by the checker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\in NP\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and \(\mathcal P'=(X',Y')\in P\) with \(X'=\{x\#c:x\in X,\ c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(x))\rfloor}\}\) and \(Y=\{y\in X:\exists c\in\{0,1\}^{\lfloor p(\operatorname{size}(y))\rfloor},\ y\#c\in Y'\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Class NP via polynomially bounded certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time verification of polynomial-length certificates for affirmative instances, with explicit one-sidedness and no search requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(\Pi\) belongs to \(\mathcal{NP}\) if and only if there exist a decision problem \(\Sigma\in\mathcal P\) and a polynomial \(\Phi\) such that, for every \(\sigma\in\{0,1\}^*\), \((\sigma,1)\in\Pi\) if and only if there exists \(\tau\in\{0,1\}^*\) for which \(((\sigma,\tau),1)\in\Sigma\) and \(|\tau|\le\Phi(|\sigma|)\). The string \(\tau\) is a succinct certificate. This condition applies only to affirmative instances and does not require an efficient method for finding \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: NP consists of decision problems whose yes-instances have polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time. It does not require certificates to be found efficiently or impose an analogous certificate condition on no-instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\in\mathcal{NP}\iff\exists\Sigma\in\mathcal P\;\exists\Phi\text{ polynomial}\;\forall\sigma:\ (\sigma,1)\in\Pi\iff\exists\tau:\ ((\sigma,\tau),1)\in\Sigma\land |\tau|\le\Phi(|\sigma|).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Sigma\) be a fixed finite alphabet containing a distinguished separator symbol \(\$\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recognition problem belongs to NP exactly when a fixed verifier and polynomial bound exist such that an input is a yes instance if and only if it has a certificate of polynomially bounded length that the verifier accepts within polynomially many steps.

The same polynomial \(p\) bounds the certificate length and the certificate-checking algorithm's number of steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\in NP\iff \exists p\,\exists a\,\forall x\in\Sigma^*:\ x\in A\iff \exists c\in\Sigma^*\text{ such that }|c|\le p(|x|)\text{ and }a(x\$c)\text{ answers yes within }p(|x|)\text{ steps}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every language \(L\), deterministic polynomial-time decidability supplies polynomially verifiable witnesses for both membership and nonmembership, so \(\mathbf{P}\subseteq\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\). Polynomial-time nondeterministic computation and its complementary acceptance condition can each be simulated using polynomial space, giving \(\mathbf{NP}\cup\mathbf{coNP}\subseteq\mathbf{PSPACE}\). These containments are unconditional; the equalities \(\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{NP}\), \(\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{coNP}\), and their negations are not assumed.

assumptions_latex: Inputs and witnesses are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet \(\Sigma\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifier characterization of NP with polynomial certificate length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) has polynomially verifiable witnesses if there exist a polynomial \(p\) and a deterministic algorithm \(V\), running in time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\), such that for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\), \[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists y\in\Sigma^*\;\bigl(|y|\le p(|x|)\ \land\ V(x,y)=1\bigr).\] The string \(y\) is a membership certificate. The class of languages admitting such a verifier is exactly \(\mathbf{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP membership claim has a certificate of polynomial length that a deterministic algorithm can verify in polynomial time.

children.title: Good Characterizations
children.top_down_role: Complementary efficiently checkable evidence for opposite outcomes.

assumptions_latex: Instances are finite strings, and both certificate relations are decidable in polynomial time.
Certificate lengths are bounded by polynomials in the instance length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\in\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity-theoretic form of a good characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) has a good characterization when there exist polynomially bounded certificate relations \(R_{+}\) and \(R_{-}\), each decidable in deterministic polynomial time, such that every instance \(x\) satisfies \[x\in L\iff\exists y\,R_{+}(x,y),\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\,R_{-}(x,z).\] Consequently, membership and nonmembership both possess succinct, efficiently checkable certificates, and therefore \(L\in\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\). This conclusion alone does not provide a polynomial-time algorithm deciding \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A good characterization provides short, efficiently checkable certificates for both yes and no instances, placing the decision problem in NP intersect co-NP.
knowledge_statements.title: Good Characterizations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed NP intersect co-NP consequence matches the intended notion of a good characterization, but its historical and technical sense needs an authoritative source. The statement also uses Sigma without introducing it and leaves the domains and explicit polynomial length bounds for y and z implicit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a property \(A\in\mathbf{NP}\), a good characterization consists of a property \(B\in\mathbf{NP}\) such that \(A\iff\neg B\); an equivalent min-max theorem may provide such a characterization. This certificate is polynomially verifiable when feasibility, both objective values, and equality can be checked in polynomial time from \((x,p,d)\).

children.title: Certificate Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on converting complementary certificates into algorithmic tractability.

assumptions_latex: The integer vertex-cover formulation and its linear relaxation are taken on the three-cycle \(C_3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}(C_3)=2>3/2=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(C_3)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality gaps obstruct equivalence between LP certificates and integer optimality certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vertex cover on \(C_3=(V,E)\), consider \(\min\sum_{v\in V}x_v\) subject to \(x_u+x_v\ge1\) for every \(uv\in E\). With \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\), every cover uses at least two vertices, so the optimum is \(2\). After replacing integrality by \(0\le x_v\le1\), the assignment \(x_v=1/2\) has value \(3/2\) and is LP-optimal. Thus LP primal-dual equality certifies only the relaxed optimum; without integrality or another exact min-max theorem, it cannot certify the integer optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a triangle, vertex cover has integer optimum 2 but LP optimum 3/2, so an exact LP certificate does not certify integer optimality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle integrality-gap example is correct and is an appropriate failure boundary, but no source supports the exact formulation or optimum values. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An encoded minimization or maximization problem \(\Pi\) belongs to \(\mathbf{NPO}\) when feasible solutions \(y\) have length polynomially bounded in \(|x|\), feasibility \(R(x,y)\) is decidable in polynomial time, and the integer objective \(m(x,y)\) is computable in polynomial time. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial, strongly polynomial, and weakly polynomial time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial time for rational inputs and its classification by dependence on encoded numerical data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm with rational input is polynomial-time if there is an integer \(k\) such that it runs in \(O(n^k)\) time, where \(n\) is the encoded input size, and every number occurring in intermediate computations can be stored with \(O(n^k)\) bits. An algorithm with arbitrary input is strongly polynomial if there is an integer \(k\) such that it runs in \(O(n^k)\) time on every input consisting of \(n\) numbers and is polynomial-time on rational input. The case \(k=1\) is linear time. An algorithm that is polynomial-time but not strongly polynomial is weakly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial time for rational input requires polynomially many steps in encoded input size and polynomially bounded intermediate encodings. Strong polynomiality instead bounds the step count polynomially in the number of input numbers and also requires polynomial time on rational inputs. Exponent one is linear time; polynomial but not strongly polynomial time is weakly polynomial.
assumptions_latex: n\text{ is encoded input size in the polynomial-time definition}
n\text{ is the number of input numbers in the strongly polynomial definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Weakly polynomial time means polynomial time without strongly polynomial time; }k=1\text{ gives linear time.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial time and transfer from arithmetic to bit complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bit-model polynomial time, gives a sufficient arithmetic-to-bit transfer condition, and preserves the boundary that bit-polynomial solvability does not imply a known arithmetic-model polynomial algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(t\) be the bit length of an encoded input. An algorithm is polynomial-time in the bit model when its bit-operation count is \(O(t^k)\) for some fixed \(k\). If it performs polynomially many elementary arithmetic operations in \(t\), every intermediate number has bit length \(O(t^r)\) for some fixed \(r\), and those arithmetic operations have polynomial bit cost in their operand lengths, then the algorithm is polynomial-time in the bit model. Conversely, the existence of a bit-model polynomial-time algorithm does not establish that an arithmetic-model polynomial-time algorithm is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial time means polynomially many bit operations in the encoded input length. A polynomial arithmetic-operation bound transfers to the bit model when intermediate numbers have polynomially bounded bit length and the elementary arithmetic operations can be implemented in polynomial bit time. The reverse inference is not valid as a statement about known algorithms.
assumptions_latex: t\text{ is the bit length of the encoded input.}
\text{For the transfer claim, the number of elementary arithmetic operations is polynomial in }t.
\text{Every intermediate number has bit length polynomial in }t.
\text{Each elementary arithmetic operation has bit cost polynomial in the operand bit lengths.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{time}_{\mathrm{bit}}(t)=O(t^q)\quad\text{for some fixed }q.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the encoded instance space, feasible-solution relation, objective, optimization goal, heuristics, exact algorithms, and reduction interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An NP optimization problem is a quadruple \(\mathcal P=(X,(S_x)_{x\in X},c,\operatorname{goal})\) such that: \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) is decidable in polynomial time; each \(S_x\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) is nonempty; some polynomial \(p\) satisfies \(\operatorname{size}(y)\le p(\operatorname{size}(x))\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in S_x\); membership in \(\{(x,y):x\in X,\ y\in S_x\}\) is decidable in polynomial time; \(c(x,y)\in\mathbb Q\) is computable in polynomial time; and \(\operatorname{goal}\in\{\min,\max\}\). Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(x)=\operatorname{goal}\{c(x,y):y\in S_x\}\). A heuristic returns a feasible \(y\in S_x\) for every instance, and it is exact if \(c(x,y)=\operatorname{OPT}(x)\) for every instance. The problem has nonnegative weights when \(c\ge0\). It may be represented as the computational problem whose valid outputs are its optimum solutions, so polynomial reductions apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP optimization problem has a polynomial-time recognizable binary instance set, nonempty feasible sets whose solutions have polynomially bounded encoding length and are polynomial-time verifiable, a polynomial-time computable rational objective, and a minimization or maximization goal. OPT is the best feasible objective value. A heuristic returns a feasible solution for every instance and is exact when it always attains OPT. Objectives may additionally be designated nonnegative. Viewing optimum solutions as valid outputs makes polynomial reductions applicable.
assumptions_latex: \(S_x\ne\varnothing\) for every \(x\in X\), feasible solutions have polynomially bounded encoding length, and feasibility is polynomial-time decidable.
\(c:\{(x,y):x\in X,\ y\in S_x\}\to\mathbb Q\) is polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(x)=\operatorname{goal}_{y\in S_x}c(x,y)\), and an algorithm is exact precisely when it returns a feasible \(y\) satisfying \(c(x,y)=\operatorname{OPT}(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic decision algorithm is in the exponential-time regime when its worst-case running time is bounded by \(2^{p(n)}\) for some polynomial \(p\), where \(n\) is total input bit length. The associated class is \[\mathbf{EXP}=\bigcup_{k\ge1}\operatorname{DTIME}(2^{n^k}).\] A bound \(O(c^n\operatorname{poly}(n))\) with fixed \(c>1\) is called single exponential and is a special case. This definition is an upper-bound classification and does not assert that exponential time is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EXP consists of decision problems solvable in deterministic time exponential in a polynomial of the input length; single-exponential time is a narrower regime.
