knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity is measured relative to encoded input length; numerical parameters such as capacities have logarithmic-length encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm is exponential-time if its worst-case running time cannot be bounded by a polynomial in the encoded input length. For instance parameters \(n,m,C,U\), an algorithm is pseudopolynomial-time if its running time is polynomially bounded in the numerical values \(n,m,C,U\), although it need not be polynomially bounded in \(n,m,\log C,\log U\). Thus bounds such as \(O(m+nC)\) and \(O(mC)\) can be exponential in the encoded input length. Under the similarity assumption, pseudopolynomial-time algorithms become polynomial-time algorithms, though their bounds may remain unattractive when \(C\) or \(U\) is a high-degree polynomial in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponential-time algorithm has worst-case running time that is not polynomially bounded by the encoded input length. A pseudopolynomial-time algorithm runs in time polynomial in numerical parameter values such as n, m, C, and U, but not necessarily in their bit lengths. Under the source's similarity assumption, such an algorithm becomes polynomial-time, although its bound may still be large.
assumptions_latex: \text{Numerical parameters such as }C\text{ and }U\text{ contribute through their encoded lengths, including }\log C\text{ and }\log U.
\text{The final polynomial-time conclusion assumes the source's similarity assumption.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(n,m,C,U)=\operatorname{poly}(n,m,C,U)\ \text{need not be }\operatorname{poly}(n,m,\log C,\log U);\ \text{under the similarity assumption it is polynomial-time.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-time and broadly defined exponential-time algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's broad terminology: “exponential time” includes every runtime not polynomially bounded, even functions such as n^{\log n} that are not ordinarily called exponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For functions on nonnegative input lengths, \(f(n)=O(g(n))\) means that there exists a constant \(c\) such that \(|f(n)|\le c|g(n)|\) for every \(n\ge0\). An algorithm is polynomial-time if its time-complexity function \(T(n)\) satisfies \(T(n)=O(p(n))\) for some polynomial \(p\), where \(n\) is the input length. Under the stated broad convention, an algorithm is exponential-time if no polynomial \(p\) satisfies \(T(n)=O(p(n))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Big-O means that one function is bounded in absolute value by a constant multiple of another for every nonnegative input length. An algorithm is polynomial-time when its running time is Big-O of some polynomial in the input length. Under this source's broad convention, every algorithm whose running time has no such polynomial bound is called exponential-time, including nonpolynomial functions that are not exponential in the usual narrow sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{PolyTime}(A)\iff \exists p\text{ polynomial}:T_A(n)=O(p(n));\qquad \operatorname{ExpTime}_{\mathrm{broad}}(A)\iff \nexists p\text{ polynomial}:T_A(n)=O(p(n)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-time consequence and conjectural boundary of NP-completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Informal characterization and the principal polynomial-time consequence of NP-completeness, with the conjectural status of intractability made explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Informally, an NP-complete problem is computationally as hard as every problem in the relevant class. For all NP-complete problems P and Q, if P admits a polynomial-time algorithm, then Q admits a polynomial-time algorithm. Thus, if any NP-complete problem is polynomial-time solvable, all NP-complete problems are. The assertion that no NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm—and hence that exact solution necessarily requires exponential worst-case time—is presented as a conjectural belief, not a proved consequence of NP-completeness. The cited NP-complete problem families include TSP, integer linear programming, satisfiability, and three-matroid intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP-complete problem is informally as hard as every problem in the relevant class. If one NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm, then every NP-complete problem does. NP-completeness alone does not prove that polynomial-time algorithms are impossible or that exponential worst-case time is necessary; those claims are conjectural in the extract. TSP, integer linear programming, satisfiability, and three-matroid intersection are given as examples.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ admits an algorithm polynomial in the encoded input size}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ admits an algorithm polynomial in the encoded input size}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource functions for a fixed encoding and machine model, together with polynomial-resource classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an encoding and a deterministic \(t\)-tape Turing machine algorithm. Its time complexity is \(f(n)=\max\{\operatorname{steps}(I):|I|\le n\}\), and its space complexity is \(g(n)=\max\{\sum_{i=1}^t \operatorname{maxlen}_i(I):|I|\le n\}\), where \(\operatorname{maxlen}_i(I)\) is the maximum tape-string length occurring on tape \(i\) during the computation. The algorithm is polynomial-time, respectively polynomial-space, if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that \(f(n)\le p(n)\), respectively \(g(n)\le p(n)\), for every \(n\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Time complexity is the maximum number of machine steps over instances of encoded length at most n. Space complexity is the corresponding maximum total tape space used. An algorithm is polynomial-time or polynomial-space when the relevant worst-case function is bounded by a polynomial for every input length.
assumptions_latex: \text{the encoding scheme and deterministic }t\text{-tape machine model are fixed}

\text{Polynomial time: }\exists p\in\mathbb R[n]\;\forall n\in\mathbb N,
 f(n)\le p(n);\qquad \text{polynomial space: }\exists p\in\mathbb R[n]\;\forall n\in\mathbb N,

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly polynomial, linear, and semi-strongly polynomial time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-count regimes for inputs divided into numerical parts, including intermediate-number size control and the source's arithmetic-model boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let input part i contain n_i numbers whose maximum encoding size is s_i. An algorithm is strongly polynomial-time if it performs at most p(n_1,\ldots,n_k) operations for some polynomial p independent of s_1,\ldots,s_k, and every number occurring during execution has size O(\max_i s_i). It is linear-time when p may be chosen linear. It is semi-strongly polynomial-time when rounding a rational is counted as one operation. If the problem has no numerical input, strongly polynomial-time and polynomial-time coincide. Under the stated elementary-arithmetic model, computing \lfloor x\rfloor and even deciding whether an integer is odd or even are not strongly polynomial-time operations in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If input part i contains n_i numbers of maximum encoding size s_i, an algorithm is strongly polynomial-time when its operation count is bounded by a polynomial in the array lengths n_i that is independent of the numerical sizes s_i, while every intermediate number has size O(max_i s_i). The corresponding linear-time definition requires a linear operation bound. Semi-strong polynomial time counts rational rounding as one operation. For problems without numerical inputs, strong and ordinary polynomial time coincide. In the stated arithmetic model, rational flooring and integer parity testing are not strongly polynomial-time in general.
assumptions_latex: \text{Input part }i\text{ contains }n_i\text{ numbers of maximum encoding size }s_i.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\le p(n_1,\ldots,n_k)\ \text{with }p\text{ independent of }s_1,\ldots,s_k,\qquad \operatorname{size}(z)=O\!\left(\max_i s_i\right)\ \text{for every intermediate number }z.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the problem's pseudo-polynomial upper bound, fixed-K consequence, and Turing-reduction lower bound without reproducing the reduction proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\), \(s:A\to\mathbb Z_{>0}\), \(B\le s(A)\), and \(K\le2^n\), Kth Largest Subset is solvable in time polynomial in \(|A|\,K\,\log s(A)\), and therefore in polynomial time for each fixed \(K\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Number problem and the polynomial-bound boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines number problems and states when pseudo-polynomial time collapses to polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(\Pi\) is a number problem if there is no polynomial \(p\) such that \(\operatorname{Max}[I]\le p(\operatorname{Length}[I])\) for every \(I\in D_\Pi\). knowledge_statements.title: Many-One Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time many-one reductions between binary decision languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(L,K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(L\) to \(K\) is a total function \(f:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}^*\), computable in deterministic polynomial time, such that for every string \(x\), \[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)\in K.\] Thus one transformed instance and one answer for \(K\) determine the answer for \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time computable transformation maps each source instance to one target instance while preserving yes and no answers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a Karp reduction between decision problems, together with the stated implication and transitivity properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_i=(X_i,Y_i)\) be decision problems. A polynomial transformation from \(\mathcal P_1\) to \(\mathcal P_2\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f:X_1\to X_2\) such that, for every \(x\in X_1\), \[x\in Y_1\iff f(x)\in Y_2.\] Such a transformation is also called a Karp or polynomial-time many-one reduction and implies a polynomial-time Turing reduction. Polynomial-time many-one reductions and polynomial-time Turing reductions are transitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time many-one or Karp reduction maps every yes-instance to a yes-instance and every no-instance to a no-instance through one polynomial-time computable function. Every such reduction is also a polynomial-time Turing reduction, and both reduction relations are transitive.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Turing Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic polynomial-time adaptive oracle reductions between decision languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(L,K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), an adaptive polynomial-time Turing reduction from \(L\) to \(K\) is a deterministic oracle machine \(M^K\) that decides whether \(x\in L\) in time polynomial in \(|x|\). Each oracle query may depend on \(x\), the machine state, and answers to earlier queries. The polynomial running-time bound includes writing every query, so both the number and lengths of queries are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time machine decides the source problem using target-oracle queries whose contents may depend on earlier oracle answers.
assumptions_latex: Oracle membership queries have unit answer cost, while query construction is charged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The existence of \(M^K\) establishes \(L\le_T^p K\).

notation.meaning: machine M with membership-oracle access to K

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polynomial-time reducibility through oracle access to another problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial-time Turing reduction from \Pi to \Pi' is a polynomial one-oracle Turing machine (T;\Pi') that solves \Pi using \Pi' as its oracle. When such a machine exists, \Pi is polynomial-time Turing reducible to \Pi'. In particular, \Pi'\in\mathcal P implies \Pi\in\mathcal P.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem is polynomial-time Turing reducible to another if a polynomial-time oracle machine solves the first using the second as its oracle. A polynomial-time solver for the oracle problem then gives a polynomial-time solver for the source problem.
assumptions_latex: (T;\Pi')\text{ is a polynomial one-oracle Turing machine solving }\Pi
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\le_T^p\Pi',\qquad \Pi'\in\mathcal P\Longrightarrow\Pi\in\mathcal P.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time Turing Reduction of String Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines oracle Turing reducibility for possibly multivalued string relations and records transitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For string relations \(R,R'\) over \(\Sigma\), a polynomial-time Turing reduction from \(R\) to \(R'\) is an oracle Turing-machine program \(M\) such that, for every function \(g:\Sigma^*\to\Sigma^*\) realizing \(R'\), the relativized program \(M_g\) runs in polynomial time and computes a function \(f_M^g\) realizing \(R\). This relation, denoted \(R\propto_T R'\), is transitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time Turing reduction from a string relation R to R' is an oracle program that, for every oracle function realizing R', runs in polynomial time and computes a function realizing R. Polynomial-time Turing reducibility is transitive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\propto_T R'\text{ via }M,\qquad (R\propto_T R'\land R'\propto_T R'')\Rightarrow R\propto_T R''

children.title: Nonadaptive Truth-Table Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions fixing all target queries before receiving answers.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonadaptive Truth-Table Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time nonadaptive truth-table reductions between decision languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(L,K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a polynomial-time truth-table reduction from \(L\) to \(K\) computes from \(x\) a list of queries \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\) and a Boolean function \(g_x:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\), all within time polynomial in \(|x|\), such that \[\mathbf 1_L(x)=g_x\bigl(\mathbf 1_K(q_1),\ldots,\mathbf 1_K(q_m)\bigr).\] Every query is fixed before any oracle answer is received.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All target queries are generated in advance, and a polynomially computed Boolean rule combines their answers into the source answer.
assumptions_latex: The query list and an evaluable representation of \(g_x\) have polynomial size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed computation establishes \(L\le_{tt}^p K\).

children.title: Oracle-Access Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reduction frameworks parameterized by access to an abstract target oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Access Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General oracle-machine formulation underlying query-access reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a computational task and let \(O\) be an oracle mapping admissible query strings to answers. An oracle-access reduction of \(F\) to \(O\) is an algorithm \(A^O\) that, on every valid input \(x\), may submit queries to \(O\) and must output \(F(x)\). Its resource bound charges all ordinary computation and query construction while assigning the stipulated oracle cost to each answer. Adaptivity is permitted unless the reduction definition explicitly forbids it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algorithm solves one task by querying an idealized interface for another task under an explicit cost and adaptivity convention.
assumptions_latex: The admissible queries, oracle answers, and oracle cost convention are specified.
\(F(x)\) is defined for every valid input \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every valid \(x\), the oracle algorithm satisfies \(A^O(x)=F(x)\) within the stated resource bound.

notation.meaning: algorithm A with access to oracle O

children.title: Cross-Interface Reduction Family
children.top_down_role: Transformations among problem interfaces with witness and solution recovery.

children.title: Decision-to-Search Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations using decision access to recover requested objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-to-Search Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direction means solving the decision interface with access to its associated search interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,y)\) be a polynomially decidable relation with polynomially bounded witnesses, let \(D_R(x)=1\) exactly when some \(y\) satisfies \(R(x,y)\), and let \(S_R(x)\) return such a witness or the symbol \(\bot\) when none exists. A decision-to-search reduction is an oracle algorithm that computes \(D_R(x)\) using access to \(S_R\). Canonically, it makes one query and returns \(1\) exactly when the response is not \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The existence decision is obtained from a search oracle by checking whether it returns a witness or reports that none exists.
assumptions_latex: Every witness has length polynomially bounded in \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_R(x)=\mathbf 1[S_R(x)\ne\bot]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The trivial computation is mathematically coherent under the stated total search interface, but no evidence is supplied for calling this direction a decision-to-search reduction or for requiring the search oracle to return a no-witness symbol. A source fixing the directional and interface conventions is required.

children.title: Search-to-Decision Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations using construction access to resolve binary questions.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-to-Decision Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time witness recovery using an associated decision oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,y)\) be a polynomially decidable relation with witnesses bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\), and define \(D_R(x)=1\) exactly when \(\exists y\,R(x,y)\). A search-to-decision reduction is a polynomial-time oracle algorithm \(A^{D_R}\) such that, for every \(x\) with \(D_R(x)=1\), it outputs a string \(y\) satisfying \(R(x,y)\); when \(D_R(x)=0\), it outputs \(\bot\). Existence of such a reduction is an additional self-reducibility property, not automatic for every relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time algorithm uses yes-or-no queries to recover a valid witness; this self-reducibility need not hold for every search relation.
assumptions_latex: Witness length is polynomially bounded in \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_R(x)=1\Rightarrow R(x,A^{D_R}(x))\), and \(D_R(x)=0\Rightarrow A^{D_R}(x)=\bot\).

notation.meaning: existence decision problem for relation R

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional definition correctly notes that witness recovery from a decision oracle is not automatic for every relation. However, no source supports the directional terminology or this exact self-reducibility formulation, so the record cannot be accepted as sourced candidate knowledge.

children.title: Optimization-to-Decision Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations resolving optimization tasks through related decision queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-to-Decision Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-valued bounded minimization reduced to threshold decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*(x)=\min_{y\in F(x)}c(x,y)\), where feasible objective values are integers in a known interval \([L(x),U(x)]\), and let the decision oracle answer whether \(v^*(x)\le t\). Initialize \(\ell=L(x)\) and \(u=U(x)\). While \(\ell<u\), set \(t=\lfloor(\ell+u)/2\rfloor\); replace \(u\) by \(t\) after a yes answer and replace \(\ell\) by \(t+1\) after a no answer. Stop with output \(\ell=v^*(x)\), using at most \(\lceil\log_2(U(x)-L(x)+1)\rceil\) queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary search over a known integer objective range computes the optimum value using threshold-decision queries.
assumptions_latex: Every feasible objective value is integral and lies in the known interval \([L(x),U(x)]\).
The threshold oracle correctly decides whether \(v^*(x)\le t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(v^*(x)\) after at most \(\lceil\log_2(U(x)-L(x)+1)\rceil\) oracle queries.

notation.meaning: known integral range containing the optimum

children.title: Solution-Recovery Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions preserving enough information to reconstruct target solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Recovery Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovers an optimizer from oracle access that initially supplies only objective information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an optimization problem with feasible set \(F(x)\), objective \(c(x,y)\), and optimum value \(v^*(x)\), a polynomial-time solution-recovery reduction is an oracle algorithm \(A^O\) that outputs some \(y^*\in F(x)\) satisfying \(c(x,y^*)=v^*(x)\). The oracle \(O\) exposes only the specified value or restricted-instance interface, and the total number and encoded lengths of queries, together with all non-oracle computation, are polynomial in \(|x|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time oracle procedure reconstructs an actual optimal solution from value information or equivalent queries on restricted instances.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface and query encoding are fixed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition is plausible, but value-oracle and restricted-instance recovery are materially different interfaces, and no citation establishes a common convention covering both. A source must specify the oracle interface and the exact optimizer-recovery guarantee.

children.title: Objective-Structure Preservation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Optimization transformations preserving objective information or feasible-object structure.

children.title: Value-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations retaining exact or controlled objective-value information.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimum-value preservation, allowing an explicitly specified decoding map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be optimization problems with optimum-value functions \(v_P\) and \(v_Q\). An exact value-preserving reduction consists of polynomial-time computable maps \(f\) and \(h\) such that \(f(x)\) is a valid instance of \(Q\) for every valid instance \(x\) of \(P\), and \[v_P(x)=h\bigl(x,v_Q(f(x))\bigr).\] In the strict form, \(h(x,z)=z\), so \(v_P(x)=v_Q(f(x))\). The value identity alone does not require recovery of a source optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transformed problem’s optimum determines the original optimum exactly through a polynomial-time decoder; strict preservation makes the two values equal.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) have well-defined attained optimum values on valid instances.
\(f\) and \(h\) are computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_P(x)=h(x,v_Q(f(x)))\) for every valid source instance \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed decoder identity is internally coherent, but value-preserving reduction has multiple non-equivalent conventions across optimization and approximation literature. No source is supplied for this exact decoder-based convention or its strict subtype.

children.title: Structure-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations retaining relevant feasible-object or incidence structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized definition relative to an explicitly named combinatorial invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\) be optimization problems and let \(\sigma_P,\sigma_Q\) assign a specified combinatorial structure to their instances or feasible solutions. A \(\sigma\)-structure-preserving reduction consists of a polynomial-time instance map \(f\), a polynomial-time solution map \(g_x\), and a declared correspondence \(\phi_x\) such that \(g_x\) maps relevant solutions of \(f(x)\) to solutions of \(x\) and \[\sigma_P\bigl(x,g_x(z)\bigr)=\phi_x\bigl(\sigma_Q(f(x),z)\bigr)\] for every relevant target solution \(z\). The preserved structure and relevance class must be stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduction preserves a named combinatorial invariant through declared instance, solution, and structure correspondences; preservation is meaningless unless that invariant is specified.
assumptions_latex: The structure assignments \(\sigma_P\) and \(\sigma_Q\) and correspondence \(\phi_x\) are explicitly specified.
The instance and solution maps are polynomial-time computable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declared structural correspondence holds for every target solution in the specified relevance class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The title does not identify a particular preserved invariant, and the statement quantifies over a 'relevant' solution class without formally defining that class. Because structure-preserving reduction is domain-dependent and no source fixes this parameterized convention, authoritative evidence and a fully specified relevance domain are required.

children.title: Joint Preservation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on simultaneously retaining objective information and solution structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Preservation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary predicate for reductions required to preserve both objective values and a specified combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let optimization problems \(A,B\) have objective functions \(v_A,v_B\), and let \(S_A,S_B\) be predicates on feasible solutions. A polynomial-time reduction with instance map \(f\) and solution map \(g\) jointly preserves value and structure when computable functions \(a(x)>0\) and \(b(x)\) satisfy \[v_A(g(x,y))=a(x)v_B(y)+b(x)\] for every feasible \(y\) of \(f(x)\), and simultaneously \[S_A(g(x,y))\Longleftrightarrow S_B(y).\] The joint-preservation boundary is reached when no single pair \((f,g)\) satisfies both conditions, even if separate reductions satisfy them individually.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint preservation requires one reduction to transfer both objective values and the chosen structural predicate; separate value- and structure-preserving reductions do not meet this condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are computable in time polynomial in the encoded input and solution lengths.
\(g(x,y)\) is feasible for \(A\) whenever \(y\) is feasible for \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[v_A(g(x,y))=a(x)v_B(y)+b(x)\bigr]\land\bigl[S_A(g(x,y))\Longleftrightarrow S_B(y)\bigr]\)

notation.meaning: Instance and solution maps of the reduction.

review_flags: The intended preservation formalism is not fixed by the supplied path.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed affine value relation, predicate equivalence, and impossibility boundary are mathematically coherent but are not fixed by the path and have no cited source. A source is needed to determine the intended joint-preservation convention.

children.title: Approximation-Preserving Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reduction interfaces transferring approximation behavior; detailed taxonomies are downstream.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Preserving Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General ratio-transfer interface for positive-objective minimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization problems \(A,B\) with positive optima, an approximation-preserving reduction consists of polynomial-time maps \(fightarrow B\) and \(g\rightarrow A\), together with a nondecreasing transfer function \(h:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying \(h(1)=1\). For every instance \(x\) of \(A\) and every feasible solution \(y\) of \(f(x)\), it must satisfy \[\frac{v_A(g(x,y))}{\operatorname{OPT}_A(x)}\le h\!\left(\frac{v_B(y)}{\operatorname{OPT}_B(f(x))}\right).\] Thus any factor \(r\) approximation for \(B\) yields a factor \(h(r)\) approximation for \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduction maps instances and solutions in polynomial time and converts every approximation ratio for the target problem into a controlled ratio for the source problem.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x,y)\) is feasible for \(x\) whenever \(y\) is feasible for \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_B(y)\le r\Longrightarrow R_A(g(x,y))\le h(r)\)
review_flags: Several inequivalent AP-, L-, PTAS-, and gap-reduction conventions exist.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: AP-, L-, PTAS-, and gap-reductions impose inequivalent requirements. No source identifies this ratio-transfer definition, and the displayed descriptions of f and g do not specify their domains and codomains.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Peak Elimination for Polynomial-Time Computable Distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The probability bound applies to the pushforward distribution induced by the constructed encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a polynomial-time computable distribution over strings. There exists a polynomial-time computable function \(g\) such that, for all strings \(x,z,y\), \(g(x)=g(z)\iff x=z\), \(|g(x)|\le |x|+1\), and \(\Pr_{g\circ\mathcal D}[y]\le 2^{-|y|+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every polynomial-time computable distribution admits a polynomial-time computable injective encoding that adds at most one bit and makes every output string's probability at most 2 to the power of one minus its length.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Definition of the Polynomial Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines all three standard class families and records their first two levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\Sigma_0^p=\Pi_0^p=\Delta_0^p=\mathrm P\). For every integer \(k\ge 0\), define \(\Delta_{k+1}^p=\mathrm P^{\Sigma_k^p}\), \(\Sigma_{k+1}^p=\mathrm{NP}^{\Sigma_k^p}\), and \(\Pi_{k+1}^p=\operatorname{co}\!\left(\Sigma_{k+1}^p\right)\). Consequently, \(\Sigma_1^p=\mathrm{NP}\), \(\Pi_1^p=\mathrm{coNP}\), \(\Delta_1^p=\mathrm P\), \(\Delta_2^p=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}\), and \(\Sigma_2^p=\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{NP}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polynomial hierarchy starts with P at level zero. At each next level, Delta is deterministic polynomial time with an oracle for the preceding Sigma level, Sigma is nondeterministic polynomial time with that oracle, and Pi is the complementary class of Sigma. Thus the first Sigma and Pi levels are NP and co-NP, respectively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_{k+1}^p=\mathrm P^{\Sigma_k^p},\quad \Sigma_{k+1}^p=\mathrm{NP}^{\Sigma_k^p},\quad \Pi_{k+1}^p=\operatorname{co}(\Sigma_{k+1}^p).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomially bounded subproblems and strong NP-completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong NP-completeness and records the associated pseudo-polynomial-to-polynomial restriction principle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decision problem \(\Pi\) and an integer polynomial \(p\), define \(\Pi_p=\{I\in\Pi:\operatorname{Max}[I]\le p(\operatorname{Length}[I])\}\). Then \(\Pi_p\) is not a number problem. If \(\operatorname{Max}[I]\) and \(\operatorname{Length}[I]\) are polynomial-time computable and \(\Pi\) has a pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm, then \(\Pi_p\in\mathrm P\). The problem \(\Pi\) is strongly NP-complete when \(\Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\Pi_p\) is NP-complete for some integer polynomial \(p\). In particular, every NP-complete problem that is not a number problem is strongly NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict a decision problem to instances whose largest numerical value is bounded by a polynomial in their encoding length. The restricted problem is not a number problem, and a pseudo-polynomial algorithm for the original problem becomes polynomial on this restriction when the size measures are polynomial-time computable. Strong NP-completeness means that some such restriction remains NP-complete; hence an NP-complete non-number problem is strongly NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a polynomial over the integers.
For the algorithmic implication, \(\operatorname{Max}[I]\) and \(\operatorname{Length}[I]\) are computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_p\) is not a number problem; pseudo-polynomial solvability of \(\Pi\) implies \(\Pi_p\in\mathrm P\); and \(\Pi\) is strongly NP-complete iff \(\Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\Pi_p\) is NP-complete for some \(p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Similarity Assumption and Strong versus Weak NP-Completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the similarity assumption, its consequence for pseudo-polynomial bounds depending on the bounded magnitudes, and the induced strong/weak NP-completeness classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The similarity assumption states that, for some fixed integer $k$, the relevant numerical magnitudes satisfy $C=O(n^k)$ and $U=O(n^k)$. Consequently, a pseudo-polynomial running-time bound whose nonpolynomial input dependence is through $C$ or $U$ becomes polynomial under this assumption; for example, $O(m+nC)=O(m+n^{k+1})$ when $C=O(n^k)$. An NP-complete problem is strongly NP-complete if it remains NP-complete when the similarity assumption is imposed, and weakly NP-complete if it is NP-complete without that restriction but is not NP-complete under the restriction. Knapsack and constrained shortest path are weakly NP-complete, while traveling salesman, Hamiltonian path, longest path, integer generalized flow, and $0$--$1$ integer programming are strongly NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the similarity assumption, relevant numerical magnitudes such as C and U are bounded by a fixed polynomial in the instance dimension. A pseudo-polynomial bound depending on those magnitudes then becomes polynomial. An NP-complete problem is strongly NP-complete if NP-completeness persists under this restriction and weakly NP-complete if it does not. The extract classifies knapsack and constrained shortest path as weak, and traveling salesman, Hamiltonian path, longest path, integer generalized flow, and 0–1 integer programming as strong.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Pseudo-polynomial bounds depending on }C\text{ or }U\text{ become polynomial under the similarity assumption, which distinguishes strong from weak NP-completeness.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The malformed relation-membership notation in the extract is resolved using its explicit explanatory sentence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an NDTM program \(M\), define \(R_M=\{\langle x,y\rangle:\exists z\text{ such that }M\text{ on input }x\text{ and guess }z\text{ halts with output }y\}\). A language \(L_1\subseteq\Sigma_1^*\) is \(\gamma\)-reducible to \(L_2\subseteq\Sigma_2^*\), written \(L_1\propto_\gamma L_2\), if there is a polynomial-time NDTM \(M\) such that \(\forall x\in\Sigma_1^*\), some \(y\in\Sigma_2^*\) satisfies \(\langle x,y\rangle\in R_M\), and \(\forall\langle x,y\rangle\in R_M\), \(x\in L_1\iff y\in L_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gamma reduction is a polynomial-time nondeterministic computation that has at least one halting output on every input and whose every halting output belongs to the target language exactly when the input belongs to the source language.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_1\propto_\gamma L_2\iff \bigl(\forall x\in\Sigma_1^*\ \exists y\in\Sigma_2^*: \langle x,y\rangle\in R_M\bigr)\land\bigl(\forall\langle x,y\rangle\in R_M:\ x\in L_1\iff y\in L_2\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boolean formulas, satisfiability, CNF, and k-CNF
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Boolean-formula evaluation and the CNF representation used by SAT and k-SAT.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Boolean formula \(\varphi\) over variables \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) is formed using \(\land,\lor,\neg\). For \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\), \(\varphi(z)\) is its truth value under assignment \(z\). The formula is satisfiable iff \(\exists z\in\{0,1\}^n\) such that \(\varphi(z)=1\), and is otherwise unsatisfiable. It is in conjunctive normal form if \(\varphi=\bigwedge_i\bigl(\bigvee_j v_{i_j}\bigr)\), where every literal \(v_{i_j}\) is a variable or its negation; each disjunction is a clause. A \(k\)-CNF formula is a CNF formula whose clauses contain at most \(k\) literals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean formula is evaluated under a binary assignment and is satisfiable exactly when some assignment makes it true. A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each clause being a disjunction of variables or their negations. In k-CNF, every clause has at most k literals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \exists z\in\{0,1\}^n:\varphi(z)=1;\quad \varphi\in k\text{-CNF}\iff \varphi\text{ is CNF and every clause has at most }k\text{ literals}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision problems over a finite alphabet, using polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Pi,\Lambda\subseteq\Sigma^*\), \(\Pi\) is polynomial-time reducible to \(\Lambda\) if a polynomial-time algorithm maps each \(w\in\Sigma^*\) to an \(x\in\Sigma^*\) satisfying \(w\in\Pi\iff x\in\Lambda\). Hence \(\Pi\le_p\Lambda\) and \(\Lambda\in\mathrm P\) imply \(\Pi\in\mathrm P\), while \(\Pi\le_p\Lambda\) and \(\Lambda\in\mathrm{NP}\) imply \(\Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\). A problem \(\Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\) is NP-complete if every problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\) is polynomial-time reducible to \(\Pi\). Consequently, if an NP-complete problem belongs to \(\mathrm P\), then \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time many-one reduction transforms each instance of one decision problem into an equivalent instance of another. Such reductions transfer membership in P or NP back to the source problem. An NP problem is NP-complete when every NP problem reduces to it; therefore a polynomial-time algorithm for any NP-complete problem would imply P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\le_p\Lambda\Longrightarrow\bigl(\Lambda\in\mathrm P\Rightarrow\Pi\in\mathrm P\bigr)\land\bigl(\Lambda\in\mathrm{NP}\Rightarrow\Pi\in\mathrm{NP}\bigr),\qquad (\Pi\text{ NP-complete}\land\Pi\in\mathrm P)\Rightarrow\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completeness and Hardness under Polynomial Transformability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General reduction-based definitions used by the classical NP completeness and hardness classifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a class $C$ of languages, $L$ is complete for $C$ with respect to polynomial transformability if $L\in C$ and, for every $L'\in C$, $L'\propto L$. The language $L$ is $C$-hard if, for every $L'\in C$, $L'\propto L$; membership of $L$ in $C$ is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A language is complete for a class when it belongs to that class and every language in the class polynomially transforms to it. It is hard for the class when the transformation condition holds, without requiring membership in the class.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a class of languages.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\text{ is }C\text{-complete}\iff\left(L\in C\land\forall L'\in C,\ L'\propto L\right),\qquad L\text{ is }C\text{-hard}\iff\forall L'\in C,\ L'\propto L.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-time Karp reducibility, NP-hardness, and NP-completeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for binary languages under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(A,B\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), write \(A\le_p B\) if there exists a polynomial-time computable function \(f:\{0,1\}^*\to\{0,1\}^*\) such that \(\forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\ x\in A\iff f(x)\in B\). A language \(B\) is NP-hard if \(\forall A\in\mathbf{NP},\ A\le_p B\), and NP-complete if it is NP-hard and belongs to \(\mathbf{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A is polynomial-time Karp reducible to B when a polynomial-time computable mapping preserves membership in both directions for every binary string. B is NP-hard when every language in NP reduces to it, and NP-complete when it is also in NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\le_p B\iff\exists f\text{ polynomial-time computable }\forall x\,[x\in A\iff f(x)\in B];\quad B\text{ is NP-hard}\iff\forall A\in\mathbf{NP},\ A\le_p B;\quad B\text{ is NP-complete}\iff B\text{ is NP-hard and }B\in\mathbf{NP}.

Moreover, if a \(\Sigma_k^p\)-complete language belongs to \(\Sigma_{k-1}^p\), then \(\Sigma_k^p=\Sigma_{k-1}^p\); the analogous adjacent-level collapse statements hold for the \(\Pi^p\) and \(\Delta^p\) hierarchies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A language is complete for a Sigma level when it belongs to that level and every language in the level polynomially transforms to it; Pi and Delta completeness are defined analogously. If a complete language for level k already lies at level k−1 of the same hierarchy, those two levels coincide, with analogous results for Pi and Delta.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\in\Sigma_{k-1}^p\implies\Sigma_k^p=\Sigma_{k-1}^p,\quad\text{with analogous implications for }\Pi_k^p\text{ and }\Delta_k^p.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Problem restrictions and strong NP classifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines restrictions of decision and optimization problems and then defines strong NP-hardness and strong NP-completeness for numeric-list problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decision problem \(\mathcal P=(X,Y)\) and \(X'\subseteq X\), its restriction is \(\mathcal P'=(X',X'\cap Y)\). For an optimization problem \(\mathcal P=(X,(S_x)_{x\in X},c,\mathrm{goal})\), its restriction is \(\mathcal P'=(X',(S_x)_{x\in X'},c,\mathrm{goal})\). If every instance of \(\mathcal P\) is a list of numbers and \(p\) is a polynomial, let \(\mathcal P_p\) be the restriction to instances \(x\) consisting of nonnegative integers with \(\operatorname{largest}(x)\le p(\operatorname{size}(x))\). Then \(\mathcal P\) is strongly NP-hard if \(\mathcal P_p\) is NP-hard for some polynomial \(p\), and strongly NP-complete if \(\mathcal P\in\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\mathcal P_p\) is NP-complete for some polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restriction retains only instances from a chosen subset, together with the corresponding yes-instances or optimization feasible sets. For problems whose instances are numerical lists, a polynomially magnitude-bounded restriction retains nonnegative-integer instances whose largest number is polynomially bounded by instance size. A problem is strongly NP-hard when one such restriction is NP-hard, and strongly NP-complete when it belongs to NP and one such restriction is NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is a decision or optimization problem}
\mathcal P\text{ has instances consisting of lists of numbers when defining strong NP classifications}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P\text{ is strongly NP-hard}\iff\exists p\;\mathcal P_p\text{ is NP-hard};\qquad \mathcal P\text{ is strongly NP-complete}\iff\mathcal P\in\mathrm{NP}\land\exists p\;\mathcal P_p\text{ is NP-complete}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines PSPACE and polynomial-reduction PSPACE-completeness and records the resulting class-collapse implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \mathrm{PSPACE} is the class of languages recognized by polynomial-space-bounded deterministic Turing machines that halt on every input. A language L is \mathrm{PSPACE}-complete under polynomial-time transformations if L\in\mathrm{PSPACE} and, for every L'\in\mathrm{PSPACE}, L'\le_p L. If L is \mathrm{PSPACE}-complete, then L\in\mathrm P iff \mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE}, and L\in\mathrm{NP} iff \mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}. Moreover, if L\in\Sigma_k^p for some k, then the polynomial hierarchy collapses at level k and \Sigma_j^p=\Sigma_k^p=\mathrm{PSPACE} for every j\ge k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PSPACE consists of languages recognized by polynomial-space deterministic machines that halt on all inputs. A language is PSPACE-complete when it belongs to PSPACE and every PSPACE language polynomially transforms to it. A PSPACE-complete language lies in P exactly when P equals PSPACE, and lies in NP exactly when NP equals PSPACE. If such a language belongs to a fixed level of the polynomial hierarchy, the hierarchy collapses there to PSPACE.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\in\mathrm P\iff\mathrm P=\mathrm{PSPACE};\quad L\in\mathrm{NP}\iff\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{PSPACE};\quad L\in\Sigma_k^p\Rightarrow\forall j\ge k,\ \Sigma_j^p=\Sigma_k^p=\mathrm{PSPACE}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transitivity of Karp reductions and consequences of NP-hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic consequences of polynomial-time Karp reducibility, NP-hardness, and NP-completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages \(A,B,C\): (i) if \(A\le_p B\) and \(B\le_p C\), then \(A\le_p C\); (ii) if \(A\) is NP-hard and \(A\in\mathbf P\), then \(\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}\); (iii) if \(A\) is NP-complete, then \(A\in\mathbf P\iff\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial-time Karp reducibility is transitive. A polynomial-time algorithm for any NP-hard language would imply P equals NP. Consequently, an NP-complete language is in P exactly when P equals NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (A\le_p B\land B\le_p C)\Rightarrow A\le_p C;\quad (A\text{ NP-hard}\land A\in\mathbf P)\Rightarrow\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP};\quad A\text{ NP-complete}\Rightarrow(A\in\mathbf P\iff\mathbf P=\mathbf{NP}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Sufficient Criterion for NP–coNP Collapse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A collapse consequence under the source's stated NP-oracle reduction conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_0,L_1,L_2\) be languages. If \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are NP-complete, \(L_1^c\propto_c^{\mathrm{NP}}L_0\), and \(L_2^c\propto_c^{\mathrm{NP}}L_0^c\), then \[L_0\in\mathrm{NP}\cup\mathrm{coNP}\implies \mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}.\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}

knowledge_statements.title: NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time many-one hardness for decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(H\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions if, for every language \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\), there exists a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that, for every encoded input \(x\), \[x\in L\Longleftrightarrow f(x)\in H.\] Membership of \(H\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\) is not required. For an optimization problem, NP-hardness conventionally means that an associated decision version is NP-hard or that polynomial-time exact optimization would polynomially solve an NP-hard decision problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every problem in NP reduces to an NP-hard problem in polynomial time; the hard problem itself need not belong to NP.
assumptions_latex: Languages use finite encodings, and running time is measured in encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall L\in\mathrm{NP},\;L\le_m^p H\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complement Closure of NP-Hardness Under Turing Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the complement of a decision problem and states the NP-hardness consequence of mutual Turing reducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decision problem \(\Pi\) with domain \(D_\Pi\) and yes-set \(Y_\Pi\), its complement \(\Pi^c\) has domain \(D_\Pi\) and yes-set \(D_\Pi\setminus Y_\Pi\). The problems \(\Pi\) and \(\Pi^c\) Turing-reduce to each other. Hence, if \(\Pi\) is NP-complete or NP-hard, then \(\Pi^c\) is NP-hard, irrespective of whether \(\Pi^c\in\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of a decision problem reverses its yes and no instances on the same domain. A problem and its complement are mutually Turing-reducible, so the complement of an NP-complete or NP-hard problem is NP-hard even though membership of the complement in NP need not be known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi^c=(D_\Pi,D_\Pi\setminus Y_\Pi),\qquad \Pi^c\text{ is NP-hard}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is NP-complete}\Longleftrightarrow C\in\mathrm{NP}\land C\text{ is NP-hard}\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by membership and polynomial reductions, with consequences under the stated separation hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(A\) is NP-complete if \(A\in\mathbf{NP}\) and every problem in \(\mathbf{NP}\) has a polynomial-time reduction to \(A\). Hence a polynomial-time algorithm for any NP-complete problem yields polynomial-time algorithms for every problem in \(\mathbf{NP}\). Under \(\mathbf P\ne\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\), one has \(\mathbf P\cap\mathbf{NPC}=\varnothing\). Graph perfectness belongs to \(\mathbf{NP}\cap\mathbf{coNP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An NP problem is NP-complete when every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. Solving one NP-complete problem in polynomial time would solve every NP problem in polynomial time. Under the stated P versus NP-intersect-co-NP hypothesis, no NP-complete problem lies in P. Graph perfectness lies in both NP and co-NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[(\forall B\in\mathbf{NP})\;B\leq_p A\bigr]\Rightarrow A\in\mathbf{NPC},\qquad \mathbf P\cap\mathbf{NPC}=\varnothing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines NP-completeness and records its polynomial-time solvability consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A decision problem \(B\) is NP-complete if \(B\in\mathrm{NP}\) and, for every decision problem \(A\in\mathrm{NP}\), there is a polynomial-time reduction \(A\le_p B\). Consequently, if \(B\) is solvable in polynomial time, then every problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\) is solvable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision problem B is NP-complete when B belongs to NP and every decision problem in NP can be reduced to B in polynomial time. Therefore, a polynomial-time algorithm for B would yield polynomial-time algorithms for all problems in NP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\in\mathrm{P}\implies \mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{P}\quad(\text{hence }\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP})

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial equivalence and the induced reduction order
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines mutual polynomial reducibility and records the order-theoretic interpretation stated for P and the NP-complete degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Languages L_1 and L_2 are polynomially equivalent exactly when L_1\propto L_2 and L_2\propto L_1; likewise for decision problems. Transitivity of \propto makes mutual reducibility an equivalence relation and induces a partial order on the resulting equivalence classes. In the stated framework, \mathrm P is the least class, while the NP-complete languages form a class containing the hardest languages in \mathrm{NP}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two languages or decision problems are polynomially equivalent when each polynomially transforms to the other. Mutual reducibility partitions problems into equivalence classes, and one-way reducibility orders those classes; in the source's framework, P is least and the NP-complete class is hardest within NP.
assumptions_latex: L_1,L_2\text{ are languages, or }\Pi_1,\Pi_2\text{ are decision problems}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_1\equiv_p L_2\iff(L_1\propto L_2\land L_2\propto L_1),\quad [L_1]\preceq[L_2]\iff L_1\propto L_2

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines clauses of at most three literals, satisfiability by a Boolean assignment, and the resulting decision problem; the extract also classifies it as NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let B_1=\{x_i,\neg x_i:i\ge 1\}. Let B_2 consist of clauses (w_1\vee\cdots\vee w_k) with w_j\in B_1 and 1\le k\le 3, and let B_3 consist of finite conjunctions of clauses from B_2. A formula f\in B_3 is satisfiable if there exists (\alpha_i)_{i\ge1}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N} such that f(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots)=1. The problem 3\text{-SAT} asks, given f\in B_3, whether f is satisfiable; 3\text{-SAT} is \mathcal{NP}\text{-complete}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A 3-SAT instance is a finite conjunction of clauses, each containing between one and three Boolean literals. It is satisfiable when some Boolean assignment makes the formula true. The decision problem asks whether such an assignment exists, and 3-SAT is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 3\text{-SAT asks whether }\exists(\alpha_i)_{i\ge1}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}:f(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\ldots)=1,\quad 3\text{-SAT is }\mathcal{NP}\text{-complete}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines deterministic log-space many-one reducibility between languages over possibly different alphabets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For languages L_1\subseteq\Sigma_1^* and L_2\subseteq\Sigma_2^*, a function f:\Sigma_1^*\to\Sigma_2^* is a log-space transformation from L_1 to L_2 if f is computable by a deterministic Turing machine using at most \left\lceil\log_2 n+1\right\rceil work space on inputs of length n and, for every x\in\Sigma_1^*, x\in L_1\iff f(x)\in L_2. Writing L_1\leq_{\mathrm{LOG}}L_2, this relation implies polynomial-time many-one reducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A log-space transformation maps instances of one language to another using logarithmic deterministic workspace and preserves membership in both directions. Every such reduction is also a polynomial-time reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_1\leq_{\mathrm{LOG}}L_2\implies L_1\leq_p L_2

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines magnitude-restricted problem families and strong NP-completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A$ be a computational problem and $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$. Define $A_f:=\{I\in A:\operatorname{number}(I)\le f(|I|)\}$, where $|I|$ is the encoding length of $I$. The problem $A$ is strongly NP-complete if $A_p$ is NP-complete for some polynomial $p$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict A to instances whose largest numerical value is at most f of their encoding length. A is strongly NP-complete if this restriction is NP-complete for some polynomial bound f=p.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_f:=\{I\in A:\operatorname{number}(I)\le f(|I|)\},\qquad A\text{ is strongly NP-complete}\iff \exists p\text{ polynomial such that }A_p\text{ is NP-complete}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Boolean objects and satisfaction relation underlying SAT.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{u_1,\ldots,u_m\}\) be a finite set of Boolean variables. A truth assignment is a function \(t:U\to\{T,F\}\). For each \(u\in U\), the literals are \(u\) and \(\bar u\); \(u\) is true under \(t\) iff \(t(u)=T\), while \(\bar u\) is true iff \(t(u)=F\). A clause over \(U\) is a set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and is satisfied by \(t\) iff at least one of its literals is true. A collection \(C\) of clauses over \(U\) is satisfiable iff there exists a truth assignment \(t\) satisfying every clause in \(C\); such a \(t\) is a satisfying truth assignment for \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A truth assignment assigns true or false to each Boolean variable. A positive literal is true exactly when its variable is true, and a negated literal is true exactly when its variable is false. A clause is satisfied when at least one of its literals is true. A collection of clauses is satisfiable exactly when some truth assignment satisfies every clause simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: U=\{u_1,\ldots,u_m\}\text{ is a finite set of Boolean variables}
C\text{ is a collection of clauses over }U
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \exists t:U\to\{T,F\}\;\forall K\in C,\;\exists \ell\in K\text{ such that }\ell\text{ is true under }t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to specified numerical-magnitude and encoding-length measures for two decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi=(D_{\Pi},Y_{\Pi})\) and \(\Pi'=(D_{\Pi'},Y_{\Pi'})\) be decision problems equipped respectively with measures \(\operatorname{Max},\operatorname{Length}\) and \(\operatorname{Max}',\operatorname{Length}'\). A pseudo-polynomial transformation from \(\Pi\) to \(\Pi'\) is a function \(f:D_{\Pi}\to D_{\Pi'}\) such that, for every \(I\in D_{\Pi}\): (a) \(I\in Y_{\Pi}\iff f(I)\in Y_{\Pi'}\); (b) \(f(I)\) is computable in time polynomial in \(\operatorname{Max}[I]\) and \(\operatorname{Length}[I]\); (c) for some polynomial \(q_1\), \(\operatorname{Length}[I]\le q_1(\operatorname{Length}'[f(I)])\); and (d) for some two-variable polynomial \(q_2\), \(\operatorname{Max}'[f(I)]\le q_2(\operatorname{Max}[I],\operatorname{Length}[I])\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-polynomial transformation preserves yes-instances in both directions, is computable in time polynomial in the source instance's maximum numerical value and encoding length, does not compress source length beyond a polynomial relation, and bounds the target's maximum numerical value polynomially in the source magnitude and length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is pseudo-polynomial exactly when conditions (a)--(d) hold.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interprets the opening characterization of NP-complete problems as problems in NP. Universal reducibility alone establishes NP-hardness, not NP-completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polynomial-time reduction from a decision problem \Pi' to a decision problem \Pi is a polynomial-time transformation mapping each instance w to an instance v such that w\in\Pi'\iff v\in\Pi. A problem \Pi is \mathcal{NP}\text{-complete} if \Pi\in\mathcal{NP} and, for every \Pi'\in\mathcal{NP}, there exists such a reduction from \Pi' to \Pi.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time reduction transforms instances in polynomial time while preserving yes- and no-answers. A problem is NP-complete when it belongs to NP and every problem in NP polynomial-time reduces to it. The universal-reduction condition without NP membership gives only NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\text{ is }\mathcal{NP}\text{-complete}\iff \Pi\in\mathcal{NP}\ \land\ \forall\Pi'\in\mathcal{NP},\ \Pi'\leq_p\Pi

children.title: Membership Requirement Boundary
children.top_down_role: The verification distinction separating hardness from completeness.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership Requirement Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The additional membership condition separating NP-hardness from NP-completeness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) be NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions. The boundary between NP-hardness and NP-completeness is membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\): there must exist a polynomial \(p\) and a polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that \[x\in H\Longleftrightarrow \exists w\in\{0,1\}^*\;\bigl(|w|\le p(|x|)\land V(x,w)=1\bigr).\] Under the NP-hardness assumption, \(H\) is NP-complete exactly when this certificate condition holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an NP-hard decision problem, NP membership—equivalently, polynomial-size certificates verifiable in polynomial time—is exactly the additional condition required for NP-completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
\(V\) runs in time polynomial in the combined encoded length of \(x\) and \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\text{ is NP-complete}\Longleftrightarrow H\in\mathrm{NP}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Weak NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-versus-unary encoding definition for numeric decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a numeric decision problem whose instances contain nonnegative integers. Write \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\) for ordinary binary encoding and \(P_{\mathrm{unary}}\) for the same problem with every numeric datum encoded in unary. In the encoding-based convention, \(P\) is weakly NP-hard when \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\) is NP-hard but \(P_{\mathrm{unary}}\) is solvable in polynomial time. Thus the hardness depends on the logarithmic compression of potentially large numerical values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numeric problem is weakly NP-hard when binary encoding is NP-hard but replacing all numbers by unary encodings yields a polynomial-time problem.
assumptions_latex: All nondigital combinatorial data retain the same encoding in \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\) and \(P_{\mathrm{unary}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{bin}}\text{ is NP-hard}\land P_{\mathrm{unary}}\in\mathrm{P}\)

children.title: Strong NP-Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness persisting when relevant numerical magnitudes remain polynomially bounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness persisting when all numerical magnitudes are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numeric decision problem \(P\) is strongly NP-hard if there exists a polynomial \(q\) such that the restriction of \(P\) to instances \(x\) whose every numeric datum \(a\) satisfies \(a\le q(|x|)\) remains NP-hard. Equivalently under standard explicit encodings, hardness persists when numerical data are written in unary. Strong hardness therefore cannot be attributed solely to exponentially large binary-encoded numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numeric problem is strongly NP-hard when it remains NP-hard even after all numerical values are restricted to polynomial magnitude, equivalently under standard unary encoding.
assumptions_latex: Instances contain explicitly represented nonnegative integer data.
The bound \(|x|\) measures the nondigital combinatorial encoding together with the bounded numeric encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists q\in\mathbb{Z}[t]\;\text{such that}\;P\!estriction\!\{x:\max a(x)\le q(|x|)\}\text{ is NP-hard}\)

notation.meaning: A numeric datum occurring in instance x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong NP-Hardness and Its Polynomial-Time Consequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strong NP-hardness for search problems through a polynomially bounded NP-hard subproblem and distinguishes its consequence from the biconditional available for NP-complete problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A search problem is strongly NP-hard if it contains an NP-hard subproblem on which the relevant maximum numerical parameter is bounded by a polynomial in the encoded instance size. Any NP-hard problem, including a strongly NP-hard one, cannot be solved in polynomial time unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\); unlike an NP-complete problem, NP-hardness alone does not justify the converse assertion that \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) would make the problem polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search problem is strongly NP-hard when it remains NP-hard on a subproblem whose relevant numerical magnitudes are polynomially bounded. Such a problem cannot be polynomial-time solvable unless P equals NP, but NP-hardness alone does not give the converse implication.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{Max}(I)\le p(|I|)\text{ for instances }I\text{ of }\Pi'\text{ and some polynomial }p
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi\text{ is strongly NP-hard};\qquad \Pi\in\mathrm P\Rightarrow\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}

children.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Tractability Boundary
children.top_down_role: The relationship between numerical magnitude, pseudo-polynomial algorithms, and hardness strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Polynomial Tractability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between pseudo-polynomial algorithms, unary encodings, and strong NP-hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm for a numeric problem runs in time polynomial in the combinatorial encoding length \(n\) and the maximum numeric value \(M\), rather than in \(n+\log M\). It is pseudo-polynomial. On instances satisfying \(M\le q(n)\) for a polynomial \(q\), its running time is polynomial in the ordinary input length. Consequently, if a strongly NP-hard problem had a pseudo-polynomial exact algorithm, its polynomially bounded NP-hard restriction would lie in \(\mathrm{P}\), implying \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudo-polynomial algorithm becomes polynomial when numbers are polynomially bounded; therefore strongly NP-hard problems admit no such exact algorithm unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is exact and runs in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,M)\).
The problem is strongly NP-hard under polynomial-time reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow\text{no exact pseudo-polynomial algorithm exists}\)

notation.meaning: Length of the combinatorial portion of the encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Reduction-Source Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transitivity principle justifying the use of standard NP-complete source problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be an established NP-complete decision problem and let \(T\) be a decision problem. If \(S\le_m^p T\), then \(T\) is NP-hard. If additionally \(T\in\mathrm{NP}\), then \(T\) is NP-complete. Established problems such as satisfiability, 3-satisfiability, clique, vertex cover, and Hamiltonian cycle may therefore serve as canonical reduction sources once their NP-completeness under the same reduction convention has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time many-one reduction from any established NP-complete source problem to a target proves the target NP-hard; target membership in NP additionally proves NP-completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ is NP-hard}\), and \(T\in\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow T\text{ is NP-complete}\)

children.title: Inapproximability Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Boundary connection from exact hardness to gap and approximation hardness.

knowledge_statements.title: Inapproximability Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap-reduction interface from decision hardness to approximation hardness for maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be an NP-hard language and \(P\) a maximization problem. Suppose a polynomial-time map \(f\) and constants \(a>b>0\) satisfy \[x\in L\Longrightarrow \operatorname{OPT}_P(f(x))\ge a,\qquad x\notin L\Longrightarrow \operatorname{OPT}_P(f(x))\le b.\] If a polynomial-time algorithm always returns a feasible value at least \(\operatorname{OPT}_P/r\) for some \(r<a/b\), then comparing its value with \(b\) decides \(L\) in polynomial time. Therefore, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no such factor-\(r\) approximation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomially created optimum gap from at least a to at most b rules out approximation factors better than a/b unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: All feasible objective values used by the comparison are computable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow P\text{ has no polynomial-time }r\text{-approximation for }r<a/b\)

notation.meaning: Completeness and soundness thresholds of the gap.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports gap reductions or inapproximability.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximization gap statement and factor threshold are mathematically plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits, but no inspectable citation supports the gap-reduction hypotheses or inapproximability conclusion.

children.title: Tractability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Changes in computational status caused by representation, numerical scale, or structural restrictions.

children.title: Tractable Restrictions of Hard Problems
children.top_down_role: Graph-class, dimension, width, and matrix-structure islands of tractability.

knowledge_statements.title: Tractable Restrictions of Hard Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal criterion for a polynomial-time island inside a globally hard problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a decision problem and \(R\) a polynomial-time recognizable class of its instances. The restriction of \(P\) to \(R\) is \[P|_R=\{x:x\in P\land x\in R\}.\] The class \(R\) is a tractable restriction of \(P\) when \(P|_R\in\mathrm{P}\), even if \(P\) on unrestricted instances is NP-hard. Typical restrictions may bound graph width, dimension, rank, or impose a special matrix or graph class; tractability must be established for the explicitly encoded restricted family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tractable restriction is a polynomial-time recognizable instance class on which a globally hard problem can be solved in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: Instances of \(P|_R\) use the same explicit encoding convention as instances of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P|_R\in\mathrm{P}\)

notation.meaning: Restriction of P to instances in R.

review_flags: The supplied locators do not directly support the formal restriction criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restriction criterion is coherent and definition is an appropriate content kind, but the record supplies no source for this formalization or its recognition requirement.

children.title: Hard Extensions of Tractable Problems
children.top_down_role: Hardness introduced by side constraints, multiple commodities, nonlinearities, or succinct inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard Extensions of Tractable Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal criterion for added modeling features to create an NP-hard extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_0\in\mathrm{P}\) be a base decision problem and \(Q\) an extended problem. The problem \(Q\) is a hard extension of \(P_0\) when there is a polynomial-time embedding \(e\) satisfying \[x\in P_0\Longleftrightarrow e(x)\in Q,\] the image of \(e\) is the subclass where the added features are disabled, and \(Q\) is NP-hard on its full instance class. The added features may be side constraints, multiple commodities, nonlinear objectives, or succinct representations, but hardness is attributed to them only after the base subclass and encoding are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard extension contains a polynomially solvable base problem as the case with added features disabled, while the full extended problem is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: The embedding \(e\) is computable in polynomial time.
The added features and their disabled values have explicit finite encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\text{ is NP-hard}\land P_0\text{ embeds as the disabled-feature subclass of }Q\)

notation.meaning: Embedding of base instances into extended instances.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly formalizes hard extensions and disabled-feature embeddings.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disabled-feature embedding gives a coherent formalization and fits a definition container, but no source establishes that this is the intended hard-extension criterion or supports attribution of hardness to the added features.

children.title: Hardness Source Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Distinction between magnitude-driven and structural difficulty.

children.title: Magnitude-Driven Hardness
children.top_down_role: Difficulty arising primarily from large or finely encoded numerical parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Magnitude-Driven Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies weak NP-hardness associated with binary-encoded numerical magnitudes and pseudopolynomial solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\) be the length of the nonnumerical part of an instance, let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb Z\) be its numerical parameters, let \(U=\max_i|a_i|\), and let \(\ell=s+O\!\left(m+\sum_{i=1}^m\log(1+|a_i|)\right)\) be its binary encoding length. Call an NP-hard problem family magnitude-driven when it has an exact algorithm whose running time is polynomial in \(s\), \(m\), and \(U\). This running time is pseudopolynomial in the binary model, while it becomes polynomial on restrictions satisfying \(U\leq(s+m)^c\) for a fixed constant \(c\), and under a unary encoding whose length accounts for the magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is magnitude-driven when binary encoding gives an NP-hard family but an exact algorithm is polynomial in the numerical values, making bounded-magnitude or unary-encoded restrictions polynomial-time solvable.
assumptions_latex: \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb Z\) are binary encoded in the unrestricted family.
An exact algorithm has running time polynomial in \(s\), \(m\), and \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated tractability boundary depends on the encoded numerical magnitudes.

notation.meaning: length of the nonnumerical instance data

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Structure-Driven Hardness
children.top_down_role: Difficulty arising from combinatorial interactions independent of large magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Driven Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies NP-hardness that persists without unbounded numerical coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete optimization family has structure-driven hardness when its decision version remains NP-hard on a restriction in which all numerical parameters are absent or take values in a fixed finite set \(D\) independent of the instance size. This restricted hardness shows that unbounded coefficient magnitudes are not necessary for the NP-hardness boundary; the remaining obstruction is carried by the admissible combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is structure-driven when an NP-hard restriction remains after numerical data are removed or confined to a fixed finite set.
assumptions_latex: The restricted decision problem is defined by the same decision predicate as the unrestricted family.
\(D\) is fixed independently of the instance size, and NP-hardness uses polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: NP-hardness persists without unbounded numerical magnitudes.

notation.meaning: fixed finite set of permitted numerical values

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Complexity, Oracles, and Numerical Computation p. 21

children.title: Mixed-Source Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness produced by coupled numerical and combinatorial effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Source Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies hardness arising from interaction between numerical magnitudes and combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Call the hardness of a discrete optimization family mixed-source when both of the following restrictions yield polynomial-time solvable subfamilies: fixing the relevant structural parameter \(k\) by a constant, and bounding the largest numerical magnitude \(U\) polynomially in the structural input size; yet instances with both \(k\) and binary-encoded \(U\) unbounded form an NP-hard family. Under this operational definition, neither magnitude nor structure alone explains the stated boundary: hardness occurs in their joint unbounded regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is mixed-source when bounding either structural complexity or numerical magnitude restores tractability, but allowing both to grow yields NP-hardness.
assumptions_latex: A structural parameter \(k\) and maximum numerical magnitude \(U\) are specified.
The two restricted subfamilies and the jointly unbounded family use the same decision predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The observed tractability boundary depends jointly on \(k\) and \(U\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is plausible as an operational taxonomy, but no source establishes this exact two-parameter classification. The phrase “fixing k by a constant” also requires uniform quantifiers and a precise structural parameter before the boundary is reliable.

children.title: Representation-Sensitive Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by explicit, succinct, lifted, or oracle representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares complexity only after fixing how feasible objects, constraints, and access operations are encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a fixed abstract optimization problem and let \(R\) be a representation of its instances. Complexity is measured as a function of the representation length \(|R(I)|\) and the permitted access operations. Consequently, polynomial-time solvability is not invariant under arbitrary changes of representation: an explicit list may have exponential length relative to a succinct encoding, while an oracle representation charges for queries and omits the oracle's implementation cost. Complexity claims for \(P\) must therefore name the encoding or oracle model and use reductions that translate representations with polynomial overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same abstract problem can have different complexity under explicit, succinct, lifted, or oracle representations, so every bound must specify its representation model.
assumptions_latex: Each representation has a defined length and access model.
Representation translations are evaluated by their computational and size overhead.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial bound relative to one representation need not be polynomial relative to another.
