knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Simplex Algorithm and Nondegenerate Finite Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General primal simplex procedure for a standard-form minimization problem; finite termination under arbitrary improving-column choices is asserted here only when degeneracy is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from a basic feasible solution, return it as optimal if $\bar c_j\ge 0$ for all $j$. Otherwise choose $j$ with $\bar c_j<0$. If $x_{ij}\le 0$ for every basic row $i$, declare the objective unbounded below. Otherwise set $\theta_0=\min_{i:x_{ij}>0}x_{i0}/x_{ij}$, choose a minimizing row $k$, and pivot on $x_{kj}$. If every executed pivot is nondegenerate, so $\theta_0>0$, each pivot strictly decreases the objective; no basic feasible solution repeats, and the procedure terminates after finitely many pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a negative-reduced-cost entering column. If it has no positive tableau coefficient, it determines an unbounded feasible direction; otherwise apply the minimum-ratio test and pivot. Without degeneracy, every pivot strictly lowers the objective, so the method finitely terminates at an optimal basic feasible solution or detects unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ is an initial basic feasible solution of }\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}
\text{there are finitely many basic feasible solutions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure terminates finitely with an optimal basic feasible solution or detects unboundedness below.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Start from a basis matrix \(B\) with nonbasic index set \(N\), \(x_B=B^{-1}b\ge0\), and \(x_N=0\). At each iteration compute \(y^{\mathsf T}=c_B^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}\) and \(\bar c_j=c_j-y^{\mathsf T}A_j\) for \(j\in N\). If every \(\bar c_j\ge0\), return the current basic feasible solution. Otherwise select \(j\in N\) with \(\bar c_j<0\), set \(d=B^{-1}A_j\), and, when some \(d_i>0\), select a leaving basic index by minimizing \((x_B)_i/d_i\) over those indices, using the fixed anticycling rule to break ties. Pivot and repeat. If no \(d_i>0\), return the ray \(r\in\mathbb R^n\) defined by \(r_j=1\), \(r_B=-d\), and all other components zero; it satisfies \(Ar=0\), \(r\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}r=\bar c_j<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal simplex maintains primal feasibility, enters a variable with negative reduced cost, and uses the ratio test to preserve nonnegativity. It terminates at an optimum or returns a feasible improving ray proving unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LP Bases, Basic Solutions, and Reduced Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form maximization LP with a full-row-rank constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P'=\max\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). For a basis \(\beta\) with nonsingular \(A_\beta\) and complementary nonbasis \(\eta\), the associated basic solution is \(x_\eta^*=0\), \(x_\beta^*=A_\beta^{-1}b\); it is primal feasible exactly when \(x_\beta^*\ge0\). For \(D'=\min\{b^Ty:A^Ty\ge c\}\), the associated dual basic solution satisfies \(A_\beta^Ty^*=c_\beta\), hence \(y^*=A_\beta^{-T}c_\beta\). The reduced costs are \(\bar c_\eta=c_\eta-A_\eta^Ty^*\), and the basis is dual feasible exactly when \(\bar c_\eta\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis sets the nonbasic variables to zero and uniquely determines the basic variables. Nonnegative basic variables characterize primal feasibility. The same basis determines a dual solution and reduced costs, whose nonpositivity characterizes dual feasibility for this maximization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_\eta^*=0,\quad x_\beta^*=A_\beta^{-1}b,\quad x_\beta^*\ge0\iff\beta\text{ is primal feasible},\quad y^*=A_\beta^{-T}c_\beta,\quad \bar c_\eta=c_\eta-A_\eta^Ty^*,\quad \bar c_\eta\le0\iff\beta\text{ is dual feasible}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Simplex Method with Phase I and Lexicographic Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-feasible basis-pivot method for full-row-rank standard-form maximization LPs, including initialization, unboundedness detection, and finite termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P'=\max\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), begin with a primal-feasible basis \(\beta\). If \(\bar c_\eta\le0\), stop with an optimal basis. Otherwise choose a nonbasic \(j\) with \(\bar c_j>0\). If \(\bar a_{kj}\le0\) for all basic rows \(k\), then \(P'\) is unbounded. Otherwise choose \(i\in\arg\min\{x_{\beta_k}^*/\bar a_{kj}:\bar a_{kj}>0\}\) and pivot; the new basis remains primal feasible. Phase I minimizes a nonnegative artificial variable and attains value zero if and only if \(P'\) is feasible. With the perturbation \(b_i\mapsto b_i+\epsilon^i\) and its induced lexicographic ratio ordering, every pivot strictly improves the perturbed objective, no basis is revisited, and finite termination follows while the visited basic solutions remain feasible for the unperturbed problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal simplex preserves primal feasibility using the minimum-ratio test, stops when all reduced costs have the optimal sign, and detects unboundedness when an improving entering column has no positive pivot entry. Phase I finds a feasible starting basis or detects infeasibility. Lexicographic right-hand-side perturbation prevents repeated bases and gives finite termination.
assumptions_latex: \text{The perturbation ratio comparisons use the ordering induced by arbitrarily small }\epsilon>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The method obtains an optimal basis or detects infeasibility or unboundedness; under the stated perturbation rule it terminates after finitely many pivots.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Start from a basis matrix \(B\) with nonbasic index set \(N\), basic values \(x_B=B^{-1}b\), and reduced costs \(\bar c_j=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}A_j\ge0\) for every \(j\in N\). If \(x_B\ge0\), return the current optimal solution. Otherwise select a row \(r\) with \((x_B)_r<0\) according to the fixed anticycling rule. For \(\bar a_{rj}=(B^{-1}A_j)_r\), select an entering index from \(\{j\in N:\bar a_{rj}<0\}\) minimizing \(\bar c_j/(-\bar a_{rj})\), with ties resolved by that rule, and pivot. If the eligible set is empty, return the resulting primal-infeasibility certificate. Repeating these pivots preserves nonnegative reduced costs and, under the finite anticycling rule, terminates at an optimal basis or with primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual simplex maintains dual feasibility while repairing negative basic variables. With a finite anticycling rule, it terminates at an optimal basis or produces a primal-infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-perturbed dual simplex and finite termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic objective perturbation that prevents zero reduced costs and thereby removes the stated dual-degeneracy obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial dual-feasible basis, replace each objective coefficient by \(c'_j=c_j+\epsilon^j\), where \(\epsilon\) is an arbitrarily small positive indeterminate, and perform dual-simplex comparisons in the ordered field of rational functions in \(\epsilon\). Because only the objective is perturbed, the basic solutions for the original constraint system are unchanged. The induced pivots obey the ordinary dual-simplex rules at \(\epsilon=0\), preserve dual feasibility for the original objective, and make its objective value nonincreasing. For every nonbasic index \(\eta_j\), \(\bar c'_{\eta_j}=\bar c_{\eta_j}-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bar a_{i\eta_j}\epsilon^{\beta_i}+\epsilon^{\eta_j}\) is not identically zero, since \(\eta_j\notin\beta\) makes the \(\epsilon^{\eta_j}\) term uncancelled. Hence no eligible pivot has zero ratio, the perturbed basic objective decreases strictly at every pivot, and the finite number of bases implies finite termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning each objective coefficient a distinct infinitesimal perturbation leaves the constraint-system basic solutions unchanged and produces pivots compatible with ordinary dual simplex for the original objective. Every nonbasic reduced cost remains a nonzero polynomial because it contains its own distinct infinitesimal term. This eliminates the stated zero-ratio dual degeneracy, makes the perturbed objective strictly decrease, and yields finite termination over the finite set of bases.
assumptions_latex: \(c'_j=c_j+\epsilon^j\) for every objective coefficient, with \(\epsilon\) an arbitrarily small positive indeterminate.
Arithmetic and comparisons use the ordered field of rational functions in \(\epsilon\).
The linear program has finitely many bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar c'_{\eta_j}\not\equiv0\text{ for every nonbasic }\eta_j;\text{ consequently the stated dual degeneracy is avoided and the epsilon-perturbed dual-simplex method terminates after finitely many pivots.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-simplex pivot rule, outcomes, and degeneracy boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary dual simplex for a finite-basis linear program, including its infeasibility outcome and the failure of the elementary finite-termination argument under dual degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a dual-feasible basis \(\beta\). If no basic value satisfies \(x^*_{\beta_i}<0\), then the basis is also primal feasible. Otherwise, select a leaving index \(\beta_i\) with \(x^*_{\beta_i}<0\), and choose an entering index \(\eta_j\) minimizing \(\Delta=-\bar c_{\eta_j}/\bar a_{i\eta_j}\) among indices satisfying \(\bar a_{i\eta_j}<0\). If no such entering index exists, then \(P'\) is infeasible. Each pivot preserves dual feasibility, and the primal objective decreases when \(\Delta>0\). Thus, if every performed pivot has \(\Delta>0\), finiteness of the set of bases gives finite termination with either an infeasibility conclusion or a primal-and-dual-feasible basis. When \(\Delta=0\), the objective does not decrease, so this finite-termination argument no longer applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual simplex starts from a dual-feasible basis. A negative basic value determines an eligible leaving variable, and the entering variable is selected by the stated minimum-ratio rule. No negative basic value means primal feasibility has been attained, while no eligible entering variable implies infeasibility. The pivots preserve dual feasibility. Strict objective decrease yields finite termination because there are finitely many bases, but a zero-ratio, dual-degenerate pivot removes that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta\) is an initial dual-feasible basis for \(P'\).
The linear program has finitely many bases.
For a selected leaving index \(\beta_i\), eligible entering indices satisfy \(\bar a_{i\eta_j}<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Dual feasibility is preserved; if all performed pivots satisfy }\Delta>0,\text{ the method terminates finitely with infeasibility of }P'\text{ or a primal-and-dual-feasible basis, whereas }\Delta=0\text{ removes this assurance.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual simplex pivot rule and termination qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General tableau-form dual simplex method, including its dual-feasibility invariant, row-first ratio test, and degeneracy qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a basic tableau with a primal-infeasible basic solution and a dual-feasible cost row, \(x_{0j}\ge 0\) for all \(j\), choose a row \(r\) with \(x_{r0}<0\). If an eligible column exists, choose \(s\in\arg\max_{j:x_{rj}<0}x_{0j}/x_{rj}\). Under the cost-row update \(x'_{0j}=x_{0j}-(x_{0s}/x_{rs})x_{rj}\), this ratio rule maintains \(x'_{0j}\ge0\). In the absence of degeneracy, successive pivots strictly improve the objective, so finiteness of the set of bases gives termination; with degeneracy, an anti-cycling pivot rule such as Bland's rule is needed to guarantee termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a primal-infeasible basic tableau with a dual-feasible cost row, first choose an infeasible basic row. If that row has an eligible negative entry, pivot on a column maximizing the ratio of its cost-row entry to its pivot-row entry. The ratio test preserves dual feasibility. Without degeneracy, strict objective improvement and finitely many bases imply termination; with degeneracy, an anti-cycling pivot rule such as Bland's is needed to guarantee termination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\in\arg\max_{j:x_{rj}<0}\frac{x_{0j}}{x_{rj}},\qquad x'_{0j}=x_{0j}-\frac{x_{0s}}{x_{rs}}x_{rj}\ge0;\quad\text{nondegeneracy gives finite termination, whereas degeneracy requires an anti-cycling rule to guarantee termination.}

knowledge_statements.title: Revised Simplex Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-factorization implementation of primal simplex without storing a full tableau.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), maintain a nonsingular basis \(B\) and a factorization permitting solves with \(B\) and \(B^{\mathsf T}\). Compute \(x_B=B^{-1}b\), solve \(B^{\mathsf T}y=c_B\), and price nonbasic columns by \(\bar c_j=c_j-A_j^{\mathsf T}y\). If all \(\bar c_j\ge0\), return \(x\). Otherwise choose \(j\) with \(\bar c_j<0\), solve \(Bd=A_j\), apply the primal ratio test, replace the leaving basis column by \(A_j\), and update or refactor the basis factors. The generated basis sequence equals that of tableau simplex under identical pivot choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Revised simplex reproduces simplex pivots using linear solves and updated basis factors instead of maintaining the complete tableau.
assumptions_latex: The initial basis is nonsingular and primal feasible.
Basis solves and factor updates are performed exactly for the mathematical algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identical entering and leaving choices produce the same bases as primal tableau simplex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded ratio test for an entering variable at its lower bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Determines the maximal feasible step, leaving variable, bound flip, or unboundedness; the extract does not state the symmetric upper-bound formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the entering variable \(x_s\) is at its lower bound and is increased by \(\theta\). For each basic variable \(x_i=\bar b(i)-\bar a_{is}\theta\), define \(\theta_i=(u_i-\bar b(i))/(-\bar a_{is})\) if \(\bar a_{is}<0\), \(\theta_i=\bar b(i)/\bar a_{is}\) if \(\bar a_{is}>0\), and \(\theta_i=+\infty\) if \(\bar a_{is}=0\). Then \(\theta=\min\{u_s,\min_i\theta_i\}\). If \(u_s\) is limiting, \(x_s\) moves from its lower to its upper bound without a basis change; if some \(\theta_i\) is limiting, that basic variable reaches a bound and the basis changes. If every limiting value is infinite, the LP is unbounded in the improving direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an entering variable leaves its lower bound, increase it only until it or a basic variable reaches a bound. The minimum admissible step either flips the entering variable to its opposite bound without changing the basis, identifies a leaving basic variable and causes a pivot, or reveals an unbounded improving direction. The symmetric case of an entering variable at its upper bound is not specified in the extract.
assumptions_latex: x_s\text{ is nonbasic at its lower bound and is increased by }\theta\ge0
0\le x_i(\theta)\le u_i\quad(1\le i\le p),\qquad 0\le x_s(\theta)\le u_s
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta=\min\left\{u_s,\min_{1\le i\le p}\theta_i\right\},\quad \theta_i=\begin{cases}(u_i-\bar b(i))/(-\bar a_{is}),&\bar a_{is}<0,\\ \bar b(i)/\bar a_{is},&\bar a_{is}>0,\\ +\infty,&\bar a_{is}=0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of primal basis and simplex-multiplier systems using a transformed partitioned basis; pricing, ratio tests, and basis-update recomputation are outside the described procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the transformed basis \(\mathcal B'\) be partitioned into a working block \(\mathcal W\) and commodity basis blocks \(\mathcal B^1,\ldots,\mathcal B^K\). For the multiplier system, first solve \(\pi^0\mathcal W=c_{\mathcal W}\); after substitution, solve the independent commodity subsystems using their tree-basis computations. For \(\mathcal Bx_{\mathbf B}=b\), solve \(\mathcal B^k y^k=b^k\) independently, substitute these solutions to obtain and solve \(\mathcal W y^0=u'\), and recover \(x_{\mathbf B}=\mathcal D y_{\mathbf B}\). With \(p\) bundle constraints, each such computation uses one \(p\times p\) working-basis solve and \(K\) tree computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use the transformed partitioned basis instead of solving with the full basis directly. Multiplier calculations solve the working block before the commodity tree systems; primal calculations solve the commodity tree systems before the working block and then transform back. With p bundle constraints, this replaces the full linear-system calculation by K tree computations and one p-by-p solve. The extract does not specify pricing, ratio tests, or recomputation after a basis exchange.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Simplex Algorithm from a Feasible Starting Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-solve realization of primal simplex for an equality-form maximization LP. The extract supplies no anti-cycling rule or finite-termination guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), let \(B\) be a feasible basis with \(A_B\) nonsingular and \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\). Solve \(y^TA_B=c_B^T\). If \(y^Ta_i\ge c_i\) for every \(i\in T\setminus B\), stop: the current basic feasible solution is optimal. Otherwise choose \(i\in T\setminus B\) with \(y^Ta_i<c_i\), solve \(A_Bz=a_i\), and find the largest \(\epsilon\ge0\) satisfying \(x_B-\epsilon z\ge0\). If no largest such \(\epsilon\) exists, stop: the LP is unbounded above. Otherwise choose \(j\in B\) with \(z_j>0\) and \((x_B-\epsilon z)_j=0\), pivot by replacing \(B\) with \((B\cup\{i\})\setminus\{j\}\), assign the corresponding updated basic values and \(x_i=\epsilon\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible nonsingular basis for a standard-form maximization LP, compute the associated dual vector. If every nonbasic reduced-cost inequality holds, the current basic feasible solution is optimal. Otherwise choose an improving nonbasic variable, compute its basis direction, and take the largest feasible step. If feasible steps are unbounded, the LP is unbounded above; otherwise pivot out a basic variable that reaches zero and continue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall i\in T\setminus B,\ y^Ta_i\ge c_i\right)\Rightarrow x\text{ is optimal};\qquad \nexists\max\{\epsilon\ge0:x_B-\epsilon A_B^{-1}a_i\ge0\}\Rightarrow\text{the LP is unbounded above}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization path-flow multicommodity linear program with a primal-feasible revised-simplex basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a primal-feasible basis of the restricted path-flow master problem. At each iteration, compute simplex multipliers \((w,\sigma)\) so that every basic column has zero reduced cost. For each commodity \(k\), compute a shortest \(s^k\)-to-\(t^k\) path under arc costs \(c_{ij}^k+w_{ij}\), with length \(\ell_k\). If \(\ell_k\ge\sigma^k\) for every \(k\), every omitted path column has nonnegative reduced cost and the current feasible solution is optimal. Otherwise, a shortest path \(Q\) for any commodity satisfying \(\ell_k<\sigma^k\) has reduced cost \(c_Q^{\sigma,w}=\ell_k-\sigma^k<0\); add such a column, perform the ordinary simplex ratio test and pivot, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute dual prices from the current feasible restricted-master basis, price paths by one modified-cost shortest-path problem per commodity, stop when all path reduced costs are nonnegative, and otherwise add a negative-reduced-cost path and pivot.
assumptions_latex: \text{The path-flow multicommodity formulation is a minimization linear program}
\mathcal B\text{ is a primal-feasible revised-simplex basis for the restricted master}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall k,\ \ell_k=\min_{P\in\mathbf P^k}\sum_{(i,j)\in P}(c_{ij}^k+w_{ij})\ge\sigma^k\right]\Rightarrow\text{current optimality};\quad \ell_k<\sigma^k\Rightarrow\text{a shortest-path column has negative reduced cost and may enter by a simplex pivot.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Revised primal-simplex iteration and two-phase cost-row updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit inverse-basis implementation of primal revised simplex, including the stated Phase I and Phase II cost-row formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a primal-feasible basis \(B\), compute reduced costs \(\bar c_j=c_j-\pi^{\prime}A_j\). If all reduced costs are nonnegative, terminate with an optimal solution. Otherwise select \(s\) with \(\bar c_s<0\), generate \(X_s=B^{-1}A_s\), and choose \(r\in\arg\min_{t:(X_s)_t>0}\bar b_t/(X_s)_t\). If no component of \(X_s\) is positive, the objective is unbounded; otherwise pivot using \((X_s)_r\), update the compact inverse-basis data, and replace the \(r\)-th basis index by \(s\). With unit-cost artificial variables in a two-phase implementation, Phase I uses \(\bar c_j=d_j-\pi^{\prime}A_j\), where \(d_j=-\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{ij}\). On entering Phase II, replace \(d_j\) by \(c_j\) and regenerate the cost row from \(-\pi^{\prime}=-c_B^{\prime}B^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The revised primal-simplex method stores compact inverse-basis information and generates reduced costs and the entering tableau column only when needed. Nonnegative reduced costs certify optimality; an improving column with no positive tableau entry certifies unboundedness; otherwise the minimum-ratio pivot produces the next basis. The extract also specifies the cost-row changes for the two phases of simplex.
assumptions_latex: \text{The problem and reduced costs use the extract's minimization sign convention}.
\text{The variables have the standard nonnegativity restrictions required by the primal-simplex ratio and unboundedness tests}.
\text{For the two-phase specialization, artificial variables initially have unit cost and the artificial basis cost row is reduced to zero}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall j,\ \bar c_j\ge 0\right)\Rightarrow\text{optimality};\qquad \bar c_s<0\land\left(\forall t,\ (B^{-1}A_s)_t\le 0\right)\Rightarrow\text{unboundedness};\qquad\text{otherwise the minimum-ratio pivot updates the basis from compact inverse-basis data}.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Variant Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility- and representation-based choice among simplex variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear program and a proposed initial basis, select the pivot regime from the maintained invariant. If \(B^{-1}b\ge0\), primal simplex can preserve primal feasibility. If the reduced costs satisfy \(\bar c_N\ge0\), dual simplex can preserve dual feasibility. If both conditions hold, the basis is already optimal. If neither holds, a feasibility-restoration phase or another initialization procedure is required before either invariant-preserving method applies. Independently, revised implementations are appropriate when basis solves and sparse factorization updates are preferable to storing the full tableau; this implementation choice does not alter the underlying primal or dual feasibility invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose primal or dual simplex according to which feasibility invariant the initial basis satisfies; choose revised storage according to the desired linear-algebra representation.
assumptions_latex: The linear program is expressed in equality form with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal feasibility selects a primal regime, dual feasibility selects a dual regime, and absence of both requires initialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-I construction of a primal-feasible basis for equality-form linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), first multiply rows by \(-1\) where necessary so that \(b\ge0\). Introduce artificial variables \(a\ge0\) and solve the Phase-I problem
\[\min\{\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}a:Ax+a=b,\ x\ge0,\ a\ge0\},\]
starting from the artificial basis. If its optimum is positive, declare the original system infeasible. If the optimum is zero, pivot zero-valued artificial basic variables out whenever possible; delete redundant rows when no original-column pivot exists. Remove all artificial columns and return the resulting feasible basis for the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase I adds artificial variables, minimizes their sum, and either constructs an original feasible basis or certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Phase I is solved to optimality with a terminating pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero Phase-I optimum yields a feasible original basis after cleanup; a positive optimum proves infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Phase Simplex Initialization and Status Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Artificial-basis initialization for simplex, including detection of infeasibility, redundant constraint rows, rank deficiency, and unbounded cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce an artificial basis with nonnegative artificial variables $x_i^a$ and run Phase I with objective $\xi=\sum_i x_i^a$. If $\xi_{\mathrm{opt}}>0$, declare the original linear program infeasible. Otherwise, if a basic artificial variable cannot be pivoted out, mark the associated constraint row as redundant and omit it. After eliminating artificial variables and redundant rows, run Phase II with the original objective. Rank deficiency is exposed at the end of Phase I, while unbounded original cost is detected in Phase II.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introduce an artificial basis and minimize the sum of the nonnegative artificial variables. A positive Phase-I optimum establishes infeasibility. If an artificial variable remains basic and cannot be pivoted out, its associated constraint row is redundant and may be omitted. Then run simplex with the original objective; Phase I handles rank deficiency and Phase II detects unbounded cost.
assumptions_latex: \text{The input is a linear program for which an artificial basis is introduced.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi_{\mathrm{opt}}>0\Rightarrow\text{the original problem is infeasible};\qquad \xi_{\mathrm{opt}}=0\Rightarrow\text{Phase II can proceed after eliminating artificial variables and any identified redundant rows, with unboundedness detected in Phase II.}

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of a basic feasible solution in standard equality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\) has row rank \(m\). A feasible basis \(B\) defines \(x_B=B^{-1}b\) and \(x_N=0\). This basic feasible solution is degenerate with respect to \(B\) exactly when at least one component of \(x_B\) is zero. Equivalently, fewer than \(m\) basic variables are strictly positive. A feasible point is a degenerate vertex when it has a feasible basis exhibiting this condition; consequently, multiple bases may represent the same vertex, and a zero-length pivot may change the basis without changing the feasible point or objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible solution is degenerate when at least one basic variable equals zero, allowing basis changes that do not move the represented vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) consists of \(m\) linearly independent columns of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy holds if and only if \((B^{-1}b)_i=0\) for some basic index \(i\).

children.title: Anticycling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Pivot-selection regimes designed to prevent repeated basis states.

knowledge_statements.title: Anticycling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination of simplex under Bland's least-index pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider simplex applied to a finite-dimensional standard-form linear program. At each nonoptimal primal-feasible basis, choose as entering variable the eligible nonbasic variable of smallest index, and among all ratio-test minimizers choose as leaving variable the eligible basic variable of smallest index. Then no basis can recur. Because only finitely many bases exist, the algorithm terminates after finitely many pivots, either at an optimal basis or with a valid unboundedness conclusion. The assertion remains relevant under degeneracy, where arbitrary eligible pivot choices can otherwise revisit a previous basis and cycle indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bland's least-index choices prevent repeated bases, so simplex terminates finitely even when degenerate pivots are possible.
assumptions_latex: The linear program has finitely many variables and constraints.
Entering and leaving choices follow Bland's least-index rule consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No basis repeats, and the simplex run terminates after finitely many pivots.

notation.meaning: A simplex basis, drawn from finitely many column subsets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite termination under Bland's anticycling rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General simplex finite-termination guarantee using least-index entering and leaving-variable choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the simplex algorithm, choose \(j=\min\{j:c_j-z_j<0\}\). Among all rows \(i\) with \(x_{ij}>0\) attaining the minimum ratio \(x_{i0}/x_{ij}\), choose one for which the leaving basic-variable index \(B(i)\) is smallest. Then the algorithm terminates after finitely many pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If simplex chooses the lowest-index favorable entering variable and, among minimum-ratio ties, the lowest-index leaving basic variable, then it terminates after finitely many pivots.
assumptions_latex: i\text{ is selected among rows with }x_{ij}>0\text{ minimizing }x_{i0}/x_{ij}.
B(i)\text{ is minimal among the leaving basic-variable indices of the minimum-ratio rows}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The simplex algorithm terminates after finitely many pivots.}

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which direct primal-simplex initialization or Phase I cannot supply a feasible basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Direct primal simplex cannot start from a proposed nonsingular basis \(B\) when \(B^{-1}b\not\ge0\), because its primal-feasibility invariant already fails. Phase I separates this recoverable initialization failure from infeasibility: for
\[\min\{\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}a:Ax+a=b,\ x\ge0,\ a\ge0\},\]
a strictly positive optimal value means that no \(x\ge0\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), so no primal-feasible basis exists. For example, \(x=-1\) with \(x\ge0\) is infeasible, and every Phase-I construction retains positive artificial mass. A zero optimum may still require removal of zero artificial basic variables or redundant rows before ordinary simplex begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible proposed basis only blocks direct initialization; a positive Phase-I optimum establishes that no feasible basis exists at all.
assumptions_latex: Rows have been sign-normalized so the displayed artificial basis is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B^{-1}b\not\ge0\) blocks direct primal initialization, while a positive Phase-I optimum certifies infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have row rank \(m\), and let \(\mathcal B\) be the family of size-\(m\) column index sets whose submatrices are nonsingular and satisfy the chosen feasibility condition. Define the basis-exchange graph \(H\) with vertex set \(\mathcal B\), joining \(B,B'\in\mathcal B\) when \(|B\setminus B'|=|B'\setminus B|=1\). Every admissible simplex pivot that replaces one basis column moves along an edge of \(H\); a degenerate pivot may traverse such an edge while representing the same polyhedral vertex. For a connected directed graph, delete one row of its node-arc incidence matrix to obtain the full-row-rank reduced incidence matrix \(\widetilde D\). Its column bases correspond to spanning trees, and exchanging one basis column amounts to adding one non-tree arc, forming its fundamental cycle, and deleting one tree arc from that cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Admissible bases form an exchange graph in which simplex pivots replace one column. For a connected graph's reduced incidence matrix, bases are spanning trees and pivots are tree-edge exchanges along fundamental cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Simplex Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-basis simplex interface for minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible minimum-cost flow with a spanning-tree basis, compute node potentials \(\pi\) so every basic arc \((u,v)\) has zero reduced cost \(\bar c_{uv}=c_{uv}+\pi_u-\pi_v\). If all nonbasic arcs satisfy the appropriate reduced-cost sign at their active lower or upper bounds, output the flow. Otherwise choose a violating nonbasic arc and insert it into the tree, creating a unique fundamental cycle. Augment flow around that cycle until an arc reaches a bound, delete a bound-reaching cycle arc to restore a spanning tree, update potentials, and repeat. With an anticycling rule, finite termination yields an optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network simplex prices arcs with node potentials and pivots by adding an arc, augmenting on its fundamental cycle, and deleting a saturated tree arc.
assumptions_latex: The network-flow instance has a feasible tree-structured basis.
Arc bounds and supplies are finite where required by the pivot.
A deterministic anticycling rule handles degenerate pivots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination with no reduced-cost violation yields an optimal feasible flow.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of arc from u to v.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Induced Basis Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spanning-tree characterization of bases of a connected graph's reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected directed graph, let \(D\in\mathbb R^{V\times E}\) be its node-arc incidence matrix, and delete one row to obtain \(\widetilde D\). Then \(\operatorname{rank}(\widetilde D)=|V|-1\). For any \(T\subseteq E\) with \(|T|=|V|-1\), the square submatrix \(\widetilde D_T\) is nonsingular if and only if the underlying undirected edges in \(T\) form a spanning tree of \(G\). Consequently, linear-programming bases of the reduced flow-conservation equations correspond exactly to spanning trees, before bound-status data for nonbasic arcs are added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonsingular column bases of a connected graph's reduced incidence matrix are exactly its spanning trees.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and connected after arc orientations are ignored.
\(D\) uses one \(+1\) and one \(-1\) in each non-loop arc column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det(\widetilde D_T)\neq0\) if and only if \(T\) is a spanning tree.

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix with one row deleted.
A set of candidate basis arcs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible tree solution on an arc set \(E\), and let a nonbasic entering arc induce a fundamental cycle \(C\). Orient \(C\) in the augmentation direction and define \(d\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}\) by \(d_e=1\) on forward cycle arcs, \(d_e=-1\) on backward cycle arcs, and \(d_e=0\) off \(C\). The maximal feasible step is \[\theta=\min\bigl(\{u_e-x_e:e\in C,\ d_e=1\}\cup\{x_e-\ell_e:e\in C,\ d_e=-1\}\bigr).\] The network pivot is degenerate exactly when \(\theta=0\). In that case an arc attaining the minimum may leave the tree, so the basis may change while the primal flow remains \(x+\theta d=x\) and its objective value is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network pivot is degenerate when its maximum feasible augmentation around the oriented fundamental cycle is zero. The tree basis may then change even though the flow and objective value do not.

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One exact-arithmetic update for a halfspace whose boundary passes through the ellipsoid center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an ellipsoid \(E(a,A)=\{x:(x-a)^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}(x-a)\le1\}\), where \(A\succ0\), and a central cut \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le0\) with \(g\ne0\). Set \[q=\frac{Ag}{\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}},\qquad a^+=a-\frac{q}{n+1},\qquad A^+=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{Agg^{\mathsf T}A}{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\right).\] Replace \(E(a,A)\) by \(E(a^+,A^+)\). The latter contains \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le0\}\); iteration stops under the prescribed feasibility, volume, or accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersect the current ellipsoid with a center-passing halfspace and replace it by the displayed smaller enclosing ellipsoid, repeating until the chosen stopping test holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le0\}\subseteq E(a^+,A^+)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covering ellipsoid for a unit hemisphere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized geometric construction underlying the central-cut ellipsoid update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\ge2\), let
\[
S_n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x^\top x\le1\},\qquad
t=\left(-\frac1{n+1},0,\ldots,0\right)^\top,
\]
\[
B=\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{n^2}{(n+1)^2},\frac{n^2}{n^2-1},\ldots,\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\right),\qquad
E=\{x:(x-t)^\top B^{-1}(x-t)\le1\}.
\]
Then \(B\succ0\),
\[
\{x\in S_n:x_1\le0\}\subseteq E,
\qquad
\frac{\operatorname{vol}(E)}{\operatorname{vol}(S_n)}<2^{-1/(2(n+1))}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The specified shifted ellipsoid is positive definite, contains the nonpositive-first-coordinate hemisphere of the unit ball, and has volume below the stated fraction of the unit ball's volume.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\succ0,\quad \{x\in S_n:x_1\le0\}\subseteq E,\quad \frac{\operatorname{vol}(E)}{\operatorname{vol}(S_n)}<2^{-1/(2(n+1))}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Central-Cut Ellipsoid Method for Strong Nonemptiness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility algorithm for a bounded polyhedron given by integral inequalities and guaranteed to be empty or full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Cx\le d\}$, where $C,d$ are integral, and suppose $P$ is bounded and either empty or full-dimensional. Set $N:=2n((2n+1)\langle C\rangle+n\langle d\rangle-n^3)$, $R:=\sqrt n\,2^{\langle C,d\rangle-n^2}$, $A_0:=R^2I$, and $a_0:=0$. At iteration $k$, declare $P$ empty if $k=N$; return $a_k$ if $a_k\in P$; otherwise choose a violated inequality $c^Tx\le\gamma$, set $b:=A_kc/\sqrt{c^TA_kc}$, $a_{k+1}:=a_k-b/(n+1)$, and $A_{k+1}:=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}(A_k-\frac{2}{n+1}bb^T)$, and continue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the prescribed encoding-length ball, the method repeatedly uses an inequality violated by the current center to perform a central-cut ellipsoid update. It returns a feasible center or, after the prescribed number of iterations, declares the polyhedron empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns a point }a_k\in P\text{ before the iteration limit, or declares }P=\varnothing\text{ when }k=N.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central-cut ellipsoid algorithm for strict linear feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit initialization, center test, iteration limit, and central-cut update for a linear strict-inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an \(m\times n\) system \(Ax<b\) of encoding size \(L\), initialize \(j=0\), \(t_0=0\), and \(B_0=n^2 2^{2L}I\). At iteration \(j\), return \(t_j\) if \(At_j<b\); if \(j>K:=16n(n+1)L\), return \(\text{``no''}\). Otherwise choose any violated inequality \(a^\top t_j\ge b_i\), set
\[
t_{j+1}=t_j-\frac{1}{n+1}\frac{B_ja}{\sqrt{a^\top B_ja}},\qquad
B_{j+1}=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(B_j-\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{(B_ja)(B_ja)^\top}{a^\top B_ja}\right),
\]
increment \(j\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the stated large ellipsoid centered at zero. Return the current center when it satisfies all strict inequalities; otherwise update the ellipsoid using any inequality violated at the center. Return no after the stated iteration limit.
assumptions_latex: Ax<b\text{ is a linear strict-inequality system of encoding size }L
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure outputs a vector satisfying }Ax<b\text{ when found, or }\text{``no''}\text{ after exceeding }16n(n+1)L\text{ iterations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central-cut ellipsoid update for constrained convex minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ellipsoid iteration using a subgradient cut at feasible centers and a separating cut at infeasible centers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathcal E_0=\{V_0u+w_0:\|u\|_2\le1\}\supseteq C\). For each \(t>0\), if \(w_{t-1}\in C\), choose \(z_{t-1}\in\partial\Psi(w_{t-1})\); otherwise choose \(z_{t-1}\) such that \(C\subseteq\{w:(w-w_{t-1})^\top z_{t-1}\le0\}\). Set \(\widetilde z_{t-1}=(z_{t-1}^\top V_{t-1}V_{t-1}^\top z_{t-1})^{-1/2}z_{t-1}\), \(w_t=w_{t-1}-\frac1{p+1}V_{t-1}V_{t-1}^\top\widetilde z_{t-1}\), and \(V_t=\frac{p^2}{p^2-1}\left(V_{t-1}-\frac2{p+1}V_{t-1}V_{t-1}^\top\widetilde z_{t-1}\widetilde z_{t-1}^\top V_{t-1}V_{t-1}^\top\right)\). Then \(\mathcal E_t=\{V_tu+w_t:\|u\|_2\le1\}\) retains all minimizers of \(\Psi\) over \(C\), while each iteration reduces ellipsoid volume by a fixed multiplicative factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with an ellipsoid containing C. At each center, use a subgradient halfspace when the center is feasible and a separating halfspace when it is infeasible, then apply the stated center and shape updates. The resulting ellipsoids retain every minimizer of Psi over C and shrink in volume by a fixed multiplicative factor per iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in C}\Psi(w)\subseteq\mathcal E_t\quad\text{for every iteration }t,\text{ and the ellipsoid volume decreases by a fixed multiplicative factor.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine normalization of the central-cut ellipsoid update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence between the normalized unit-hemisphere construction and an arbitrary central cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B_j\succ0\), \(t_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), and let \(t_{j+1},B_{j+1}\) be obtained by Step 3 of the ellipsoid algorithm. Let \(S_n\), \(\tfrac12S_n=\{x\in S_n:x_1\le0\}\), and \(E\) be as in the normalized hemisphere construction. Then there exists an affine transformation \(T\) such that
\[
T(S_n)=\{x:(x-t_j)^\top B_j^{-1}(x-t_j)\le1\},
\]
\[
T(E)=\{x:(x-t_{j+1})^\top B_{j+1}^{-1}(x-t_{j+1})\le1\},
\]
and
\[
T(\tfrac12S_n)=\{x:(x-t_j)^\top B_j^{-1}(x-t_j)\le1,\ a^\top(x-t_j)\le0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One affine transformation maps the unit ball to the current ellipsoid, the normalized covering ellipsoid to the updated ellipsoid, and the normalized hemisphere to the half retained by the central cut.
assumptions_latex: t_{j+1},B_{j+1}\text{ are obtained by Step 3 of the ellipsoid algorithm}
S_n,\ \tfrac12S_n,\ E\text{ are as in the preceding normalized construction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ an affine transformation }T\text{ satisfying the three stated image identities.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Containment and volume contraction of the central-cut ellipsoid update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step geometric guarantees for the central-cut ellipsoid update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B_j\succ0\), \(t_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), and define \(t_{j+1}\) and \(B_{j+1}\) by Step 3 of the ellipsoid algorithm. Then \(B_{j+1}\succ0\). Moreover, if

\{x\in E_j:a^\top(x-t_j)\le0\}\subseteq E_{j+1},

\frac{\operatorname{vol}(E_{j+1})}{\operatorname{vol}(E_j)}<2^{-1/(2(n+1))}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Volume Enclosing Ellipsoid of a Central Half-Ellipsoid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact enclosing-ellipsoid formula for a halfspace cut whose boundary passes through the ellipsoid center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), \(A=A^\top\succ0\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\). Define \[E'=\{z\in E(A,x):a^\top z\ge a^\top x\},\qquad b=\frac{Aa}{\sqrt{a^\top Aa}}.\] The minimum-volume ellipsoid containing \(E'\) is \(E(A',x')\), where \[A'=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2}{n+1}bb^\top\right),\qquad x'=x+\frac{1}{n+1}b.\]

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(A',x')\text{ is the minimum-volume ellipsoid containing }\{z\in E(A,x):a^\top z\ge a^\top x\}

knowledge_statements.title: Deep-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic update for a normalized cut that strictly excludes the current center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(E(a,A)\), \(A\succ0\), and a valid cut \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\), where \(g\ne0\) and \(0<\alpha<1\). Put \(q=Ag/\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\) and set \[a^+=a-\frac{1+n\alpha}{n+1}q,\qquad A^+=\frac{n^2(1-\alpha^2)}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2(1+n\alpha)}{(n+1)(1+\alpha)}\frac{Agg^{\mathsf T}A}{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\right).\] Then replace the current ellipsoid by \(E(a^+,A^+)\), which contains the cut intersection; stop according to the specified feasibility or accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deep cut excludes the current center by positive normalized depth; the displayed update encloses the surviving intersection more tightly than the corresponding central update.
assumptions_latex: The target set lies in the displayed halfspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\}\subseteq E(a^+,A^+)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoid Cut-Strength Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized classification of parallel ellipsoid cuts by signed displacement from the center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E(a,A)\) with \(A\succ0\) and \(g\ne0\), write a parallel cut uniquely in normalized form \[g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}.\] Its signed parameter classifies its strength: \(\alpha=0\) is central; \(0<\alpha<1\) is deep; and \(-1/n<\alpha<0\) is shallow but yields a strict ellipsoidal volume reduction under the standard update. At \(\alpha=-1/n\) that update returns the original ellipsoid, while \(\alpha\le-1/n\) supplies no strict progress guarantee from this update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized signed offset alpha classifies a cut as central, deep, or shallow and identifies when the standard ellipsoid update guarantees strict progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha>0\) is deep, \(\alpha=0\) central, and \(-1/n<\alpha<0\) shallow with strict standard-update progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Deep-Cut Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric boundary for the normalized deep-cut update, including empty and lower-dimensional intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E(a,A)\) be full-dimensional and consider \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le-\alpha\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\). For \(0\le\alpha<1\), the surviving intersection can be full-dimensional and the standard deep-cut shape matrix is positive definite. If \(\alpha=1\), the intersection is at most the single boundary point \(a-Ag/\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\); if \(\alpha>1\), it is empty. Consequently, the full-dimensional deep-cut update is valid only for \(\alpha<1\), and the limiting or empty cases require separate termination or dimension-reduction handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized depth below one permits a full-dimensional update; depth one leaves at most one boundary point, and greater depth makes the ellipsoid-cut intersection empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha=1\) gives an intersection of dimension zero or less, and \(\alpha>1\) gives the empty intersection.

knowledge_statements.title: Shallow-Cut Ellipsoid Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ellipsoid update accepting a weak cut whose retained halfspace contains the current center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(E(a,A)\), \(A\succ0\), and a valid shallow cut \(g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le\beta\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\), where \(g\ne0\) and \(0<\beta<1/n\). Set \(q=Ag/\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\) and \[a^+=a-\frac{1-n\beta}{n+1}q,\qquad A^+=\frac{n^2(1-\beta^2)}{n^2-1}\left(A-\frac{2(1-n\beta)}{(n+1)(1-\beta)}\frac{Agg^{\mathsf T}A}{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\right).\] Replace \(E(a,A)\) by \(E(a^+,A^+)\). The new ellipsoid contains the retained intersection and has strictly smaller volume.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently shallow valid cut may contain the old center yet still supports a strict-volume-reduction ellipsoid update when its normalized weakness is below one over the dimension.
assumptions_latex: The target set satisfies the displayed cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E(a,A)\cap\{x:g^{\mathsf T}(x-a)\le\beta\sqrt{g^{\mathsf T}Ag}\}\subseteq E(a^+,A^+)\) and \(\det A^+<\det A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(\beta\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(0<\beta<1/n\). The cut halfspace contains and supports the scaled ellipsoid, and the standard oracle uses beta equal to one over n plus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The oracle returns a shallow }\beta\text{-cut or a tough declaration; each returned cut halfspace contains and supports }E(\beta^2A,a).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact implicit feasible-region optimization problem consists of a rational objective \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), a possibly empty bounded rational polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) represented by a specified exact oracle, and rational encoding and geometric bounds sufficient for that oracle model. Its task is to certify \(P=\varnothing\), or to return \(x^\star\in P\) satisfying \[c^{\mathsf T}x^\star=\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}.\] Weak optimization is a distinct problem and requires separately specified feasibility, objective, norm, and oracle-error tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the exact model, optimize a rational linear objective over a bounded rational polytope given through an exact oracle, returning an exact optimizer or certifying that the polytope is empty. Weak optimization requires a separately specified tolerance model.

children.title: Separation-Oracle Reductions

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong optimization from strong separation for well-described rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a bounded rational polytope with known polynomial encoding and bounding data. Suppose a strong separation oracle, on rational input \(y\), either asserts \(y\in P\) or returns rational \((a,\beta)\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in P\). Then, for every \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), the ellipsoid method solves strong linear optimization over \(P\), or detects \(P=\varnothing\), using a number of oracle calls and rational arithmetic operations polynomial in the dimension and input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a suitably encoded bounded rational polytope, strong separation oracle access suffices to solve exact linear optimization in oracle-polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a bounded rational polytope with polynomially bounded description and geometric data.
The separation oracle returns polynomially encoded strong separators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong optimization over \(P\) is polynomial-time reducible to strong separation over \(P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Oracle Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation from strong optimization for well-described rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty bounded rational polytope with known polynomial encoding and bounding data. Suppose a strong optimization oracle returns, for each \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), a point maximizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) and the exact optimum value. The optimization oracle returns exact rational optimum data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation over \(P\) is polynomial-time reducible to strong optimization over \(P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every well-described bounded rational polytope \(P\), strong separation and strong linear optimization are mutually polynomial-time oracle reducible: \[\operatorname{SEP}_{\mathrm{strong}}(P)\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{strong}}(P).\] This conclusion is model-specific: it does not imply an equivalence after replacing either side by a weak oracle, omitting polynomial encoding bounds, or allowing uncontrolled oracle error. Any weak equivalence requires its own matched accuracy, norm, geometric-radius, and error hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong separation and exact linear optimization are polynomially equivalent for well-described bounded rational polytopes. The theorem does not transfer automatically to weak or mismatched oracle models.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative validity loss when extending a normalized linear inequality from an inner parallel set to a well-bounded convex body.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Encoding Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary input length used by rational polyhedral and ellipsoid complexity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(z\), define \(\langle z\rangle=1+\lceil\log_2(|z|+1)\rceil\). For a reduced rational \(r=p/q\) with \(q>0\), define \(\langle r\rangle=\langle p\rangle+\langle q\rangle\). The encoding size of a rational vector or matrix is the sum of its entries' encoding sizes together with dimensions and structural indices. An oracle algorithm is polynomial-time in rational input data only when its arithmetic-operation count and every intermediate and output bit length are bounded polynomially in this total encoding size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational encoding size counts the binary lengths of reduced numerators and denominators; polynomial-time claims must also control intermediate and output bit lengths.
assumptions_latex: Every rational is stored in reduced numerator-denominator form with positive denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input length is the summed binary encoding length, and bit complexity must be polynomial in that length.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner- and outer-radius promises supporting finite ellipsoid iteration bounds for empty-or-full-dimensional convex feasibility.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.2, Optimization from Separation, p. 105

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex feasibility instance \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has usable full-dimensional geometric bounding data when rational centers \(a_0,a_1\in\mathbb Q^n\) and rational radii \(0<r\le R\) are supplied with the promise \[K\subseteq B(a_0,R),\qquad K\ne\varnothing\Longrightarrow B(a_1,r)\subseteq K.\] The data are polynomially usable when the binary encodings of \(a_0,a_1,r,R\) and the quantity \(\log_2(R/r)\) are polynomially bounded by the instance length. children.title: Finite-Precision Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by approximate arithmetic and finite numerical representation.

assumptions_latex: The feasible region is a bounded convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Every computed separating inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) has coefficient error at most \(\eta\), and every ellipsoid update has cumulative arithmetic error at most \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-precision validity requires explicit error budgets and geometric margins.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical validity boundary for oracle-based ellipsoid iterations, not a floating-point implementation theorem.

source_refs.locator: * 4.2 Optimization from Separation p. 105

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a queried point \(y\notin K\), suppose the exact oracle admits a normalized valid cut \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}y-\beta\geq\gamma>0\). A finite-precision oracle and update remain logically valid only when their certified errors are smaller than the available separation and containment margins; in particular, a sufficient local requirement is \(\eta+\rho<\gamma\). If no positive lower bound on \(\gamma\) is available, or if rounding can move a retained point of \(K\) outside the computed halfspace, the usual exact-arithmetic volume-reduction argument does not certify feasibility, infeasibility, or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoid guarantees survive finite precision only when certified oracle and update errors stay below the available separation and containment margins.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: * 4.2 Optimization from Separation p. 105

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the scalar condition η+ρ<γ is not justified by the stated error model: coefficient error needs a norm and a bound on relevant points, while update error and cut violation must be expressed in compatible units. The cited optimization-from-separation section does not specifically support this finite-precision condition. A source and a precise numerical model are required.

A weak response with tolerance \(\varepsilon\) may instead certify \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\leq\varepsilon\), or return a cut whose promised violation is at least the specified tolerance. A cut that excludes a feasible point, has uncertified coefficient error, or has depth below the algorithm's required threshold cannot be used to invoke the corresponding optimization-from-separation guarantee.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a polynomial \(p\) such that every vertex of \(P\), when it exists, has rational coordinates of binary length at most \(p(n,L)\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(J_0\subseteq J\). At iteration \(t\), solve the restricted master \(x^t\in\arg\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in X,\ g_j(x)\leq0\ \forall j\in J_t\}\). Apply the separation routine to \(x^t\). If it returns \(j_t\in J\) with \(g_{j_t}(x^t)>0\), set \(J_{t+1}=J_t\cup\{j_t\}\) and repeat. If it certifies \(g_j(x^t)\leq0\) for every \(j\in J\), stop and output \(x^t\). Since the restricted feasible region contains the full feasible region, this final feasible restricted-master optimum is also globally optimal.

assumptions_latex: The master linear program is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}\lambda:A\lambda=b,\ \lambda\geq0\}\), with an implicit column set \(Q\).
Each restricted master and pricing problem is solved exactly.

notation.meaning: dual multiplier for the master equality

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(Q_0\subseteq Q\) so the restricted master is feasible. At iteration \(t\), solve \(\min\{\sum_{q\in Q_t}c_q\lambda_q:\sum_{q\in Q_t}a_q\lambda_q=b,\ \lambda_q\geq0\}\) and obtain a dual optimum \(\pi^t\). Solve the pricing problem \(q_t\in\arg\min_{q\in Q}\{c_q-(\pi^t)^{\mathsf T}a_q\}\). If its value is negative, set \(Q_{t+1}=Q_t\cup\{q_t\}\). Otherwise stop: dual feasibility then holds for every full-master column, so the restricted primal solution and \(\pi^t\) are optimal for the full master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve an active-column master, price all implicit columns using its dual solution, and add a column exactly when its reduced cost is negative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pricing subproblem computes \(q^*\in\arg\min_{q\in Q}\{c_q-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_q\}\). If \(c_{q^*}-\pi^{\mathsf T}a_{q^*}<0\), then column \(q^*\) violates the full-master dual inequality \(a_q^{\mathsf T}\pi\leq c_q\) and is eligible to enter the restricted master. If the optimum is nonnegative, then \(a_q^{\mathsf T}\pi\leq c_q\) for every \(q\in Q\); hence \(\pi\) is dual feasible for all implicit columns. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Improving-neighbor local search and neighborhood-relative optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General neighborhood local search for minimization, including its conditional stopping guarantee, absence of a general global-optimality guarantee, and the LP adjacency interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c(x):x\in F\}\), fix a neighborhood mapping \(N(x)\subseteq F\), start from \(x\in F\), and repeatedly replace \(x\) by a point \(y\in N(x)\) satisfying \(c(y)<c(x)\). If it is established that no such neighbor exists, then the current point is locally optimal relative to \(N\): \(c(x)\le c(y)\) for all \(y\in N(x)\). This does not generally imply global optimality or finite termination. For a linear program, vertices joined by an edge may be regarded as neighbors, and simplex pivots may accordingly be viewed as local-search moves between adjacent basic feasible solutions, subject to the usual qualifications caused by degeneracy. When the simplex method terminates with its optimality condition, its solution is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local search starts from a feasible point and repeatedly moves to a neighboring feasible point having a strictly smaller objective value. If the absence of an improving neighbor is established, the current point is at least as good as every neighbor and is locally optimal for the chosen neighborhood. It need not be globally optimal, and the procedure is not guaranteed to terminate without additional assumptions. In linear programming, edge-adjacent vertices provide a neighborhood interpretation of simplex pivots, with degeneracy requiring care; a simplex solution satisfying its termination optimality condition is globally optimal.
assumptions_latex: \text{Stopping requires establishing that no }y\in N(x)\text{ satisfies }c(y)<c(x).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\nexists y\in N(x):c(y)<c(x)\bigr)\implies \bigl(\forall y\in N(x),\ c(x)\le c(y)\bigr),\qquad x\not\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in F}c(z).

assumptions_latex: The current solution is a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\) in a complete graph \(G=(V,E)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A k-opt neighbor is obtained by deleting k tour edges and reconnecting the resulting paths into a different Hamiltonian cycle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard traveling-salesperson exact \(k\)-opt neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact \(k\)-opt neighborhood of \(H\) is \[N_k(H)=\{H'\subseteq E:H'\text{ is a Hamiltonian cycle},\ |H\setminus H'|=|H'\setminus H|=k\}.\] Equivalently, choose \(D\subseteq H\) with \(|D|=k\), delete \(D\), and insert \(I\subseteq E\setminus H\) with \(|I|=k\) so that \((H\setminus D)\cup I\) is a Hamiltonian cycle distinct from \(H\). For a minimization objective, \(H\) is exact-\(k\)-opt locally optimal when no member of \(N_k(H)\) has smaller cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-opt tour move removes exactly k tour edges and inserts exactly k other edges so the result is again a Hamiltonian cycle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion laws for the shard's bounded set-exchange conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\in\mathcal F\), if \(p\leq p'\) and \(q\leq q'\), then \(N_{p,q}(S)\subseteq N_{p',q'}(S)\). assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a finite feasible set and \(N:S\to 2^S\) is a neighborhood map.
Instances are indexed by an input-size parameter \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\) is polynomial-size if \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\), exponential-size if \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|=2^{\Omega(n)}\) along an infinite instance family, and implicitly searchable if an improving neighbor can be found or its absence certified in polynomial time without enumerating \(N(x)\).

notation.meaning: neighbors reachable by one allowed local move

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies neighborhoods by cardinality and by the complexity of implicit improvement search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of finite minimization instances with feasible sets \(S\), neighborhood maps \(N:S\to 2^S\), and encoded size \(n\), a neighborhood is polynomial-size when \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\). It is exponential-size when \(\max_{x\in S}|N(x)|=2^{\Omega(n)}\) on an infinite subfamily. Independently of cardinality, it is implicitly searchable when a polynomial-time procedure, given \(x\), either returns \(y\in N(x)\) satisfying \(f(y)<f(x)\) or certifies that no such \(y\) exists. Thus a neighborhood may be exponentially large yet algorithmically searchable without explicit enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neighborhood regimes distinguish polynomial or exponential cardinality from polynomial-time implicit search for an improving move.

knowledge_statements.title: Improvement-Path Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the directed graph induced by strict objective improvement and distinguishes arbitrary paths from maximal trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the directed improvement graph \(G_f=(S,A_f)\) by \(A_f=\{(x,y):y\in N(x),\ f(y)<f(x)\}\). A strict improvement trajectory \((x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_T)\) is a directed path in \(G_f\). Along it, \(f(x_0)>f(x_1)>\cdots>f(x_T)\), so no vertex repeats. Consequently, every strict improvement trajectory in the finite set \(S\) is simple and has at most \(|S|-1\) arcs. If the trajectory is maximal, meaning that it continues whenever an outgoing improvement arc exists, then its terminal vertex is a sink of \(G_f\) and hence an \(N\)-local optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict improvement trajectories are simple directed paths of at most one fewer arc than there are feasible states; a maximal such trajectory terminates at a sink representing a local optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) is minimized, and \(N:S\to 2^S\) is a neighborhood map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every strict improvement trajectory is simple and has at most \(|S|-1\) arcs; every maximal strict improvement trajectory terminates at a sink of \(G_f\), which is an \(N\)-local optimum.

A deterministic tie-breaking order is fixed whenever the selected criterion has multiple minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule produces \(x_{t+1}=r(x_t)\in I(x_t)\) while improvement is possible and stops exactly when \(I(x_t)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic first-improvement and best-improvement rules for finite minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x_0\in S\), at iteration \(t\) form or search \(I(x_t)=\{y\in N(x_t):f(y)<f(x_t)\}\). If \(I(x_t)=\varnothing\), stop and output \(x_t\). A first-improvement rule scans neighbors in the fixed order and chooses the first member of \(I(x_t)\). A best-improvement rule chooses \(r(x_t)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in I(x_t)}f(y)\), resolving ties by the fixed order. Set \(x_{t+1}=r(x_t)\) and repeat. Either rule induces a unique strict improvement trajectory once its scan and tie-breaking orders are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivot rule repeatedly selects an improving neighbor by a fixed criterion and stops when no improving neighbor exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivot-Rule Selection

Since strict improvement prevents repeated states, \(T_r(x_0)\le |S|-1\). children.title: Stalled-Path Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which admissible moves cease to yield useful progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Stalled-Path Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes termination boundaries for strict-improvement local search and separates them from plateau behavior under nonworsening rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state \(x\in S\) lies on a stalled-path boundary for strict-improvement local search exactly when \(I(x)=\{y\in N(x):f(y)<f(x)\}=\varnothing\). Equivalently, \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\), so \(x\) is a sink of the strict improvement graph. Equal-value neighbors in \(B(x)=\{y\in N(x):f(y)=f(x)\}\) do not prevent stalling under a strict pivot rule. If nonworsening moves are admitted, the rule may traverse or cycle on a plateau, and its termination behavior additionally depends on its pivot, memory, and revisit policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict local search stalls exactly where no neighbor improves the objective; when equal-value moves are allowed, termination also depends on how plateau moves and revisits are handled.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite, \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\) is minimized, and \(N:S\to 2^S\) is a neighborhood map.
The primary boundary condition concerns rules permitting only strict improving moves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strict-improvement trajectory stalls at \(x\) exactly when \(I(x)=\varnothing\), equivalently when \(f(x)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in N(x)\); this equivalence alone does not characterize termination for rules admitting equal-value moves.

children.title: Local-Optimum Traps
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood structures admitting locally optimal solutions of poor global quality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) is an \(N\)-local optimum but not a global optimum, so strict local search initialized at \(a\) cannot reach the globally optimal state \(c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal finite example separating local from global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimization on \(S=\{a,b,c\}\) with \(N(a)=\{b\}\), \(N(b)=\{a\}\), \(N(c)=\{b\}\), and objective values \(f(a)=1\), \(f(b)=2\), \(f(c)=0\). At \(a\), the only neighbor is worse, so \(f(a)<f(b)\) and \(a\) is an \(N\)-local optimum. Nevertheless, \(c\) is the unique global optimum because \(f(c)<f(a)\). A strict-improvement search initialized at \(a\) therefore stops immediately and cannot reach \(c\), demonstrating a local-optimum trap created by the chosen neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-state instance has a nonglobal local optimum whose only neighbor is worse, trapping strict local search.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Optimum Traps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit three-state counterexample is valid and fits Local-Optimum Traps, but the record contains no cited evidence or marked standard-field rationale.

children.title: Search-State Cycling
children.top_down_role: Repeated-state behavior within local improvement processes.

assumptions_latex: The pivot rule permits equal-value moves and alternates to the available neighbor without memory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated trajectory \(a,b,a,b,\ldots\) cycles indefinitely; strict improvement or a no-revisit mechanism excludes this cycle.

notation.meaning: objective function constant on the two-state plateau

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycling caused by memoryless acceptance of nonworsening plateau moves.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{a,b\}\), let \(N(a)=\{b\}\) and \(N(b)=\{a\}\), and set \(f(a)=f(b)=0\). A memoryless rule that accepts nonworsening moves and selects the sole neighbor generates \(a,b,a,b,\ldots\), so it never terminates despite the finite state space. The failure arises because objective monotonicity is non-strict and therefore does not exclude repeated states. Requiring \(f(x_{t+1})<f(x_t)\), forbidding revisits, or imposing a terminating tie-breaking potential eliminates this particular cycling mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing equal-value moves without memory can cycle forever even on two states; strict descent or revisit prevention restores termination.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-State Cycling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the neighborhood sampling and temperature-dependent acceptance rule; global convergence is only asserted under suitable conditions not specified by the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At state \(x\), sample \(\bar x\in N(x)\) using probabilities that are positive for every member of \(N(x)\). If \(f(\bar x)<f(x)\), accept \(\bar x\). Otherwise accept it with probability \(\exp(-(f(\bar x)-f(x))/T)\), where \(T>0\), and reject it with the complementary probability. Larger \(T\) increases acceptance of worse solutions, while smaller \(T\) decreases it; in practice \(T\) is commonly reduced gradually. Under suitable additional conditions, randomized selection provides eventual escape from local minima and convergence to a global minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulated annealing samples every neighbor with positive probability, always accepts strict improvements, and accepts a nonimproving candidate with probability exp(-(cost increase)/T). Higher temperature makes worse moves more likely; temperature is typically reduced gradually. Global-minimum convergence requires additional suitable conditions not specified here.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(\operatorname{accept}\bar x\mid x)=\begin{cases}1,&f(\bar x)<f(x),\\ \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{f(\bar x)-f(x)}{T}\right),&f(\bar x)\ge f(x).\end{cases}

children.title: Exponential Improvement Paths
children.top_down_role: Instances whose improving trajectories may require exponentially many moves.

assumptions_latex: For each \(n\ge 1\), let \((g_0,\ldots,g_{2^n-1})\) be a binary reflected Gray-code ordering of \(\{0,1\}^n\).
Set \(N(g_i)=\{g_{i-1},g_{i+1}\}\) at interior indices, with the nonexistent endpoint neighbor omitted, and minimize \(f(g_i)=2^n-1-i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: From \(g_0\), every strict-improvement rule follows \(g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{2^n-1}\) and performs exactly \(2^n-1\) improving pivots.

notation.meaning: the state at Gray-code position i
path neighborhood along the Gray-code ordering

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit encoded family with a unique exponential-length improving path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), enumerate \(S_n=\{0,1\}^n\) as a binary reflected Gray code \((g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{2^n-1})\). Give each interior \(g_i\) the path neighborhood \(N(g_i)=\{g_{i-1},g_{i+1}\}\), with the missing neighbor omitted at each endpoint, and define \(f(g_i)=2^n-1-i\). From every \(g_i\) with \(i<2^n-1\), the unique improving neighbor is \(g_{i+1}\). Hence local search started at \(g_0\) makes exactly \(2^n-1\) improving pivots before reaching \(g_{2^n-1}\), although each state and move has an \(n\)-bit description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gray-code path on n-bit states forces every improving rule to take exactly exponentially many pivots.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Improvement Paths

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gray-code construction does yield a unique exponential-length improving path, but no source supports the construction or its encoded-state and move representation claim.

children.title: Trap-Escape Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where broader moves or selection changes overcome local obstructions.

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is locally optimal for a base neighborhood \(N_1\), and \(N_1(x)\subseteq N_2(x)\).
The objective \(f\) is minimized over a finite feasible set \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An enlarged-neighborhood escape exists exactly when \(\min_{y\in N_2(x)\setminus N_1(x)}f(y)<f(x)\); a perturbation escape exists exactly when some admissible \(z\) reaches a state whose strict improvement trajectory leaves the trap basin.

notation.meaning: states whose strict improvement trajectories terminate at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates neighborhood enlargement from perturbation-based escape conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be \(N_1\)-locally optimal and let \(N_1(x)\subseteq N_2(x)\). Direct escape by neighborhood enlargement is possible exactly when there exists \(y\in N_2(x)\setminus N_1(x)\) with \(f(y)<f(x)\). For a fixed strict pivot rule, define the basin \(\mathcal{B}(x)\) as the states whose induced trajectories terminate at \(x\). A perturbation mechanism escapes the trap exactly when it can produce an admissible state \(z\notin\mathcal{B}(x)\). Enlarging the neighborhood may preserve monotone descent; perturbation escape may require an intermediate worsening or equal-value move.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trap is escaped either by adding a newly improving move or by perturbing to a state outside the trapped local optimum's basin.
knowledge_statements.title: Trap-Escape Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The enlargement and fixed-rule basin conditions are coherent, but the terminology and claimed escape-regime correspondence lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Linear Relaxation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Continuous objective bounds supplied by linear relaxations.

assumptions_latex: Both minima are finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For minimization, \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\min_{x\in X}c^\top x\); equality holds whenever an LP optimum belongs to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bounds for finite binary minimization through feasible-set relaxation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\) be the feasible set of a minimization problem and let \(P\subseteq[0,1]^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral relaxation with \(X\subseteq P\). For \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}=\min_{x\in X}c^\top x\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\). Feasible-set inclusion gives \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}\), so the LP value is a valid lower bound. If an optimal LP solution lies in \(X\), then \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=z_{\mathrm{IP}}\) and that solution is integer-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing over a superset of integer solutions yields an LP lower bound, exact whenever an LP optimum is integer feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Relaxation Bounds
